This study also enhances our understanding of lead tolerance, elimination mechanisms, and sublethal effects in snakes.
3056: An annotated checklist of new and recent records of fish from the Mariana Islands published recently is further described. This checklist adds significantly to the known biodiversity of fishes from the archipelago. The checklist expands our use of the terms reef fishes, inshore fishes or shore fishes to include the mesophotic and rariphotic zones (and those that are found at shallower depths at higher latitudes), and below. The vast majority of these records are based only on photographs. Some of these photographs have been posted online, with or without comment on their significance, on the website www.guamreeflife.com. Others were posted by the U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s (NOAA) Ocean Exploration program.  Still others have not been reported until the publication of the checklist. The checklist included at least 117 additional species that have recently been discovered in the Mariana Islands that occur or are likely to occur at depths of approximately 500 m or less. Further, we provided photographs and other data, or otherwise validated species recorded from offshore banks, seamounts, and deep slope habitats of the archipelago.
3057: The Eastern Red-backed Salamander (Plethodon cinereus) is the most common and widespread salamander across eastern North American forests. It is well-known for its color polymorphism, which primarily manifests as two common morphs: striped and unstriped. A third, less frequently observed erythristic morph is typically entirely orange, often featuring varying degrees of black mottling. In addition to these morphs, several rare color variants are known to occur including a leucistic form characterized by partial or complete loss of skin pigmentation. We leveraged more than 80,000 images of P. cinereus downloaded from the popular community science platform iNaturalist to document color variation across the species’ range. This large crowdsourced dataset substantially expands upon limited published records of these rarer color variants and sheds new light on their spatial prevalence across the species’ range. Overall, this work provides a valuable foundation for further ecological and evolutionary research on this highly polymorphic salamander.
3058: Killdeer Plains Wildlife Area, located within Wyandot and Marion County, is a large area of preserved prairie habitat. Prior to the construction of wetlands on the property, American bullfrogs (Lithobates catesbeianus) did not occur within Killdeer Plains. The recent addition of wildlife ponds and reservoirs has attracted a large number of bullfrogs to the area. The stomach contents of 111 American bullfrogs collected from Killdeer Plains Wildlife Area, were identified and quantified based on the sex and size of the frog. Members of 14 different major taxa (orders and phyla) were found in the stomachs. Of these orders, the most frequently observed prey were beetles, followed by crayfish and other frogs. When separated by sex and size, clear dietary differences could be seen. Chi-squared tests were performed for each variable to determine statistical significance. Both tests gave a significant p-value. Male and female frogs were largely similar, though females showed a preference for vertebrate prey. The most drastic comparison came from the size groups. The smallest frogs ate substantial amounts of insects, while larger frogs ate larger prey such as crayfish and vertebrates. The research findings support the hypothesis that both sex and size play a role in the diets of bullfrogs.
3059: Africa is a major hotspot for freshwater fish biodiversity, yet large areas remain understudied. This study presents ongoing research aimed at reassessing species descriptions and revising species delimitation for Labeo found in Central Africa in Gabon. Labeo is a genus of cypriniforms found in Sub Saharan Africa and Southeast Asia. Attempts to sort Gabonese Labeo into species using available morphological keys have yielded results that conflict substantially with clusters revealed with preliminary DNA barcoding. Specifically, morphological keys suggest the presence of six morphotypes, while COI barcodes indicate three probable species-level lineages in the areas sampled. These results indicate the need to determine if these three lineages align with known species or warrant new descriptions. Using specimens collected during surveys in the Ogooué and two other rivers found within Gabon, this study will use traditional meristics and geometric morphometrics to analyze variation within and among these three genetic lineages of Labeo. The conjunction of morphological data with DNA barcoding will identify traits that distinguish each species, if they exist. Once species groups have been identified, each species will be formally described or redescribed. The main goal of this project is to successfully identify morphological characteristics that could be used to make a dichotomous key that could correctly identify all Labeo in Gabon and adjacent countries within each river’s reach, down to the species level. The insights gained from this project could lead to a reassessment of species abundance and distribution in the Ogooué and adjacent rivers.
3060: The hexaploid African barb genus Labeobarbus exhibits striking polymorphisms in jaw and lip morphology (e.g., “rubberlips” and "chisel-mouths") that make it a good system for studying morphological evolution and hybridization. However, persistent taxonomic challenges have impeded such evolutionary studies. Species descriptions have often conflated within-species variation with species-level diagnoses, and genetic data have revealed that morphotypes frequently occur in sympatry and do not align cleanly with COI phylogenies. This pattern suggests that hybridization, convergence, or plasticity may obscure true species limits, reinforcing the need for integrative analyses. To explore this further, we are conducting traditional geometric morphometric analyses of external traits and high-resolution micro-CT scans of representative Labeobarbus skulls from Gabon, a freshwater biodiversity hotspot where focal morphotypes co-occur, to assess variation in biomechanically relevant structures. Feature 3D reconstructions will illustrate how jaw shape varies among morphs, as well as among and within lineages. Preliminary results show that current diagnostic morphologies appear scattered, with no clear lineage-level patterns across five lineages, though lip morphology tends to form neat, lineage-specific clusters. These findings suggest that morphology alone might not be sufficient for delimiting species with Labeobarbus. By identifying key axes of cranial and jaw variation at this stage, we refine our analysis framework for downstream genomic and biomechanical studies. This work helps clarify the extent and sources of morphological diversity in Labeobarbus, improving our ability to test evolutionary hypotheses and build a more accurate taxonomic foundation for this complex and understudied group.
3061: Biofluorescence is a recent discovery in amphibians, with functional significance seldom established. Adults of Plethodon cinereus have sexually dimorphic green biofluorescent serous glands on the ventral portion of their tails, with males possessing more and larger glands than females. In addition, a seasonal peak in the number of fluorescent glands has been observed in males during the fall breeding season. It has been hypothesized that green biofluorescence acts as a visual signal during courtship and may be a target of sexual selection. However, color vision has not been previously tested in Plethodon, and it is unclear if salamanders can perceive this green signal. To evaluate color discernment in P. cinereus, salamanders were placed singly in test chambers for 6 hours with 30 Drosophila hydei. Each salamander was tested twice under these conditions. The flies were fed a dyed sucrose solution such that half were dyed brown and the remainder were dyed green. We hypothesized that if P. cinereus can see green, then there would be a difference in the number of brown and green flies eaten. We found that significantly more green flies were eaten than brown flies across both trials, suggesting that P. cinereus can discern green from brown. Interestingly, while no difference was found in brown flies eaten between sexes, females consumed significantly greater numbers of green flies than males, suggesting that females may be more predisposed to responding to this color.
3062: Lizards are major predators of arthropods, including chemically defended species such as spiders. We previously found two lizard species (Elgaria multicarinata, Sceloporus occidentalis) possess different degrees of resistance to black widow spider venom (BWSV). Because these lizards are not closely related, resistance might represent independent adaptations to local prey, or be a deeply rooted trait of lizards. To determine whether BWSV resistance is a derived or ancestral trait of lizards, we assessed BWSV resistance at organismal and tissue levels in three additional lizard species (Coleonyx variegatus, Takydromus sexlineatus, Iguana iguana) representing a broad phylogenetic, geographic, and ecological scope. We mapped results onto the lizard phylogeny and used a mammalian outgroup for comparison. To determine whether lizards might possess broad-spectrum resistance against many toxins, we also quantified resistance to Arizona bark scorpion venom (ABSV) in E. multicarinata and S occidentalis. Sprint trials revealed that insectivorous species (C. variegatus, T. sexlineatus) were not significantly affected by BWSV, while the herbivorous species (I. iguana) exhibited severely reduced performance. Histological analysis showed minimal to moderate muscle damage in insectivorous species, but extensive damage in I. iguana. In comparison, sprint trials with E. multicarinata and S occidentalis showed these lizards are highly susceptible to ABSV. As such, lizards are not broadly resistant to diverse toxins, but do possess a baseline level of resistance to BWSV compared to mammals, with resistance elevated in some lineages and lost in others. Thus, ecological interactions with widow spiders appear to have driven patterns of venom resistance across the lizard phylogeny.
3063: Natural selection can influence body shape within species in response to changing environmental conditions. If the strength of selection is strong enough between different regions, then a community response in body shape change may occur. Among coral and rocky reef habitats, one abundant, and varied, group of fishes are crypto benthic reef fishes (CRFs). Species comprising this group are generally <50mm in length and can comprise nearly 50% of biomass consumed on a reef, making them an essential component of reef ecosystems. However, functional morphological variation across CRF communities has not been studied in a biogeographical framework. The Tropical Eastern Pacific (TEP) is a biogeographic region separated from the Western Pacific by a semipermeable open ocean barrier, and from the Caribbean by the impermeable Isthmus of Panama, making it an ideal isolated marine region to examine functional turnover and morphological variation in CRF communities. Within this region there are more than 300 CRF species distributed amongst 12 families. In this study we examine how body shape varies in a CRF community context across the TEP using geometric morphometrics of museum specimens. Comparisons between biogeographic provinces and amongst families largely show CRF families across different biogeographic regions occupy similar regions of morphospace, as expected given their close geographic and phylogenetic proximities. However, we find significant differences in body shape disparity in certain families from different regions, suggesting selection on certain morphotypes. We discuss these findings in relationship to shared geological and evolutionary history of these species, as well as their ecology.
3064: Traditionally, species identification has required expertise in aspects of morphology that can be used to differentiate among species within a given taxon. DNA-based identification is much easier for many researchers because it does not require specialized training in morphology and can be used to evaluate inter and intraspecific diversity, including detecting cryptic species. Increasingly, techniques which do not require collection of live specimens (i.e., environmental DNA; eDNA) are also being used to understand species diversity and distribution. However, these studies require a well curated database in which DNA sequences originate from individuals that were properly identified to the species level, and preferably vouchered in a natural history collection. To this end, we have begun to assemble a resource, TX-FISH-DNA, which links whole mitochondrial genome sequences with expert identified and vouchered specimens. Currently, we have collected one or more voucher specimens from more than 300 fish species from Texas waters and assembled one or more mitochondrial genomes for more than 60 of those species. Upon completion, this data will comprise paired DNA and vouchers for over 90 percent of the ichthyofauna of Texas marine and freshwaters, providing a centralized repository for conservationist, ecologists and other researchers to support their investigations of the natural world.
3065: Larvae of spring-breeding amphibians at higher latitudes may experience sizeable diel fluctuations in temperature that may affect growth and development. As both growth and development rates may respond nonlinearly to changes in temperature, fluctuating temperature may result in differences in these rates compared to constant exposure to simple arithmetic mean temperature. Herein, we compared growth and development in Wood Frog (Lithobates sylvaticus) tadpoles exposed to diel sinusoidally cycling temperatures (10.0 to 20.0 °C) with those at a constant temperature arithmetic mean temperature of 15.0 °C. In addition, a third group of tadpoles were reared at a constant temperature equal to a derived “constant temperature equivalent” (CTE) for the fluctuating temperature regime (17.2 °C). Tadpoles were sampled at Weeks 1, 2, 4, 6, and 12 post-hatching and preserved, and Gosner developmental stage, preserved body mass, body length, and tail lengths were recorded. Tadpoles reared under fluctuating temperatures or at the CTE were generally more developed and had greater preserved body masses at a given sampling interval than were those maintained at a constant 15 °C, although neither body length nor tail length differed significantly among the three groups. These findings suggest that exposure to fluctuating temperatures accelerates growth and development compared to exposure to a constant arithmetic mean temperature. Moreover, the findings suggest that use of a derived “constant temperature equivalent” can be successfully applied to modeling thermal effects on growth and development in organisms that normally experience fluctuating temperatures.
3066: Since its increased production in the 1950s, plastic pollution has become widespread in the environment. Time, combined with exposure to the elements, repeatedly breaks plastics into smaller pieces, ultimately becoming microplastics. These microplastics are readily available for consumption by a multitude of animals at various trophic levels, including fishes. Currently there is little information regarding the prevalence of microplastics in Southern California fishes across time, limiting our understanding of how microplastics may be impacting coastal food webs in the region. To address this, we examined microplastics within the gastrointestinal (GI) tracts of four Southern California species from the 1940s to the present: Stenobrachius leucopsarus (Northern Lampfish), Chauliodus macouni (Pacific Viperfish), Cymatogaster aggregata (Shiner Perch), and Girella nigricans (Opaleye). The GI tracts of these preserved specimens provide an excellent view into microplastic pollution across time, as they give insight into the environmental conditions of a specific location at a particular moment in time. Through dissection and KOH digestion, gut contents were extracted and processed onto glass filters, and Raman spectroscopy was used for the identification of plastic types present. Here we discuss trends in the data that allow for the establishment of a historical timeline of microplastics in marine fishes of Southern California.
3067: In mammals, melatonin produced by the pineal gland signals the dark phase of the circadian cycle and inhibits the migration of circulating leukocytes to tissues under normal conditions. Following an infectious stimulus, this production is blocked, allowing the migration of circulating leukocytes to inflammatory sites. After the pro-inflammatory phase, macrophages at the inflammatory site produce melatonin locally, enhancing phagocytosis and helping the inflammatory resolution. This shift between central (pineal) and local (immune cell) melatonin production defines the immune-pineal axis that is known only in mammals. In amphibians (Rhinella diptycha, R. icterica, and Lithobates catesbeianus), our previous results described a similar decrease in central melatonin (pineal and retina) and its increase in immune tissues during an infectious stimulus, suggesting local production of melatonin by leukocytes, indicating the possible existence of an immune-pineal-ocular axis in this group. Our objective was to confirm the presence of this axis and melatonin production by immune cells in amphibians, as in mammals. Our results demonstrated that genes of enzymes of the melatonin synthesis pathway are downregulated in the retina following an infectious stimulus, reinforcing the participation of the retina during the inflammatory response in amphibians. We are currently determining the melatonin production by peritoneal and blood leukocytes of toads (R. diptycha) and its role in the phagocytosis activity of these same cells (autocrine and paracrine function). These results are fundamental for the unprecedented description of the immune-pineal-ocular axis in amphibians and expand the understanding of the evolutionary conservation of the melatonin role as an immunomodulatory hormone.
3068: Global climate change has driven shifts in marine fish distributions, including the northward expansion of the Common Snook (Centropomus undecimalis), a popular subtropical gamefish historically restricted to southern Florida and throughout the Caribbean. Since the early 2000s, snook have been documented approximately 135 miles north of their historical range boundary, with a confirmed resident breeding population near Cedar Key, Florida. Due to the relative recency of expansion and the small size of the snook’s northern population, this represents a novel opportunity to observe fine-scale characteristics of the species’ spawning behavior and the degree of reciprocal transfer between spawning and juvenile individuals. This ongoing study aims to identify key spawning locations relative to nursery habitats, analyze the spatiotemporal dynamics of young-of-year (YOY) aggregations, and estimate the effective population size of northern Gulf of Mexico (GOM) snook through close-kin genetic analysis. Field surveys are conducted across coastal ponds, tidal creeks, and estuaries between the Suwannee and Waccasassa River drainages. Using a standardized seining approach, YOY snook (<200 mm SL) are collected, measured, and fin-clipped for genetic analysis. Habitat characteristics, including vegetation type, substrate, and water quality parameters are also documented to improve understanding of juvenile habitat selection. This study intends to lay the groundwork for a long-term monitoring project to provide insights into the sustainability of this expanding population, informing fisheries management and habitat conservation efforts. Given the snook's economic and ecological importance, identifying critical nursery areas could shape long-term conservation strategies in the region.
3069: Amphibians can serve as sentinel species in the assessment of environmental quality, especially in relation to freshwater ecosystems. Agricultural activity has great potential for impacting aquatic habitats. Not only is water diverted for irrigation but runoff can introduce particulate and chemical contaminants into amphibian breeding habitats. In the agriculturally-productive central valley of California, milder winters and extended growing seasons associated with climate change may shift agricultural influences to greater overlap with the amphibian breeding season, with the potential for multiple applications of both fertilizers and pesticides to occur while egg masses and tadpoles occupy neighboring aquatic habitats. This laboratory study examined the effects of chronic exposure to a commercially-available pyrethroid pesticide, lambda-cyhalothrin, on the development of Pseudacris regilla tadpoles, as indicated by morphological measures and histological examination of the liver. Tadpoles exposed to lambda-cyhalothrin were significantly larger by Gosner stage 41 in all metrics, compared to control tadpoles; there were no notable differences in liver morphology. An examination of the mechanisms that underlie these results is recommended. As the phenologies of both natural and anthropogenic activities shift with climate change, reexamination of  the impacts of pesticides in regular use should be the subject of new studies, to assess the effects of changing practices involving chemical agents approved decades ago under different environmental regimes.
3070: Ponyfishes are a group of approximately 51 shallow marine and brackish-water species that produce light using a circumesophageal bioluminescent organ that houses bacteria in the genus Photobacterium. All species use bioluminescence transmitted through a guanine rich swimbladder with ventral transparency for ventral counter illumination, but others also emit light dorsally or laterally through transparent “windows” and multiple species have been observed to flash, with rapid illumination and then darkening. Our histological study of the light organ in this group revealed possible mechanisms or this rapid change in visible bioluminescence. For example in the genus Photopectoralis dorsal and lateral muscles are likelu able to pull guanine-containing connective tissues over “windows” in the bioluminescent organ that transmit light to the swimbladder and transparent lateral tissues. The structure in additional genera also will be described.
3071: Morphological and behavioral lateralization is an adaptation seen across species in the vertebrate world. Initial research focused on mammals and birds, finding that many species showed preferential limb use at the individual and sometimes population level. Functional lateralization had then been believed to be an adaptation related to object manipulation and arboreality produced through convergent evolution. Recent work on fish predator escape, amphibian pawedness, and reptile aggressive responses, however, provides evidence for an earlier origin of brain lateralization in vertebrates. As an earlier lineage existing on an arboreal spectrum, chameleons offer an intriguing study group at the intersection of ecology and phylogeny to further research into the origins of functional brain lateralization. This study set out to provide some of the first data on chameleon lateralization by looking for biases in their righting response. To do so, individuals of Chamaeleo calyptratus, Bradypodion damaranum, and Calumma malthe were suspended on a horizontal dowel by their tail to observe their righting response with specific attention to righting direction and limb. While some individuals (3 of 7 C. calyptratus, 1 of 5 B. damaranum, and 1 of 10 C. malthe) showed a significant righting direction bias, no species level pattern could be discerned for either righting direction or the first limb to grasp the substrate, reflecting work in other non-primates. Such results likely suggest limited selective advantage for functional lateralization based purely on arboreality and will provide the framework for further research on potential origins of lateralization in early lineages.
3072: Population dynamics of fish communities depend on predator-prey distribution, environmental factors such as tidal cycle, and anthropogenic activity. This study utilizes underwater camera systems as an effective tool to passively monitor fish assemblages and track forager activity across time and habitats. For this project, I quantified the diversity of demersal fish communities across the seascape of Harrington Sound, Bermuda, by analyzing continuous photo surveillance collected over 11 days in 2024 at two sites characterized by a variety of habitats: Gibbets Island (inlet) and Green Bay (inshore sound). Species presence, abundance, and foraging behavior were recorded relative to fish communities at each site, focusing on mesopredators. Preliminary results suggest variable mesopredator presence across sites, with Green Bay having the greatest abundance of mesopredators compared to Gibbets Island. These observations demonstrate the importance of benthic, sandy-bottom ecosystems as a hotspot for mesopredatory fishes.
3073: Pelvic fins in fishes have been repeatedly modified into specialized organs used to generate suction and adhere to the benthos.  Well known examples of this have evolved independently in clingfishes, lumpsuckers, snailfishes, loaches, and gobies.  Within gobies (Gobiidae), fusion of pelvic fins typically results in simple circular pelvic disk made up solely of lepidotrichia, and simple membranous anterior pelvic frenum connecting pelvic spines, and an inter-radial membrane uniting the lepidotrichia and forming the posterior of the round disk. This simple pelvic disk stands in stark contrast to the specialized pelvic morphologies in clingfishes, snailfishes and lumpsuckers, which possess highly modified papillae and fleshly pad-like structures to help create adhesion. While performing morphological analyses on coral-dwelling goby Paragobiodon lacunicula, we observed an unusual pelvic-fin morphology that has never been reported for this genus, nor in any goby. A combination of light microscopy, SEM and histology were used to examine these structures in 32 specimens of P. lacunicola, from the Burke Museum of Natural History and Culture and the Bishop Museum. We found that P. lacunicula possesses a complex arrangement of elongate, pedestal-shaped fleshy papillae in the central section of the pelvic fin disc, which were unassociated with lepidotrichia.  Similarly, there are numerous smaller fleshy papillae-like structures covering the distal margin of the pelvic disc, which seem to originate from the tips of highly branched pelvic rays. Collectively, these fleshy papillae form a suction apparatus that is analogous to those seen in clingfish, lumpsuckers and snailfishes, representing a striking example of convergent evolution. We provide a description of this structure and compare it to other obligate coral-associated gobies and discuss potential functional significance of this organ.
3074: The zeiform family Parazenidae traditionally includes three genera: Parazen, Cyttopsis and Stethopristes. Morphological support for this familial relationship has been based on a single character (one anal-fin spine). Subsequent molecular analyses, however, challenged this relationship and suggested that Parazenidae are not monophyletic, strongly supporting a sister-group relationship between Cyttopsis and Stethopristes, but only weakly recovering Parazen as sister to either those two genera or to Zenion.  Morphometric analyses based on overall body shape and jaw shape further suggested that the shallower body shape, larger eye placed more laterally, and shorter jaws of Parazen evolved divergently from comparable traits of Cyttopsis and Stethopristes, both of which resemble the primitive body shape of zeiforms. The number of species within Parazen has also come into question. Earlier preliminary analyses based on barcode data and body-shape morphometrics suggested that fish from the Caribbean differ from those in the Indian and Pacific oceans. This poster explores the monophyly of Parazenidae by reexamining proposed morphological characters and analyzing new phylogenomic data.  We also reexamine variation within Parazen via molecular, morphometric and meristic data and correlate these data with geographic distributions of known populations. Results from this study suggest that the family Parazenidae contains only the genus Parazen. Parazenidae are sister to a clade of “cyttopsids” consisting of Cyttopsis and Stethopristes. A new, expanded Sanger dataset and body shape morphometrics suggest that Parazen most likely consists of at least two species, with Caribbean and Atlantic populations differing from those in the Indian and Pacific oceans.
3075: Amphisbaenians are a group of specialized fossorial squamates that often lack limbs. Due to their subterranean nature, amphisbaenians are difficult to study, resulting in basic aspects of their ecology being poorly understood. Surprisingly, one of the least understood families is Rhineuridae, the only North American amphisbaenid, and is today represented by the Florida Worm-Lizard (Rhineura floridana). Heretofore, R. floridana has putatively been documented being predated upon by three species (Dasypus novemcinctus, Lampropeltis extenuata, Micrurus fulvius), however none of these occurrences are associated with physical museum specimens, making it difficult to verify these records. Currently, the largest collection of this species is at Florida Museum of Natural History, with most specimens having associated collection data (i.e., georeferences, date, gut contents). Here we aim to compound all cases of predation upon R. floridana by vertebrates and expand the list of predators to include Aves (Buteo lineatus), with all occurrences including an FLMNH collection number. We also demonstrate a correlation between the geographic range of R. floridana, Tantilla relicta (another fossorial squamate), and the predator, L. extenuata. Using MaxEnt niche modeling, there appears to be no climatic or geographic limitations for the range of L. extenuata, suggesting prey availability may play a role. Additionally, while little published behavioral data exists for this cryptic taxon, it is popularly believed that R. floridana often surfaces during rainfall. Utilizing collection dates and associated field notes, we were able to establish a relationship between the hurricane season and increased surface activity, supporting this tentative hypothesis.
3076: Established non-native species can be used as model systems for understanding both human-mediated dispersal and how taxa change (whether it be genetic or plastic) when introduced into novel environments. Understanding the processes behind patterns in dispersion, establishment, and expansion of introduced species can illuminate strategies to reduce the occurrence of introduction and mitigate its effects. Information on source population, dispersion paths, and number of introduction events can be gained by examining the evolutionary genetics of multiple introduced populations and populations from the native range. Aspidoscelis neomexicanus (the New Mexico whiptail) is native to the Rio Grande basin in New Mexico and Trans Pecos Texas. Introduced populations exist in northern Utah (Salt Lake and Utah counties) and northeastern Arizona (Navajo and Apache counties), and putative introductions have occurred in southern Utah (Washington county) and northwestern New Mexico (San Juan county). To understand the evolutionary history of these introduced populations, we captured individuals from nine sites (five non-native and four native) and used collected DNA sequence data to perform phylogenetic population and genetic analyses. We also tested whether populations cluster based on morphology, and whether patterns reflect their estimated evolutionary history.
3077: Cods, hakes, grenadiers, and their kin (order Gadiformes) comprise an ancient and biodiverse clade of predominantly-marine fishes. With more than 620 species in 17 families, these fishes exhibit remarkable morphological variability — some members possess dorsal antennae (Bregmaceros); bioluminescent organ systems (Steindachneria, many morids and macrourids); bulbous, inflated heads (Macrouroides, Squalogadus); or glassy bodies with ornate, streamer-like appendages (Eretmophorus). This diversity is mirrored in their ecology — major global fisheries are sustained by shallow-water oceanic species like cod, pollock, and haddock, while grenadiers, gargoylefishes, and whiptails represent some of the largest and most abundant deep ocean vertebrates. However, our systematic knowledge of this order is significantly lacking. Gadiformes diversified through an ancient adaptive radiation, a massive flurry of speciation in which countless major lineages diverged from one another across a short time frame. Such biological events are confounding to most methods of phylogenetic analysis, and previous studies of gadiform systematics have failed to approach topological consensus. The present study is the first to incorporate whole-genome sequences — including 49 complete gadiform genomes — into a comprehensive phylogeny of the order including all 17 families and almost 300 species. Our approach uses the phylogenomic software ROADIES to produce a high-confidence backbone of gadiform family-level relationships, and progressively expands on this backbone using 1,119 highly-conserved exons and 3 legacy markers. We use a novel time-calibrated gadiform phylogeny to estimate morphological and ecological shifts in the order, including multiple potential gains of bioluminescence and previously-undescribed transitions between shallow- and deepwater marine habitats.
3078: Sao Tome and Principe Islands in the Gulf of Guinea form a part of the Cameroon volcanic line. Due to their Cenozoic volcanic origins, they have not been connected by land to mainland West-Central Africa. Therefore, the herpetofauna originated via overwater dispersal events. Among squamates, the islands harbor two genera and five species of gecko, three genera and five species of skink, four genera and five species of Alethinophidian snake, and one genus and two species of Scolecophidian snake. We compiled new and published DNA sequence data of the squamates of Sao Tome and Principe to produce a calibrated molecular timescale of the colonization of the islands. Results illustrate variation in inferred stem ages among taxa, and corroborate expected Cenozoic dates of divergence from mainland relatives.
3079: The Florida Box Turtle (Terrapene carolina bauri) is an understudied taxa found throughout Peninsular Florida. Though basic chemistry and health indicators have been reported in wild Woodland Box Turtles (Terrapene carolina carolina) and Ornate Box Turtles (Terrapene ornata ornata), Florida Box Turtles have litter representation in terms of published blood parameters. Given the unique ecology of Florida Box Turtles, it is unknown if their basic physiology differs from congeners. We sought to report the basic blood health profiles of wild population Florida Box Turtles in Southwestern Florida, including White blood cell counts (WBC), packed cell volume (PCV), and total protein (TP). We collected blood samples from the subcarapacial sinus during opportunistic surveys as part of a long-term population study. Total WBC averaged 3418.2 cells/µL, PCV averaged 10.9%, and TP averaged 2.4g/dL. We compared parameters between sexes but did not see a significant difference in WBCs and PCVs between males and females. However, female TP was significantly higher than that of males. This could be resultant from the extended reproductive season of the species in peninsular Florida. We also compared our data to the ranges in other taxa within the Terrapene genus, and found our WBC, PCV, and TP were all lower than most other values reported. These data may be the first baseline values reported for Florida Box Turtles and may serve as key reference values for comparisons across the range of the species.
3080: Waves of Wonder, which was supported as part of the William & Mary (W&M) Provost’s Art & Science Exchange, fostered creative, interdisciplinary collaborations between W&M Arts & Science undergraduate students and graduate students at W&M’s Batten School of Coastal and Marine Sciences at the Virginia Institute of Marine Science. Through a student salon (i.e., a creative meetup), students learned from and became inspired by one another, and 10 pairings or small groups (including a total of 30 students) were established that worked together to create visual or performance art that communicates science. Each group was charged with creating a piece to be displayed or performed in a final exhibition. For this public exhibition, incubator participants shared their pieces during a gallery-style and performing art exhibition that put the art and science side-by-side so that both disciplines communicated the shared creative narrative. The Waves of Wonder project also provided art and science communication through a public seminar titled “The Art of Ichthyology” and professional development in the form of a visual capture demonstration and workshop. This project created cross-disciplinary connections between art and science, capitalizing on the creativity that is inherent in both, to create novel methods of science communication that open doors to new audiences. By using art to create accessible channels for science communication, we can share scientific stories and approach problems from fresh perspectives. Fostering collaborations between art and science enabling more imaginative expressions of scientific concepts that could resonate with previously unreached audiences.
3081: The Eastern Red-backed Salamander, Plethodon cinereus, offers a good model for the study of behavioral variation due to its large geographic range and the persistence of two color morphs, striped and unstriped, in most populations. Levels of aggressive and territorial behavior vary greatly across the salamander’s range, with more northern populations generally being less territorial. Behavioral and ecological differences have also been observed between different color morphs, and red-striped individuals show more signs of territoriality. We hypothesized that salamanders in a polymorphic mid-Michigan population would exhibit less territorial behavior than those in southern populations and that this behavior would differ between the two color morphs. We collected adult male salamanders of both color morphs from the field and tested them in laboratory conditions. We used a setup in which resident salamanders were given time to establish a territory, then intruder salamanders were introduced into the territory and all behaviors were recorded. We expect to find low levels of territorial behavior in Michigan salamanders, but with some differences between the two morphs. These differences in behavior based on geographic location and polymorphism may help to explain the processes of evolution and speciation in amphibians.
3082: The evolution of anuran life histories involves repeated transitions from aquatic to terrestrial reproduction, often accompanied by changes in developmental trajectories. In this study, we investigated the ontogeny of the nasal chemosensory organs in Arthroleptella villiersi, a terrestrial frog developing a non-feeding (endotrophic) tadpole, which shares life-history characteristics with aquatic indirect-developing species and direct-developing species (e.g. completely terrestrial reproduction). Using μCT-based 3D reconstructions and histological sections of different ontogenetic stages, we described the development of the olfactory and vomeronasal systems. Our data reveals that A. villiersi retains several tadpole-specific traits commonly associated with aquatic feeding. However, other aspects of its chemosensory system show similarities to patterns described in direct-developing anurans. To further assess developmental modularity and potential shifts in the developmental timing, we employed heterochrony plots comparing A. villiersi with aquatic indirect-developing anurans. The analysis uncovered differential timing among chemosensory traits between species, including both pre- and postdisplacement as well as variation in developmental rates for several structures. These findings suggest that while some features of the olfactory system may be developmentally constrained, others exhibit signs of modular organization and heterochronic shifts. This may allow optimized adaptation of specific traits without necessitating global changes to the system. Our findings provide new insights into how reproductive modes shape sensory development and highlight the need for broader comparative studies to test the role of modularity and heterochrony in anuran evolution.
3083: Zoological collections are an irreplaceable resource in biological research. With many universities divesting from zoological collections, the resulting loss is devastating to the scientific community. Orphaned collections offer a unique opportunity for established collections to expand their holdings, honor past work, and preserve historical records. In September 2023, the University of Michigan Museum of Zoology (UMMZ) acquired 60,000 Ophidia from Oregon State University (OSU) and Michigan State University (MSU). Absorbing a collection of this size has presented some challenges that we have had to adapt to and overcome. Our ethanol waste increased, we faced data loss, and we had to integrate an existing organizational scheme into ours. However, these specimens have improved the research and educational utility of our collection. So far, we have accessioned 18,900 specimens and have started using them in research. This collection includes a sizable amount of extended specimen data outside the physical vouchers, too.  We are CT scanning snakes, collecting diet items, organizing tissue samples, and field diet data. We have incorporated specimens without adequate data into our teaching collections to support classroom activities and have included several in public museum exhibits at the University of Michigan Museum of Natural History (UMMNH). Orphaned collections have a unique set of challenges, but the depth of information that they offer to our knowledge base and in educating the next generation of scientists is unmatched.
3084: With over 11,000 freshwater lakes and nearly 70,000 miles of rivers and streams, Minnesota’s natural resource managers face a monumental task in monitoring the health of our vast aquatic faunal communities. Every year, the Minnesota Department of Natural Resources and Pollution Control Agency collect fish samples from hundreds of sites across the state’s waterbodies to determine the Index of Biodiversity Integrity, a metric calculated using species counts to assess water quality and inform management strategies. Since 1997, University of Minnesota students have facilitated these assessments by validating identification of fish and stewarding sample vouchers held at the Bell Museum. This yearly effort, called the Fish ID Collective, provides data validation that would otherwise be impractical to undertake in the field. In 2023, the Fish ID Collective identified over 37,000 Minnesota fishes, producing a snapshot of fish diversity crucial to the work of fisheries managers. In addition to the immediate research benefits imparted to participating Minnesota agencies, the Fish ID Collective provides auxiliary benefits to the fish researchers at the University of Minnesota and fellow institutions. Survey samples from past years provide a stable flow of data-rich specimens for accession in the Bell Museum collections, and to build out teaching collections for fish-related clubs, agencies, and neighboring universities throughout Minnesota.  In the future, we plan to develop a formal structure for fulfilling requests for teaching specimens, expand our contracted partnerships with other management divisions, and continue seeking novel ways to maximize the value and utility of this incredible yearly effort.
3085: Social media groups that offer help identifying biodiversity are now fixtures of the internet and in many communities are the go-to for rapid, accurate identification of snakes. Although they lack the structured aspects of citizen science data platforms like iNaturalist, these groups are valuable sources of accurately-identified snake images, many of which are georeferenced, from which viral, duplicate, and other irrelevant images have been filtered out by diligent moderators. The largest such groups include hundreds of thousands of users and help to identify hundreds of snake photos per day. Because many social media platforms no longer support systematic access via an API, we gathered 12,630 images from 6,784 posts across four snake ID groups specific to regions of sub-Saharan Africa by hand over about one year. Just over 60% of observations have geographic information sufficiently precise to be plotted on a map. We present taxonomic, spatial and temporal patterns of snake ID requests, data on latency to correct ID and on human-snake interactions in Africa, and some new incidental observations on snake distribution and ecology. Limitations include that searches are non-reproducible and influenced by user language, location, and group access. These images will nourish a growing snake imagery dataset for training computer vision algorithms to identify snakes at the species level.
3086: Effective management of small, isolated populations requires accurate and precise estimates of vital rates to evaluate extinction risk and the factors contributing most to population viability. Population viability analysis (PVA) is a widely used tool for assessing extinction risk in captive and wild populations, but its reliability depends on high-quality, population-specific data. As such, PVAs should be used adaptively and updated as new information becomes available. The Eastern Massasauga (Sistrurus catenatus) rattlesnake, a species federally listed as threatened, persists in highly fragmented populations that may benefit from population-specific management strategies. A prior PVA of a population in Cass County, Michigan, projected an exceptionally low probability of extinction over 100 years. However, recent evidence of inbreeding, inbreeding depression, and reduced fitness via decreased survival and lifetime reproduction raises new concerns about its long-term viability. We will conduct an updated PVA incorporating this new information to reassess extinction risk over 50 and 100 years. We will perform a sensitivity analysis to identify key drivers of viability and hypothesize that extinction risk will increase relative to the PVA that did not incorporate these previously unknown genetic effects. Results will be used to inform ongoing Eastern Massasauga conservation efforts.
3087: Organisms with limited dispersal capabilities commonly fragment over space and time into a complex of forms exhibiting complex patterns of morphological distinctiveness and lineage independence. This poses a taxonomic and biogeographic challenge that is best solved by geographic sampling. Of particular interest are the contact zones where divergent lineages interact. One example of a difficult complex is the Plethodon wehrlei complex of woodland salamanders, which has recently been split into five separate species, but transition zones between species have never been characterized. This research aims to provide more complete geographic sampling to characterize geographic ranges, patterns of population structure, and points of secondary contact. For this study, we used ddRAD sequencing to obtain thousands of SNPs. Isolation by distance was tested in R, population admixture was inferred using the program Construct, and species trees were inferred using ASTRAL and TreeMix. The impacts of these results for species delimitation and the aims of future research will be discussed.
3088: Male Eurycea bislineata head shape varies seasonally. Jaw muscles hypertrophy during the mating season (specifically the M. levator mandibulae externus) causing their heads to become more diamond-shaped from dorsal view. Considering that the skeletal muscle system and skeletal system are inherently connected, we analyzed whether skeletal features of the jaw apparatus vary seasonally, as well. We compared overall cranial shape from a dorsal view (origin point of M. levator mandibulae externus), dentary shape from a lateral view (insertion point of M. levator mandibulae externus), otic crest number, and dentary tooth number/size between male E. bislineata captured in mating condition (October through April) to those captured in non-mating condition (May through September). Our preliminary results indicate that there is no correlation between skeletal shape/features to mating condition. We therefore examined if skeletal shape/features were correlated with age by counting lines of arrested growth from histological samples of the humerus from male individuals. At present, these results are being analyzed and we hope that we can provide some more conclusions in Saint Paul, MN at the historic Joint Meeting of Ichthyologists and Herpetologists.
3089: The coupling between sex determination and downstream sexual differentiation networks is crucial to generate functional sexual phenotypes. Developmental staging series for different squamate species show that lineages vary according to the synchronicity of gonadal and genital development. In some squamate species, females develop male-like genitalia (i.e., hemipenes) concomitantly with the presence of differentiated ovaries, and hemipenis regression, forming the hemiclitoris, occurs in late embryonic stages or even post-hatching/birth. Heterochronic changes in genital sexual differentiation have been hypothesized to be associated with the type of sex determination system in lizards. Specifically, temperature-dependent sex determination (TSD) systems should be associated with asynchronous development, while the evolution of canalized genetic sex determination systems (GSD) would be associated with a higher synchronicity of these two axes. According to this hypothesis, delayed hemipenis regression in females may be important for enabling plasticity of sexual development in TSD organisms. Geckos show a great diversity of sex determination systems and recently evolved sex chromosomes, providing key taxa to understand the evolution of developmental integration of different reproductive structures. All geckos evaluated to date seem to exhibit asynchronous genital development, with females developing and maintaining a bilobed hemipenis throughout embryogenesis. Nonetheless, there is no detailed description of genital development in geckos. This work will present preliminary data on the timing of sexual differentiation of reproductive structures in gecko species with different sex determination systems by describing external morphology of the genitalia and internal morphology of the gonad and genitalia using histological techniques.
3090: We investigated the habitat preferences and seasonal habitat use of three species of aquatic snakes in wetlands that differ in hydroperiod and prey availability, within a semi-urban environment on the Florida Gulf Coast University (FGCU) campus in southwest Florida. Over the course of four years, snakes, fishes, amphibians, and aquatic macroinvertebrates were captured using minnow traps set for five nights at a time (average 18 visits/wetland). Water depth was measured on a weekly to daily basis by a network of manual and automated groundwater wells. We present details of an inverse relationship between fish and amphibian captures: catch-per-unit-effort of amphibians declined the longer wetlands held water, whereas fish CPUE increased over the same time period. Among snakes, Nerodia and Liodytes did not show clear habitat preferences, whereas Farancia were captured exclusively in long-hydroperiod cypress-dominated wetlands with high salamander densities. Temporally, Farancia were captured in February and March when water levels were at annual lows. Captures of Nerodia peaked 4-8 weeks after wetlands had refilled, regardless of time of year. Liodytes showed no clear pattern, but terrestrial movements among wetlands seemed more prevalent as wetlands were drying, as evidenced by dead-on-road encounters. By assessing the ecological needs of under-studied aquatic snake species in relation to wetland conditions, the study provides valuable insights into how hydrology influences habitat selection in semi-urban wildlife. The findings of this research will contribute to the broader understanding of habitat preferences for generalist and specialist species in dynamic environments. Additionally, these results can inform conservation and management strategies, helping to protect these species and maintain biodiversity in semi-urban areas.
3091: Amphibians are uniquely sensitive to changes in environmental conditions, making them particularly threatened by climate change. Plethodontid salamanders breathe cutaneously and therefore require a high level of moisture in their environment to maintain bodily function. Using Plethodon cinereus (the Eastern Red-backed Salamander) as a model organism, the study assessed how abiotic factors influence P. cinereus hydration state and how these influences change seasonally. Over the course of the Fall 2024 field season (October-November), salamanders were collected and subject to dehydration and rehydration trials. We weighed them between each trial to assess their ability to either resist dehydration (i.e. maintain mass) or facilitate rehydration (i.e. gain mass back after a dehydration event). Our work expanded upon previous research by including temperature treatments in the experimental trials. The trials will be repeated in the Spring 2025 field season. Preliminary results suggest that of all explored variables, the amount of precipitation in the week prior to collection has the greatest effect on their ability to rehydrate after a dehydration event. We predict that this trend will continue into the Spring 2025 field season. The goal of this study is to provide support for the creation and implementation of conservation plans. These findings will be critical for incorporating P. cinereus’ response to changing environmental conditions into such management practices.
3092: Modern technology has vastly increased our access to information. While this access is in many ways beneficial, it has also resulted in a proliferation of misleading work. Understanding how to critically evaluate different sources of information is an important aspect of science education that can help prevent misconceptions and bolster trust in scientific institutions. I designed a seminar course for upper level life-science majors to critically evaluate media sources, while teaching them how to conduct background research using the primary literature. I chose to use nature documentaries in various formats (TikTok, short tv episodes, longer movie-like documentaries) to get students thinking about how they apply their scientific knowledge in their day-to-day lives. The format of this course enabled students to gain a broader understanding of how to critically evaluate media sources while gaining the ability to search and use the primary literature to find trusted information. A theme that unexpectedly emerged throughout the class was how do scientists (and how should scientists) communicate science to a public audience that may have differing levels of interest, knowledge, and understanding of science in order to increase scientific literacy and trust in science. This poster will outline the major assignments used in the course, key take-aways about student learning, and future directions. I will provide some recommendations for those interested in developing similar courses or assignments that engage students using modern media.
3093: The James F. Scudday Vertebrate Collection at Sul Ross State University contains significant coverage of the vertebrate specimens from the Trans Pecos and surrounding area, including notable contributions from Big Bend National Park. Many of the specimens were collected by the late Dr. James F. Scudday, a leader in regional vertebrate research. This collection serves as a vital resource for research focused on the biodiversity and ecology of the region. The collection contains approximately 1,300 amphibians, 6,257 reptiles,1,243 birds, and 2,871 mammals for a total of ~11,671 specimens. This project is actively digitizing the James F. Scudday vertebrate collection and preserving and clarifying the information before it is lost. The digitization is being conducted utilizing a Canon EOS-1DX Mark II DSLR. These high-quality photographs along with their respective identification tag are saved and are available for use by students, community members, and outside researchers. The collection data is cross-referenced as photographs are taken to determine the quality of the specimen and to check if locality data may require some updating. As many researchers know, museum collections before advanced use of GPS devices relied on descriptions of the locations. Many locations are often lost with the passing of the individual that made the collection. We have discussed with local experts who collected alongside our biggest contributor to help clarify some of the specimen localities for the collection. Through this continued effort, we want to encourage people to reach out and utilize the information in our collection.
3094: Batrachochytrium dendrobatis (Bd), the amphibian chytrid fungus, exists in suitable aquatic habitats across much of the United States Midwest and East Coast. Both biotic and abiotic habitat characteristics may help explain the presence of Bd in aquatic systems. While much research has been conducted regarding how environmental factors, such as climatic variables and water quality, as well as amphibian host presence, influence Bd persistence in ecosystems, shocking little work has been conducted to understand how non-amphibian members of ecosystems may interact with this pathogen. This collection of studies aims to identify arthropod species that may be acting as pathogen reservoirs within systems, or acting as fomites which can transmit this pathogen among ponds and wetlands. Using quantitative PCR, our team has identified multiple taxa, including Daphnia, copepods, Notonectid backswimmers, and Chironomid midges, which appear to directly interact with Bd by changing its abundance in controlled experiments. Further, we have demonstrated that water striders from the family Gerridae can transmit Bd on their surface from one location to another. Together this work suggests that complex ecological interactions between amphibians, non-amphibian animals, and Bd may be contributing to the persistence and spread of Bd in aquatic habitats.
3095: The introduction of Burmese pythons in Florida resulted in an ecological disaster for the Florida Everglades, but the scope and extent of the disaster spreads further than range of pythons. Parasites that were introduced to North America from pythons are spilling over into native taxa. The focus of this study is the Asian pentastome, Raillietiella orientalis. The introduced endoparasite now infects at least 18 native snake species of Florida as adults and has been documented as larvae in frogs and lizards. The spread of these parasites has been swift: documentation of the species now extends to the Florida panhandle. This range expansion along with the potential impacts on native taxa requires a thorough examination of the species. In this study, we assess the population genetic patterns present in R. orientalis across three widespread snake hosts: Coluber constrictor, Nerodia spp., and Agkistrodon piscivorus. We compare the genetic patterning of the parasites with respect to the distribution and behavior of their hosts.
3096: Understanding natural variability in population and community dynamics of amphibians is critical to differentiate those dynamics from true population declines. We monitored an amphibian community using a partial drift fence around an ephemeral pond on the Southern Illinois University Edwardsville campus from 2023-2024. We monitored it daily from the start of the amphibian breeding season (~February) until pond drying in each summer. We detected eight amphibian species in each year, with Southern leopard frogs being the most common adult anuran and smallmouth salamanders the most common adult caudate. Most adult movement patterns were tied to rainfall events and in a predictable pattern each year: tiger salamanders arrived first, followed by smallmouth salamanders, Southern leopard frogs, boreal chorus frogs, spring peepers and American toads arriving last. Recruitment differences in each year were driven by hydroperiod. The pond dried in late May in 2023, resulting only two individuals across all species completing metamorphosis. In 2024, where pond drying occurred in early July, tiger and smallmouth salamanders, Southern leopard frogs, spring peepers and American toads all had substantial (> 100 individuals) recruitment. This work highlights the importance of hydroperiod on amphibian population dynamics and sets baseline population and community levels for ongoing monitoring at this study site.
3097: Cryptobenthic reef fishes (CRFs) are small (less than 5 cm) fishes that live in crevices on or near the benthos. CRFs represent at least 40% of all reef fish species, though remain under-described due to their small size, limited mobility, and rapid diversification among niches. Our study examines a species complex within the cryptobenthic dwarfgoby Eviota lachdeberei to determine whether genetic and morphological data support the recognition of multiple species.  Our DNA barcoding data indicate the presence of 4 divergent mitochondrial lineages within the Coral Triangle. We compared morphometric and meristic characteristics of 18 specimens that include our genetic vouchers and type specimens of Eviota lachdeberei and Eviota partimacula, a morphologically similar species. E. lachdeberei specimens came from the Coral Triangle (a region including Indonesia, Papua New Guinea, the Philippines, and the Solomon Islands); E. partimacula specimens came from the Marshall Islands. We conducted a principal component analysis (PCA) to compare morphological traits across all specimens and to compare these groupings with the E. lachdeberei groupings from our COI tree.  Our ongoing molecular and morphological analyses will help clarify the taxonomy of these cryptic species, potentially revealing new patterns in reef biodiversity and speciation within the most diverse marine ecoregion in the world.
3098: Salamanders with biphasic life cycles (aquatic larvae to terrestrial adults) offer a unique opportunity to investigate how eye morphology adapts to ecological transitions, particularly in species that differ in their post-metamorphic use of aquatic habitats. We compare eye structure between two groups: (1) permanently terrestrial salamanders (Dicamptodon tenebrosus and Ambystoma gracile) that abandon water after metamorphosis and (2) newts (Taricha granulosa and T. rivularis) that return to aquatic environments as breeding adults. Using microCT data obtained from MorphoSource and new scans of specimens deposited in the Vertebrate Museum at Cal Poly Humboldt, we test whether these groups exhibit divergent ocular adaptations. Following findings from a recent study on frogs showing aquatic species retain spherical lenses while terrestrial forms develop flatter lenses, we predict that (1) permanently terrestrial species will develop flatter lenses (lower sphericity) as adults, optimizing vision in air, and (2) newts will retain more spherical, larval-like lenses to accommodate both terrestrial and aquatic vision. Our study leverages innovative imaging to link morphological variation with ecological divergence in salamanders, providing a broad comparative analysis of eye structure evolution in this group. Results will clarify how repeated transitions between aquatic and terrestrial habitats shape sensory anatomy, with implications for understanding the plasticity of visual systems across vertebrates.
3099: African pompano (Alectis ciliaris) is an important species in commercial markets and can fetch up to $25/pound. Despite this, nothing is known about their basic biology which is often used when making management decisions. We sought to fill this gap and describe the age, growth, diet and reproduction of the African pompano from Georgia, South Carolina and North Carolina. Following collection by fishermen, basic morphological variables were measured and gonads, guts and otoliths were removed. We found that this species is a rapidly growing fish reaching 5.5 kg in their first two years. The oldest individual analyzed here (9 years) weighed 17.7 kg. Though most stomachs were empty, we found that this species feeds primarily on cephalopods including squid and octopus. Fish parts were infrequently found inside the guts. Finally, reproductive capacity was highly variable among individuals. We found a positive relationship between the relative weight made up by the gonads and total weight. Furthermore, we found a positive relationship between female fecundity and age. Surprisingly, there was no relationship between fecundity/egg condition and date collected suggesting that these fish spawn all summer rather than preparing for a massive spawning event. With this research we reveal some important basic biological features of the African pompano. Additionally, this information can be used by managers worldwide to create science backed management policies.
3100: Recent phylogenetic studies have reshaped our understanding of the genera Noblella and Psychrophrynella (Anura: Strabomantidae). Inferred relationships based on molecular data revealed that, despite their similar morphology, species of Noblella actually belong to two non-sister clades. One clade ranges from northern Peru to Ecuador and southeastern Colombia, while the other one, which is paraphyletic with respect to Psychrophrynella, extends from southeastern Peru through northeastern Bolivia and into adjacent regions of Brazil. Recent studies provided new genetic data through the rediscovery and sequencing of the type species of those genera, N. peruviana and P. bagrecito that led to the synonymization of Psychrophrynella with Noblella. However, the assignment of the name N. bagrecito to a population did not rely on name-bearing types. To test this assignment, we extracted and sequenced DNA from a formalin-fixed paratype of N. bagrecito. The resulting sequence is genetically identical to an unnamed clade that was not recognized as N. bagrecito, suggesting that current taxonomic assignments may not reflect the original type designation. Our findings demonstrate the critical role of obtaining molecular data from name-bearing types to ensure taxonomic decisions are anchored to their original definitions. They also illustrate the value of museum collections in clarifying taxonomic uncertainties.
3101: We used three decades of long-term amphibian data for three species (Pseudacris maculata, Lithobates sylvaticus and Ambystoma mavortium) and a Bayesian occupancy modeling framework to estimate changes in occupancy, colonization, and persistence of amphibians across Rocky Mountain National Park and explore mechanisms (e.g., precipitation, drought, visitor use) behind observed changes. Our results indicate that the probability of colonization of previously unoccupied catchments is low, the probability of persistence is declining for all three species; and that occupied catchments are increasingly isolated. A higher proportion of popular trails in a catchment affected initial probability of occupancy negatively, and increasing visitor use negatively affected the probability of persistence of amphibians. In contrast, increased complexity in vegetation was associated with increased persistence and colonization. This information provides a perspective across time in a protected area where change may be less obvious or occur more slowly than in unprotected areas and is useful in planning and implementing appropriate management and conservation actions.
3102: Science illustrations are accurate and informative visualizations created for the purpose of communicating science. They can be a powerful tool to support scientific research by visually explaining and enhancing the accessibility for the viewer. Biological research including evolution, ecology, genetics, physiology, pathology, systematics, conservation etc. concerns intangible or invisible processes. Visual aids can help conceptualize the idea, and can be useful for visualizing 1) the morphological traits of the specimen, and 2) the mechanisms of phenomena. First, illustrations allow the artist and researcher full control over the presentation of visual information. For example, a subject could be rendered with neutral lighting to depict accurate colors, or in an idealized posture for comparisons across taxa. This can be especially important in herpetology and ichthyology because of their highly diverse interspecific and intraspecific variations. While photography is a great tool for documentation, a photo will always be affected by the quality of the light source and a subject's irregularities or imperfections, which may be difficult to capture sufficient detail alone. Second, the ability to visualize mechanisms or processes through abstraction is another strength of illustration. The artist can choose how to simplify findings to deliver information most efficiently in a diagram, graph, or through data visualization. For example, graphical representation can better communicate the phylogenetic relationships, physiological reactions or its role in the ecosystem. The poster would highlight a variety of science illustration methods which can support research and enhance viewer understanding and participation in various ways.
3103: The majority of marine biogeography and biodiversity studies have focused on the tropics, especially ‘biodiversity hotspots’ like the Coral Triangle and Caribbean. However, recent work suggests that speciation rates are higher at high latitudes, likely associated with greater physiological adaptation required by colder and deeper waters. One high-latitude area of interest is the 1.5 million square miles of waters surrounding Alaska, which supports high biodiversity and biomass, fueling booming commercial fisheries that average $4.5 billion/year. This vast area encompasses multiple biogeographic regions, including the temperate Gulf of Alaska, the diverse Aleutian Islands, the productive Bering Sea, and the ice-influenced Arctic. Each area has been sculpted by a dynamic geologic history of glaciers, sea level changes, land bridges, ice cover, and currents. Here we investigate how complex geologic and oceanographic history has driven speciation in the region, creating a high-latitude biodiversity hotspot, using both phylogeographic analyses (population genetics, time calibrated trees, and ancestral range reconstruction) and population ecology (hierarchical clustering, alpha-, beta- and gamma-diversity metrics). Specifically highlighting evolutionary relationships of fish species complexes that span these regions and share similar phylogeographic histories. Utilizing contemporary biodiversity data from the Alaska Fisheries Science Center groundfish surveys we model species distributions, investigate patterns of species richness, and examine current biogeographic region boundaries. Our findings may help refine management units to ensure conservation of both species and genetic diversity and showcase why cold waters deserve just as much focus as the tropics.
3104: The field of herpetology has been an inspiration for many individuals and continues to allow for an intersection of multiple fields of research to converge on the Class Reptilia and Amphibia. Study of herpetology is increasingly important given that many species are experiencing declines. Historically, systemic barriers have limited participation in the field, particularly for individuals from underrepresented backgrounds. The Herpetologists’ League (HL) is committed to addressing and dismantling these barriers to actively build community by fostering community, supporting equitable access, and expanding opportunities for engagement at all career stages. Through new initiatives, we seek to magnify connections across geographical space and foster new collaborations throughout the field. With ongoing efforts, including a student mentoring program, a free student membership drive, the revitalization of the student committee, and efforts to broaden participation through travel support, virtual resources, and recorded professional development workshops, the HL Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion Committee remains committed to supporting and building community among current and future herpetologists. We share current initiatives and seek feedback on new and creative efforts to promote access to the field of herpetology.
3105: Amphilius, a genus of mountain catfishes, native to African freshwaters, represent a fascinating group for studying biodiversity and evolutionary relationships. These fishes tend to radiate into clades of morphologically similar species, presenting challenges for accurate identification and highlighting the importance of integrating morphological and genetic analysis to uncover cryptic diversity within this group. This pilot study combines preliminary mitochondrial COI gene sequences with traditional morphometrics and radiograph-enabled meristics to explore the diversity and relationships within Amphilius in the West Central African country of Gabon. Our results revealed seven distinct mitochondrial lineages within the samples, several of which may represent species previously unknown to science. These findings suggest that the current taxonomy of Amphilius in this region underestimates its true diversity. The analysis set the stage for future exploration of landmark-based geometric morphometrics to evaluate variations in body shape and microCT scanning to generate detailed 3D reconstructions of skeletal structures. These investigations will assess whether there are multiple, distinct species that have not been recognized or described due to their morphological similarities and if these species are genetically distinct, representing separate evolutionary lineages. The findings from this preliminary study will lay the groundwork for the development of accurate taxonomic keys and a suitable framework for species identification.
3106: Understanding the immune system of wild vertebrates is essential for assessing the health of populations, including both survival and reproductive potential. Reptile immune performance, and how it is affected by the natural environment, has been historically understudied. Our study examined the relationship between parasitism and immunocompetence in a population of red-sided garter snakes (Thamnophis sirtalis parietalis) in Manitoba, Canada, specifically focusing on males that display overt signs of parasitism. Some males in the population have shortened, swollen ("stubby") tails caused by trematode infection (Alaria mesocercariae) that confers a significant fitness deficit by reducing mating competitiveness. We therefore asked if parasitized males may exhibit altered immunity compared to non-parasitized males. During the spring breeding season (May 2024) at a well-studied hibernaculum, we opportunistically collected stubby (n=25) and normal males (n=311). All snakes were weighed and measured and the data log-transformed to obtain body condition (linear residuals). From the plot, each parasitized male was then size-matched with a similar control male (n=25) to control for any condition effects. Blood samples were then collected to create smears and obtain plasma for performing bacterial killing assays (BKA). Total cell counts were conducted per slide via Ilastik (AI-based software) and ImageJ, and immune cell types, including heterophils, lymphocytes, and monocytic cells (monocytes and azurophils), were counted manually. We saw no effect of overt parasitism on any aspect of the immune cell counts, and after combining the stubby and control male datasets we found that the proportion of monocytes/total leukocytes was negatively correlated with both lymphocyte and heterophil proportions. Further, lymphocyte proportion was negatively correlated with male body size, corroborating studies in multiple groups of vertebrates. Our study is unique in that all males were actively courting females at the time and had recently emerged from long-duration brumation (~8 months), indicating that the immunity patterns we observed may represent a biological optimum for sustained, high-endurance activity.
3107: Among Lake Malawi cichlids, feeding behaviors span a continuum from suction to scraping, likely influenced in part by cranial morphology. To investigate this relationship, we used geometric morphometrics to assess shape variation in the neurocranium of wild-caught cichlids from four rock-dwelling genera—Labeotropheus, Tropheops, Petrotilapia, and Maylandia. We then conducted a principal component analysis (PCA) which revealed interspecific variation in the vomer, a bone at the anterior tip of the neurocranium, with angles ranging from acute to obtuse (relative to the parasphenoid). To test functional implications, we recorded feeding strikes (i.e. suction and scraping) in lab-reared individuals of the same genera using high-speed video (550 fps). Fish were fed Daphnia to elicit suction behavior, and preliminary analyses suggest a relationship between vomer angle and jaw movement. Individuals with acutely angled vomers, such as Labeotropheus and Tropheops, tend to rotate their jaws ventrally during strikes, while those with more obtuse angled vomers, such as Petrotilapia, and Maylandia, project their jaws anteriorly. Fish were given an algal mat to elicit scraping behavior, where we note an association between vomer angle and body orientation. For example, at the extremes, we observe Labeotropheus consistently feeding with a shallow body angle (~45°) relative to the substrate, aligning with its ventral jaw protrusion. In contrast, Petrotilapia feeds nearly perpendicular (~90°) to the substrate, using its anteriorly projecting jaws to graze. Together, these data aim to clarify how variation in vomer morphology influences feeding behavior and contributes to differences in ecological specialization among closely related cichlid species.
3108: The genus Agama is a group of highly conspicuous diurnal, insectivorous lizards with striking sexually dimorphic coloration.
