Despite their abundance and nearly universal presence in the region, a high degree of morphological conservatism, incomplete taxon sampling, and inadequate geographic coverage has resulted in uncertainties with respect to species boundaries and the validity of certain taxa. Existing work on southern African ground agamas has historically emphasized patterns within South Africa, but the ranges of two highly widespread taxa (A. anchietae, A. aculeata) extend well beyond its borders. In this study, we utilize more representative geographic coverage across their ranges (chiefly by the inclusion of specimens from Angola and Namibia) and increased gene sampling to generate robust molecular phylogenies in maximum likelihood and Bayesian frameworks using a combination of two mitochondrial genes (ND4, 16s) and three nuclear genes (PDKREJC, PNN, SETX). We uncover reciprocally monophyletic, previously undescribed deep divergences within A. aculeata and A. anchietae with geographical significance. We have obtained and annotated low-coverage genomic sequences for most taxa, which represent the first genomic data available for the genus Agama.  Mitochondrial gene order is generally considered to be highly conserved, especially within vertebrates. Currently, only 112 incidences of mitogenomic rearrangements have been confirmed within all of Lacertilia. Whole mitochondrial sequences in all sampled taxa of southern African Agama share a mitochondrial gene rearrangement previously undescribed in any other vertebrate, which lends credence to the growing notion that the conserved nature of mitochondrial gene order may be overstated due to poor sampling.
SSAR Siebert - Conservation, Evolution and Systematics
3109: Gender equality remains a major issue globally. Though progress has been made, the number of women is lower than that of men at all career stages, and data shows that representation decreases as the career stage increases. Societal structures, cultures, norms, and traditions have been identified as factors contributing to gender inequality. However, exposure to diverse role models and broader representation within STEM have a positive effect on the recruitment and retention of students and early-career biologists, especially from underrepresented groups in STEM. To increase the visibility of women in herpetology across disciplines, regions, and cultural backgrounds, we formed the Global Women in Herpetology Project and gathered herpetologists from 50 countries and regions. Collectively, we published “Women in Herpetology: 50 Stories from Around the World,” which contains short stories in which each herpetologist shares a personal narrative that intersects their gender, cultural background, and professional journey. We then used the profits of the book to establish a conference scholarship for female students in underrepresented regions around the world. Through this initiative, we hope to promote further opportunities for collaborations and mentorships for women in the field of herpetology and to engage more people to join our efforts. The next phase of this project is to widely translate the “Women in Herpetology” book into different languages, starting with Spanish and Chinese. Through this initiative, our aim is to collectively place a spotlight on the diversity of women in our field and encourage more young people to enter the field of herpetology.
3110: For many nocturnal animals, moonlight—the primary source of natural nighttime illumination—is a key determinant of predation risk. Nocturnal prey often rely on non-visual senses and have poor dim-light visual acuity, whereas visually oriented predators typically experience improved hunting success under brighter conditions. As such, non-visual prey are generally expected to suppress activity during moonlit periods to avoid detection. Because the moonlight cycle varies in a complex but predictable manner, some nocturnal species may anticipate moonlight timing  via an endogenous circalunar rhythm. However, this has rarely been demonstrated. We document a striking case of moonlight avoidance in the electric sand knifefish (Gymnorhamphichthys rondoni), which inhabits Amazonian streams where visual predators are common. These fish rely on active electroreception to forage in darkness, but its short range (<10 cm) is ineffective for predator detection. Using custom field loggers to detect electric signals, we monitored their activity across a lunar cycle alongside moonlight illuminance measurements. Sand knifefish tracked the shifting timing of moonlight, hiding in the sand during moonlit periods and sacrificing ~25% of their foraging time over the lunar cycle. An increase in electric discharge rate during the afternoon—an indicator of readiness to emerge that night—was observed on days when the moon was due to rise after sunset. This anticipatory increase was significantly reduced during full moon and two days prior, when bright moonlight was already present after sunset. These results suggest that sand knifefish anticipated moonlight conditions hours before nightfall while still buried during the day.
3111: Traditionally, baited hoop-nets and fyke nets are the primary means by which aquatic turtles have been detected during surveys, but when the goal is to map distributions, capturing turtles is a time-consuming excess compared to a birding-derived approach called digiscoping. Nets cannot be deployed in rivers during flood conditions, especially when the water is full of debris. Moreover, where we work, in Kansas, nearly all rivers are privately owned, so public access is limited to rights-of-way along roads at bridges. Riverine turtles are, thus, relatively rarely encountered and documented by museum herpetologists or on iNaturalist.com. Digiscoping opens that frontier. We survey ~150 m up and downstream at bridges with a spotting scope and photograph turtles at 80–300´ for vouchers. Prior to our visual surveys, Graptemys geographica was known in Kansas from 9 specimens collected 1911–1952 in 6 counties, went unrecorded 1953–1989, was rediscovered in 1990–1991 through extensive trapping that yielded 10 individuals in 4 counties, went unvouchered 1992–2016, and was found in 2017–2019 with laborious trapping that yielded 8 individuals. In fall 2018, we started digiscoping and, via modest efforts through early 2022, found 135 individuals at 79 locations (including 9 new county records). Consequently, Graptemys geographica was recently removed from state-threatened status. Digiscoping also yielded many other Emydid (6 taxa), Trionychid (2 spp.), and Chelydra serpentina records. Only Sternotherus odoratus went almost undetected. Graptemys geographica aside, we now average 0.67 new county records and 2.7 new drainage records within counties per field day.
3112: Alligator mississippiensis populations have recovered throughout so much of their range that regulated harvest now occurs in all but one state. The northwestern range limit of A. mississippiensis extends to southeastern Oklahoma, and little is known about the status of the population there. To better inform future management actions, we conducted surveys for alligators at 39 water bodies across 6 counties in southeastern Oklahoma. We also monitored reproductive effort at Red Slough Wildlife Management Area (RSWMA) by conducting nest and hatchling surveys. We documented sources of mortality by monitoring nests and dens with game cameras and direct observations. Alligators were detected in 4 counties, but detection rates were very low in 3 of those counties. The vast majority of detections occurred at RSWMA. Alligator surveys conducted at RSWMA several years prior reported much lower detections than we found in our current study. Data from nest and hatchling surveys indicate an overall increase in reproductive effort, but the number of nesting females remains fairly low. Major sources of mortality were predation of eggs, primarily by raccoons, and death of young alligators during freezing events. Predation by raccoons in 2024 resulted in 100% mortality of known nest sites at the WMA. Our results indicate that the alligator population is relatively small and primarily concentrated in one area of the state. Populations there would potentially benefit from actions that mitigate mortality in early life stages.
3113: Deep reefs fishes are a poorly studied community due to their depths exceeding recreational SCUBA limits. This has severely limited the amount of knowledge that exists regarding the trophic relationships among deep reef fishes and their shallow-water counterparts. Most of what is known about these species is inferred from behavior based on comparison with shallow water sister taxa. This study seeks to examine the percentages of δ15N and δ13C in four common deep reef fishes and to start to map trophic relationships for the ecosystem. δ15N acts as a proxy for determining trophic position while δ13C serves to track carbon sources and estimate trophic plasticity. The specimens were collected from four species that occur exclusively on deep reef reef slopes in Curacao using the submersible Curasub: Pronotogrammus martinicensis (Serranidae), Chrionema squamentum (Bembropidae), Symphysanodon beryi (Symphysanodontidae), and Epigonus sp. (Epigonidae).  These species are some of the most common fishes present on deep reefs and therefore should serve as a good baseline to which further work studying food webs can amend. Samples will be taken from various tissue types to have a broader time range of stable isotope measurements as the tissues chosen have distinct cell turnover rates. These values will be compared with samples from invertebrates and primary producers as well as fishes collected from shallow reefs to build a comprehensive food web of the ecosystem.
3114: Some amphibians have developed a close relationship with bromeliads, utilizing them for moisture, prey, shelter, and reproduction. This association has been so extreme that some species entirely depend on this microhabitat, also known as bromeligenous species. The environmental change hypothesis posits that shifts in species distribution are associated with temporal variation in environmental factors. Amphibian selection of suboptimal microhabitats,  such as ground bromeliads, can be ecologically important, possibly increasing disease risk. Amphibians may avoid bromeliads that maintain low moisture levels. In contrast, bromeliads that maintain high moisture conditions may attract amphibians but also promote pathogen transmission. We tested whether the frequency of occurrence of Phyllodytes gyrinaethes, a bromeligenous treefrog endemic to the Brazilian Atlantic rainforest, increases (1) with canopy cover, (2) during the rainy season in suboptimal microhabitats such as ground bromeliads, and (3) is associated with higher chytrid fungus infection in ground bromeliads and other suboptimal microhabitats shared with other amphibian species. We sampled 131 bromeliads for P. gyrinaethes presence. The frequency of occurrence of P. gyrinaethes increases during the rainy season, at high pH, and with large numbers of bromeliad leaves. The prevalence of chytrid fungus, but not infection loads, varied seasonally in ground bromeliads during the rainy season.
3115: The Dusky Gopher Frog (Lithobates sevosus) is one of the most critically endangered frog species in the United States. One major threat to their persistence is habitat loss and fragmentation. To prevent further species loss, the Memphis Zoo spearheaded the establishment of a captive population to both serve as an assurance colony in the event of species extinction in the wild and to be a source population to help boost wild populations. The first important step for the program was establishing a reintroduction site in Southern Mississippi. Under the guidance of the USFWS and Memphis Zoo, this site underwent significant habitat restoration by the Army Corp of Engineers. From 2017-2024 the Memphis Zoo and collaborators released a combined 10,738 zoo-bred tadpoles and juvenile frogs. As a result of these efforts, we are now at a turning point for this recovery program, where assessment of the establishment of this population is urgently needed for the program to advance. To monitor the status of the reintroduced population we are implementing camera traps using a version of the AHDrift method. We have fully enclosed the pond with a drift fence, with trail cameras in upside-down buckets with openings serving as entrances to and from the pond. These cameras will capture movement of both adults and metamorphs during and after the breeding season. With these images we will determine population estimates and recruitment of juveniles. This will allow us to determine if this population is self-sustaining and where to direct future reintroduction efforts.
3116: Anolis scriptus, also called the Silver Cay Anole, is widespread across the southern Lucayan Archipelago, including the Inaguas, Plana Cays, and Mayaguana of the Bahamas, as well as the Turks and Caicos Islands (TCI). It thrives in diverse habitats throughout this range, from dense tropical dry forests to pine savannas and small vegetated cays. Phylogenetic studies place A. scriptus within the Puerto Rican Anole radiation, closely related to species like A. cristatellus, A. desechensis, and A. ernestwilliamsi. Despite its resemblance to A. cristatellus, A. scriptus likely dispersed from Puerto Rico to the TCI around the beginning of the Pliocene. This migration may have occurred via over-water dispersal aided by currents and hurricanes or by island-hopping across the now-submerged Silver, Mouchoir, and Navidad banks. Potential biogeographic boundaries exist on each of these island banks within the range of A. scriptus. For example, the Turks Bank and the Caicos Bank are separated by the ~20km Turks Island Passage and were never connected. I sequenced 38 individuals at a ~1200bp mitochondrial locus, including individuals from two islands on the Caicos Bank and three islands on the Turks Bank. I then aligned these sequences and conducted phylogeographic analysis using the package ape in R. Despite drastic phenotypic differences, I found no evidence of distinct Turks Bank and Caicos Bank lineages. Rather, there are northern and southern lineages that cross the Turks Island Passage. These data will be important as additional systematic and population genetic work is done on this species elsewhere in its range.
3117: Pacific salmon migration from the ocean to freshwater to spawn impacts a number of species that consume live and dead adult salmon.  We examined trends in the spawning migration timing of Auke Creek pink (Oncorhynchus gorbuscha), coho (O. kisutch), and sockeye salmon (O. nerka) since 2011.  By observing their migration patterns, we were able to determine changes in migration timing, run duration, and relationships between migration timing and stream flow. Consistent with analyses prior to 2011, we found that sockeye migration timing has not advanced, but coho and pink salmon continue to spawn earlier in the year in this warming stream. The duration of spawning migration has a high variance over recent years for all three salmon species with no significant trends.  We explored residuals in the run timing trend for each species to determine whether abiotic variables could explain annual variation in the spawning migration.
3118: Tetracheilostoma carlae was first described by S. Blair Hedges sixteen years ago from Barbados. It is the smallest species of snake currently known, with a total length of 104 millimeters at maximum and a maximum snout-vent length of 98 millimeters. In this study, we use high-resolution computed tomography of two specimens, the holotype (USNM564819) and the paratype (USNM564818), to study the cranial and axial skeletal anatomy of this species. The morphology of the snout is narrow but expands at the neurocranial region. The antero-medial process of the parietal wedges between the frontals. The nasals, rather than being perforated by multiple foramina as in other Typhlopoids, are solid and have an opening in the lateral side of the nasofrontal suture. Each dentary bears five procumbent teeth, and no teeth are present in the premaxilla or maxilla. Compared with Typhlopoids of similar size (Antillotyphlops grantii), the posteromedial border of the parietal is rounded rather than transverse, and the supraoccipital bones are absent. We will continue investigating the individual cranial elements to produce a detailed description of the cranial morphology.
3119: Painted turtles (Chrysemys picta) are famous for their supercooling ability and for surviving long periods of anoxia without further damage in tissues and organs, making them an ideal model for ecology, evolution and biomedicine. For years, turtle research has been hampered for their slow maturation, seasonal reproduction, and the difficulty of having them in captivity. To overcome these difficulties, our lab recently developed the first adult stem cell-derived turtle organoids from liver. Organoids are 3D structures that recapitulate the microanatomy and physiology of their tissue of origin allowing for in vitro testing and experimentation without constantly harvesting donor tissue and screening offspring. Here we present the isolation and characterization of hepatic organoids from three different turtle species: painted, snapping and soft-shell turtles. The isolation of multiple turtle species organoids demonstrated that our protocol is suitable for the generation of organoids in chelonians, allowing the development of most needed tools that are currently missing to study these emerging models.
3120: The marine hatchetfishes (Sternoptychidae) are one of the largest deep-sea families with 10 genera and 79 species. Species in Argyropelecus, Polyipnus, and Sternoptyx have anteriorly deep and posteriorly shallow bodies that resemble a hatchet in lateral view, while the seven remaining genera have a more uniform, slender body. These two morphologies have typically been recognized as the Sternoptychinae and Maurolicinae, respectively. All previous molecular studies have failed to recover the family or every genus as monophyletic. We investigate the evolutionary relationships of the Sternoptychidae using  415 mitochondrial and nuclear loci (including ultraconserved elements) and 149 morphological characters. We will present the results of our combined phylogenetic analysis that recognizes a monophyletic Sternoptychidae, paraphyletic Sternoptychinae, and polyphyletic Maurolicinae. Further all genera represented my multiple species were recovered as monophyletic.
3121: The NSF Bio-LEAPS Advisory Board has outlined recommendations to improve accessibility and inclusivity at the Joint Meeting of Ichthyologists and Herpetologists (JMIH) conference. A key suggestion is the introduction of a separate accommodations survey during the registration process, allowing attendees to request child care, dietary accommodations, language support, and more. Additionally, the formation of an accessibility team, trained to manage these requests, is recommended to ensure smooth implementation during the event. The Board also advocates for clear visa letters for international attendees, detailing their accepted abstracts and participation. The Advisory Board emphasizes the importance of a user-friendly conference app with accessibility features, alongside providing physical maps and announcements to ensure equal access to information. The inclusion of opt-out options for attendee names on registration lists is also recommended to respect privacy. In terms of conference venue and logistics, the Board urges JMIH to select accessible locations with public transport options, safe environments, and ADA-compliant hotels. Conference rooms should be accessible, with adequate space for mobility devices, accessible bathrooms, and multiple food options that cater to dietary restrictions. The use of microphones, captions, and accessible podiums for presentations is recommended, along with the creation of sensory-friendly spaces for those with sensory sensitivities. Further suggestions include offering affinity and language badges to foster community, ensuring free access for caregivers, and providing affordable childcare. Finally, the Board stresses the importance of ensuring safety through clear guidelines on photography and videography, and a review of the Code of Conduct during the opening ceremony.
3122: The ringed salamander, Ambystoma annulatum, is a species of mole salamander that is endemic to the Ozark Plateau regions of the Midwest in the United States. They are found in and near ponds during their fall breeding season and lay eggs in the wetland, with larvae overwintering in ponds until the following spring. There are few studies conducted on the population dynamics of this species, and because of its small geographic range, it is considered a species of concern for this region. This study aims to assess the presence or absence of ringed salamanders in areas where urbanization is encroaching. Secondarily, I will also examine occupancy patterns of other species to explore which taxa may be less susceptible to the negative effects of urbanization. I will sample up to ninety ponds across varying habitats during two seasons surrounding St. Louis, Missouri. Dip netting will occur in all accessible areas near the bank and encompass all potential microhabitats at each pond. All captured individuals of all species will be identified and released, and their life stage, species, and sex (if apparent) will be documented. Candidate models will be compared using locally recorded and spatial factors using Akaike’s Information Criterion (AIC) to determine which factors affect the occurrence and implemented into a GIS software map. I predict that study sites that have an increase of fragmentation, are in closer proximity to roads, and have had recent increases in forest clearcutting will negatively affect amphibian populations, therefore decreasing A. annulatum occurrence and abundance.
3123: Stable isotopes of carbon and nitrogen are commonly used to examine food web structure, diet composition, and resource use within communities. In many cases, the whole organism is homogenized to obtain isotope ratios from bulk-tissue, or muscle samples from carcasses are used. Often, non-lethal subsamples, including fin, toe, and scale clips, are preferred for logistical, conservation, or animal welfare reasons. Firstly, we compare δ13C and δ15N values of nonnative Cuban treefrogs (Osteopilus septentrionalis) and African jewelfish (Hemichromis bimaculatus) to determine if non-lethal sampling methods (toe clips for anurans and fin clips for fish) give an equivalent isotope measure to that of bulk-tissue. Preliminary results show that δ13C values are similar among tissue types. δ15N values of anuran toe clips and bulk-tissue samples are similar, and thus non-lethal samples may be substituted for lethal samples. For fish, bulk-tissue samples are depleted in δ15N values compared to fin clips, which may be due to the fast metabolic rate of muscle. Due to variation in δ15N values, it is important to compare “like with like” when measuring relative isotopic niche space by keeping the use of lethal or non-lethal samples consistent within species. Secondly, we conduct a meta-analysis to determine the combined effects of preservation methods on stable isotopes of museum specimens. Although changes to δ13C and δ15N values of alcohol-preserved specimens have been documented, they are predictable and can be corrected for. We validate the use of non-lethal samples as a less-destructive means of sampling museum specimens for long-term food web studies.
3124: Will County is the most herpetologically rich county in northeastern Illinois and is home to a diverse community of anuran species. Although the Forest Preserve District of Will County safeguards an extensive network of local habitats, the county has also been experiencing significant urbanization. Given the strong link between amphibian breeding and recruitment with environmental conditions, there is a growing concern about how land-use change, such as urbanization, may impact anuran species. From 2022 to 2025, we conducted resurveys of forest preserves in Will County to understand how the herpetofauna survived, thrived, or were displaced since the last comprehensive compilation was published in 2015. We examine how calling phenology, a proxy for breeding phenology, varied across species and sites. We used passive acoustic monitoring to record anuran calling activity in wetlands of five forest preserves. To identify calls to species, we analyzed the audio data with a machine learning algorithm, which yielded a higher performance for some species than others. For species in which the algorithm allowed us to classify calls with a high confidence, we describe phenological patterns and determine how environmental and habitat factors affect variation in phenology. Calling activity exhibited species and site-specific variation. Understanding the drivers of variation in phenology across species and localities is increasingly important in the context of global change, as it can inform conservation strategies and management practices aimed at preserving biodiversity in rapidly changing landscapes.
3125: As rapid population growth, urbanization, and landscape alteration continue to increase, so too will anthropogenic inputs to ecological systems across spatio-temporal scales. Reptiles and amphibians, among Earth's most imperiled taxa, are particularly sensitive to these changes and, as such, exist at the center of the human-nature intersection. This increasingly shifting condition of their existence threatens to compromise the pivotal roles these species enact in the maintenance of biodiversity and ecosystem functioning. Responding to these challenges will require a methodological praxis which accounts for the social, political, economic, and cultural aspects involved in socio-ecological systems. This will necessitate the engagement of new, interdisciplinary approaches and epistemological frameworks, as well as increased collaboration and reflexivity in our research. Moreover, it will require the deconstruction of systems of oppression which contextualize and pervade our field in addition to interrogation of the roles we play in reifying them. A growing body of scholarship is elucidating the ways these structures, such as settler colonialism and racial capitalism, have historically operated -- and continue to operate -- to the detriment of ecology and natural history, including herpetology. In addition to upholding barriers to participation and perpetuating exclusivity and inequity in the field, these systems also affect our scholarship -- not just shaping who performs herpetology, but how it's performed and what it produces. This poster gives an overview of some of herpetology's oppressive history, offers examples of its implications, and proposes strategies and tools for systemic dismantling, embodying more critical approaches, and identifying potential areas of intersect.
3126: Crotalus ravus (Cope, 1865) is an endemic mountain rattlesnake that ranges across the Trans-Mexican Volcanic Belt (TMVB). This region is located between the Nearctic and Neotropical biogeographical realms and is recognized as a center of diversification in many taxa due to its environmental heterogeneity and relatively recent geologic origin. C. ravus has undergone several taxonomic changes throughout its history, and a recent phylogeographic study revealed previously unknown genetic diversity in populations across an east-west axis. Here, we present an integrative taxonomic approach incorporating different lines of evidence with the aim of evaluating whether the reported genetic diversity is reflected in morphology and environmental preferences, specifically through traditional morphology (meristic and mensural characters), hemipenial morphology, geometric morphometrics of head shape, and ecological niche overlap. None of the morphological lines of evidence showed significant differences between both lineages, while an ecological niche similarity test showed low overlap between lineages. Although our results suggest bioclimatic conditions differ across the distribution of C. ravus, these do not seem to influence the morphological characteristics considered. This study also suggests cryptic diversification processes in a species with a highly conservative morphology, highlighting the importance of carrying out integrative studies that incorporate genetic, morphological, and ecological data with the aim of understanding the evolutionary history of species distributed in biogeographically complex regions.
SSAR Siebert - Conservation, Evolution and Systematics
3127: The Hell Hollow Slender Salamander (Batrachoseps diabolicus) is a species of plethodontid salamander that occurs in the lowlands of the Sierra Nevada foothills in California. This lungless salamander occupies one of the most fire-prone regions of the state—one that is also rapidly growing in terms of human footprint.  At the time of description in 1998, this species was noted to encompass staggering genetic diversity, with extremely divergent populations found in the central portion of the species’ range. Our work uses modern molecular approaches and expanded sampling to describe how populations of this data-deficient species interact with each other and exchange genetic information. Specifically, our study examines the range-wide population structure and phylogenetic relationships of this species complex at a genomic scale to assess genetic diversity and the conservation status of this species. Through several years of fieldwork, we have more than doubled the elevational range that this species was thought to occupy and have discovered populations in novel habitat types. As a result, we have greatly expanded the extent of samples for divergent populations in the center of the range of B. diabolicus, with 10x the quantity of samples from this region included in our study as compared to prior publications, helping add context to the evolutionary history of this divergent lineage. Overall, this work has produced new insight into habitat preferences, range extent, and population genomic diversity for a member of an at-risk salamander group.
SSAR Siebert - Conservation, Evolution and Systematics
3128: Several species of barbs (Cyprinidae, Smiliogastrinae) were examined using vital fluorescent staining (4-di-2-ASP) and scanning electron microscopy to examine the distribution, shape, and physiological orientation (axis of best physiological sensitivity to flows) of the neuromast receptor organs of the mechanosensory lateral line system. As neuromasts were studied in detail, other structures were found in the skin on the head, trunk and tail in scanning electron micrographs. Breeding tubercles were found on the head and caudal fin of some species and taste buds were identified on the lips and barbels in some species. However, multicellular structures similar to taste buds, with what appear to be short microvilli, were also found in the epidermis on the head and overlying the scales, but also along the posterior edge of scales and, most surprisingly, in a ring around the entire circumference of the corneal epithelium. At least some of these structures are likely to be taste buds (given reports of wide distribution of taste buds in cyprinids), but the identity of the others remain enigmatic.
3129: Tooth morphology reflects the relationship between a fish and its prey, with different teeth suited for different tasks like piercing, slicing, and crushing. However, dental function is mediated by replacement (i.e. polyphyodonty) and damage to teeth (loss, breakage, blunting, etc). This study investigates tooth replacement patterns and damage across four species of prickleback (Stichaeidae), Xiphister mucosus, Xiphister atropurpureus, Phytichthys chirus, and Anoplarchus purpurescens, a group of fishes exhibiting ontogenetic dietary variation and differences in jaw and tooth morphology/mechanics. We assessed patterns of tooth replacement and damage across species and ontogeny. Our results indicate that replacement patterns and proportions are conserved across species, suggesting a phylogenetically controlled mechanism despite morphological differences. Species display differences in tooth damage, as fish that have a crushing morphotype incur more damage than fishes with a piercing morphotype. Finally, we compared replacement and damage over ontogeny, and found evidence of changes in tooth count, replacement, and damage over ontogeny for some of the species. These findings suggest that, while tooth replacement remains consistent, tooth damage reflects the forces placed upon teeth during feeding.
3130: Global declines of reptiles are caused by factors such as habitat degradation and invasive species. Understanding the impacts of nonnative cichlids and other tropical aquarium fishes in the southeastern USA is multi-faceted because these fishes probably act as both prey and competitors of aquatic reptiles. We surveyed abundance and diversity of native and non-native fishes, amphibians, and reptiles in southwest Florida wetland ecosystems using minnow trapping and asked how the presence, abundance, biomass density and diversity of prey might drive watersnake occupancy, capture rates, and prey selection. Non-native fishes made up the vast majority of biomass and of watersnake stomach contents. However, the proportionally greater relative abundance (amphibians were 3.5% of captures but 14% of stomach contents) and larger relative prey mass of amphibians in snake stomachs (max 11% for fishes vs. 31% for frogs) suggests that despite their low availability, amphibian prey are likely preferred when selection is possible. Overall, understanding how prey availability impacts snake and other predator populations can help guide conservation and decision-making efforts for these important species.
3131: We present a database to aid in the identification of the presently recognized 625 genera and 4260 species of snakes from around the world using scale characters. There are numerous snake genera for which morphological data and keys are not available, even to professional herpetologists. This compilation is based upon 1) examination of many thousands of museum specimens, 2) published scientific and lay literature, and 3) unpublished data from colleagues and museum collections, all collated by V. Wallach. Searchable characters include number of dorsal scale rows, ventral and subcaudal counts, scale carination, and head scalation. Filtering by global region, elevation, higher taxonomy, and body size is implemented. The database was recently published by DeepScience and a companion ShinyApp was developed by J. Williams and A. Durso. This resource should be of value to any herpetologist seeking to identify snakes based on their scale counts.
3132: Nearly 50 years ago, in 1976, Joseph S. Nelson published the first edition of Fishes of the World. That modest work built on a foundation laid by L.S. Berg and others, and attempted to summarize the diversity, classification, phylogeny, and characteristics of all the world’s fishes. Since that time, four more editions have been published. During recent decades, our understanding of fish evolution and systematics has changed dramatically, owing to the efforts of researchers, the advent of molecular phylogenetics, and the application of morphological tools such as µCT scanning, 3-D virtual reconstruction, and multivariate morphometrics. The pages of Fishes of the World record many dramatic changes in fish discoveries and phylogenies. The new 6th Edition of Fishes of the World, with publication scheduled in 2026, will incorporate new ideas proposed during the past 10 years about fish relationships. This poster focuses on three areas of fish evolution where relationships have been controversial and in flux. One is the phylogeny and classification of chondrichthyans, both extant taxa and their numerous fossil stem-group relatives. A second area is the controversial relationships of the basal-most extant acanthomorphs, including lampriforms, paracanthopterygians, trachichthyiforms, beryciforms, and holocentriforms. A third focus of discussion is the dramatically altered composition of the percoids relative to earlier volumes, and the placement of key taxa among a predominantly scorpaeniform radiation. The purpose of this poster is to invite the conference community to offer input, comments, and suggestions about these and other groups that are under active discussion.
3133: Amphibians are the most threatened vertebrate group on the planet and have been seen as harbingers of the Sixth Mass Extinction. It is with this alarm call that AmphibiaWeb was founded in 2000 and has been operating uninterrupted since then. AmphibiaWeb (amphibiaweb.org) is a non-profit initiative whose mission is to connect people around the world by synthesizing and sharing information about amphibians to enable research, education, and conservation. We do this by providing up-to-date scientific information on amphibian natural history, conservation, taxonomy, and global decline. The website amalgamates information from scientists and experts with the latest in biodiversity informatics. Features include: up-to-date tracking of newly described amphibian species, expert-based species accounts for over 30% of the world’s amphibians, some in multiple languages; dynamic species range and occurrence mapping; detailed pages on amphibian declines and its causes with ongoing literature updates; community- contributed multimedia files (sound, video and photos); and a community of scientists responsive to the latest taxonomic and research developments in amphibian biology and conservation to any inquiries from the public. Here we will provide a guide to how to effectively use this amphibian resource and outline how herpetologists like you can contribute and share your knowledge and photos! Please come visit our poster and meet members of the AmphibiaWeb steering committee!
3134: Fragmentation of natural landscapes disrupts individual movement and population connectivity. With continued anthropogenic change, it is increasingly important to understand how specific landscape features impact populations. The Northern Red-legged Frog (Rana aurora) is native to the Pacific Northwest and is a designated surrogate species for other riparian-associated species. We investigated how particular landscape features influence genetic diversity and connectivity among populations in the Portland, Oregon Metropolitan Region. Genomic data (RADseq) were generated for 158 individuals sampled across the region. We characterized the environmental conditions and land-use features within and between breeding sites. With a reference-aligned RADseq dataset and geospatial data, we estimated standard population genetic metrics, developed gravity models, and conducted a Maximum Likelihood Population Effect (MLPE) regression analysis to determine relationships between landscape features and population connectivity. Given the natural history and ecology of this species, we hypothesized that forested habitat, wetland corridors, and cooler, wetter climates would increase connectivity while human-modified features would decrease connectivity. We found evidence for a genetically distinct site suggesting possible human-assisted migration. At-site features did not affect gene flow among sites. Both gravity models and MLPE analyses indicated that wetland and deciduous forest corridors facilitate connectivity consistent with our expectations. These findings help us understand how human-altered landscapes affect amphibian movement and also contribute important data for improving habitat connectivity in the region for this and other species.
3135: Cryptobenthic fishes are small-bodied, short-lived inhabitants of reef habitats around the world. Recently, our understanding of the ecological importance of cryptobenthic fishes has increased, with their taxonomic diversity and varied ecological roles of particular note. However, there is relatively little detailed information on the anatomy of these fish, especially in comparison to their diversity, to allow for in-depth investigations into their adaptations to such specialized lifestyles. Here we present CryptoVert, a digitization project led by the Department of Ichthyology at the Natural History Museum of Los Angeles County, in support of the openVert project (oVert). This project digitizes at least one species per genus for each cryptobenthic fish family through macro-photography, and two µCT scans: one to document the skeletal anatomy and a second using contrast-enhanced CT scans to examine soft tissue anatomy, including muscle, digestive, circulatory, and nervous systems. In total, over 400 scans have been made across 12 families of cryptobenthic fishes. These scans have been uploaded to MorphoSource and are freely available for download. We anticipate these scans will support research into general trends in vertebrate anatomical evolution associated with body size and will be a valuable resource for the development of new questions and hypotheses in a variety of scientific disciplines. Additionally, we showcase educational models created from these scans that will be useful for classrooms ranging from high school biology to graduate-level ichthyology courses.
3136: Desert reptiles exhibit numerous adaptations, such as high blood osmolality, high operative temperatures, and low cutaneous evaporative water loss (CEWL) to survive drought. It is well known that between closely related squamate species, those inhabiting hotter and drier habitats tend to exhibit more extreme versions of those adaptations than relatives in milder climates. However, very little is known about whether these adaptations vary intraspecifically. The Yellow-backed spiny lizard (S. magister uniformis) conveniently inhibits a transect of increasing aridity and temperature from the San Joaquin to the Mojave Deserts in California. I hypothesized that lizards sampled from hotter and drier sites will exhibit higher operative temperatures, higher blood osmolality, and lower CEWL than those sampled from cooler and wetter environments. I established six field sites across this gradient and sampled 20 lizards each for blood osmolality and CEWL measurements. A subset of 10 more lizards per site were outfitted with light-level geolocators (GLS) to determine their voluntary thermal maximum in combination with operative temperature models placed in full sun, shade, and burrows. The use of GLS is particularly exciting as these devices are extremely lightweight (<1g w/o harness) and can provide high accuracy temporal measurements of thermoregulatory behavior without labor intensive direct observations. My project will still be ongoing by the time of this conference, but I will have presentable preliminary data by June. My project will add to our understanding of desert reptile physiology overall and inform landscape-scale conservation measures targeting species experiencing a diverse array of climatic conditions.
3137: Different environments have distinct light characteristics that place evolutionary constraints on vision. Over time, evolution under these constraints has resulted in the dynamic and specialized photosystems visual systems seen across various animal groups. Environments where light is limited or absent are expected to relax the effects of selection on vision-related genes, resulting in evolutionary regression of the visual system as other sensory systems are favoured. Many aspects of visual system regression have been well studied in fossorial mammals but remain understudied in fossorial amphibians and reptiles. Caecilians and several independent lineages of fossorial squamates have convergently evolved similar morphological adaptations to their fossorial lifestyles, but the molecular underpinnings of the changes to their visual systems have not been studied. We predict that vision-related genes will show convergent patterns of regression across independent evolutionary transition to fossoriality. However, in addition to regression, we hypothesize that a subset of genes will show evidence of adaptation, where those genes, and their proteins, have been selected for alternative functions within the fossorial light environment. To test these predictions, we supplement existing amphibian and squamate genomic resources through the sequencing of additional genomes from fossorial taxa. Vision-related genes from fossorial and non-fossorial taxa will be compared to determine the extent of gene loss across taxa and molecular evolutionary models will be used to estimates selection pressures included test for relaxed and positive selection. Preliminary results suggest many fossorial taxa maintains many more vision-related genes than expected suggestion potential adaptive evolution or co-option for non-visual functions.
SSAR Siebert - Conservation, Evolution and Systematics
3138: The Atlantic cownose ray (Rhinoptera bonasus) is a highly migratory batoid occurring along the eastern coasts of North and South America and throughout the Gulf of Mexico (GoM), frequently observed in large schools. Although R. bonasus possess an extremely vulnerable life history and has historically been targeted in directed fisheries, a formal stock assessment has never been conducted, inhibiting management and making it difficult to assess population fluctuations. Cownose rays have been frequently documented using estuaries during reproductive and young-of-year (YOY) life stages, increasing potential anthropogenic interactions during delicate life stages. While cownose ray movement behavior has been extensively described on the US East coast, movement data in the GoM is limited. In this study, 36 cownose rays (mature and YOY males and females) were acoustically tracked in Apalachicola Bay, Florida. Both life stages used the estuary extensively, with mature females making unique, directed movements to specific seagrass-dominated areas after parturition/mating. A large proportion of mature individuals exhibited seasonal residency in the Apalachicola Bay system, with mature females demonstrating the strongest fidelity to the estuary and mating area. Tagged animals remained in the bay for durations of weeks to months, primarily using mud habitat near the river mouth during the spring and summer. Sporadic winter detections on the eastern side of the system and near inlets suggest that cownose rays do not migrate great distances after departing the system. This study provides a novel assessment of habitat use, seasonal residency, and mating behavior of cownose rays in the GoM.
3139: The Atlantic sharpnose shark (Rhizoprionodon terraenovae) is the most abundant shark species found in the coastal waters of the Gulf of Mexico (GoM). Due to their relatively small size, they have developed life history strategies such as rapid growth and maturation, to counteract various pressures. Understanding the diet of young-of-year (YOY) individuals is crucial for assessing maternal influence on early feeding behaviors, which play a key role in promoting rapid growth. This study examined YOY diet composition in St. George Sound, FL, using a combination of gut-content analysis and stable isotope analysis (δ13C and δ15N). Diet composition was quantified using the Index of Relative Importance (%IRI), incorporating the percent number of prey (%N), percent weight of prey (%W), and percent frequency of occurrence (%O) to assess dietary significance of different prey taxa. Preliminary results indicate that of the YOY sampled (n=167; n= 67 empty), guts were dominated by Teleostei (n=75; %N: 53.9, %W:69.6, %O: 62.5, %IRI: 84.05), followed by Malacostraca (n=31; %N: 26.5, %W: 9.6, %O: 30.2, %IRI: 11.89). Unidentified animals made up 12 of the contents (%N: 10.3, %W: 2.3, %O: 11.36, %IRI: 1.57), then Cephalopoda (n=9; %N: 7.7, %W: 15.5, %O: 9.4, %IRI: 2.4) and Sipuncula (n=2; %N: 1.7, %W: 3.1, %O: 2.1, %IRI: 0.1).These findings align with previous studies completed in the northeastern GoM, further supporting the role of teleost fish in the species' diet. Future results will explain isotopic shifts across fork length (cm) in conjunction with gut-contents, providing further insights into ontogenetic dietary shifts.
3140: Skates are an important, yet poorly studied taxonomic group, with multiple species often co-occurring in space and time. We compared the relative abundance of three species of skate to examine trends in phenology compared to oceanographic conditions and explore niche overlap using a fisheries independent survey. Three of the most abundant skate species in the Mid-Atlantic Bight (MAB) are Clearnose Skates Rostroraja eglanteria, Little Skates Leucoraja erinaceus, and Winter Skates Leucoraja ocellata. We found that off of New Jersey, peaks of Clearnose Skate abundance occur at higher temperatures compared to Little and Winter Skates (center of temperature distribution for Clearnose Skates = 17.6°C, Little Skates = 11.3°C, Winter Skates = 10.3°C). Correspondingly, Little and Winter Skates abundance peaked in the early spring. In addition to variance in seasonal occurrence, interspecific variations were documented in terms of spatial habitat occupancy in the coastal oceans off the coast of New Jersey. Clearnose Skates displayed a more southerly center of distribution compared to Little Skates, and Winter Skates. Notably, the centers of distribution for all three species occurred at higher latitudes during summer months suggesting a seasonal north-south migrational life history strategy. Additionally, we found inter and intraspecific depth distributions for each species. Overall, our results demonstrate the occurrence of niche partitioning between these species based on differences in habitat occupancy and create a foundation upon which future investigations into skates in the MAB can build upon.
3141: The Guana and Tolomato Rivers provide essential habitat for several ecologically and economically important species and serve as nursery habitat for a variety of Atlantic coastal shark species, including scalloped hammerhead (Sphyrna lewini), sandbar (Carcharhinus plumbeus), and bull sharks (Carcharhinus leucas). Spanning the northeastern Florida coast, the rivers are home to over 50 endangered or threatened species and host several habitat restoration projects due to their ecological significance and proximity to development along the coast. The effects of human influence and pollution, and specifically toxic metal mercury (Hg), has not been well studied in this system. Mercury is known to biomagnify through the food web, therefore posing significant health risks to high level consumers that possess elevated concentrations, such as elasmobranchs. Therefore, this presentation will highlight the completed first section of my master’s thesis, investigating the presence of mercury in fishes and elasmobranchs of the Guana and Tolomato Rivers and its movement through the food web. Mercury concentrations were analyzed in elasmobranchs and their prey species, using the current federal guidelines for safe mercury concentrations in fish as set by the EPA (0.3 mg/kg/ of wet-weight) and the FDA (1.0 mg/kg of wet weight). Additionally, trophic levels were determined through stable isotope analysis to better illustrate the transfer and magnification of mercury within this system.
3142: The lemon shark, Negaprion brevirostris, is a large-bodied inshore species of shark that is well documented in tropical waters of the Western Atlantic. Until 2019, this species has been largely absent from coastal surveys in Georgia. In 2019, a potential lemon shark nursery was identified for the species on Little St. Simons Island (LSSI) – a first for the state. The lemon sharks around LSSI were determined to have a strong selectivity for surf and inlets, which likely offered shelter at high tides. In this study, we hypothesized that lemon sharks were also present on other Georgia barrier islands. Using aerial imagery, we selected habitats with similar characteristics to the lemon shark nurseries on LSSI and sampled them using the same methods used previously on LSSI. In 2021–2022, we documented 108 lemon shark captures, including 28 recaptures, in surf and inlet habitat on Little St. Simons, Ossabaw, and St. Simons islands. Additionally, juvenile lemons were observed in 2022 on St. Catherines Island but were not successfully captured during sampling. These results suggest nursery habitats may exist in those additional locations, and that Georgia has an underassessed presence of juvenile lemon sharks. The documentation of these novel nurseries provides important information about habitat preference and the geographic extent of nursery habitat for this species, which is critical to the proper management of these highly migratory sharks.
3143: The Brassy Jumprock (Moxostoma sp.) is a known yet undescribed species of freshwater fish that has long remained in taxonomic uncertainty. Initially discovered in 1956, the species was erroneously diagnosed as Moxostoma robustum, a species originally described in 1870 but unseen since. However, the subsequent rediscovery of a population matching the original description of M. robustum in 1992 clarified the identity of M. robustum, leaving the Brassy Jumprock without a valid scientific name. Herein, in the effort to compose a formal description for the species, morphological and meristic characters from a total of 215 Brassy Jumprock specimens were examined, representing every major river basin where they are known to occur. Furthermore, 154 specimens of comparative material were examined consisting of coexisting, morphologically similar congeners sympatric with the Brassy Jumprock. These analyses were able to identify a suite of characters that can be used to distinguish the Brassy Jumprock as a unique species. In conjunction with formalizing a description, we sought to examine the population structure of the species. A series of historical geographic records from museum collections and state agencies was used to define a precise distribution range for the species. Population structure was then examined via RADSeq data from individuals throughout the geographic range to determine the degree of population connectivity between drainages and to search for any unrecognized cryptic diversity. This comprehensive approach provides the foundation for the formal recognition and description of the Brassy Jumprock.
3144: Unionid mussels have severely declined, and reintroduction represents a valuable conservation tool. Fishes serve as hosts for early life stages of mussels (glochidia), and recolonization is dependent on the ability of fish hosts to disperse to suitable mussel habitat. The Mission Reach of the San Antonio River is an urban reach with ‘flashy’ hydrology, and restoration has involved the construction of 31 erosion control structures across an eight-mile (12.8 km) segment. These structures have not been evaluated for fish passage. Although juvenile mussels have been reintroduced, natural recolonization by sexually mature mussels that persist has not been documented. One hypothesis for the lack of recolonization success is that movement by fish hosts may be limited by installed structures or hydrologic variables, thereby reducing connectivity between mussel populations and suitable rearing habitat. Our objective was to determine whether fish are passing erosion control structures and evaluate predictors of passage. We used passive integrated transponder (PIT) tags to evaluate movement across seven structures within the Mission Reach. We PIT tagged 1,140 individuals representing 20 species and used a mobile antenna system to redetect individuals. We redetected 229 individuals and documented 22 passage events. Passage was correlated with fish length, Julian date, and several structure-specific characteristics, indicating that larger individuals pass structures more frequently and that some structures may pass fish more efficiently than others. Our results will inform future mussel reintroduction efforts and indicate that structures comparable to those in the Mission Reach do not represent complete barriers to movement by fishes.
3145: Aphredoderus are a widespread genus of lowland freshwater fish native to the Eastern United States. Along the southeastern coastal plain, Aphredoderus exhibit widespread sympatry with little to no evidence of admixture between sister taxa. Using biogeographic, genomic, and temporal data we evaluate relationships between sympatric species of Aphredoderus. We find incompatibilities between spatial and temporal data of one Aphredoderus species, and evidence of pervasive ancestral introgression in both allele-frequency and haploid sequence data. Our data support extensive early-to-mid Pleistocene introgression and reticulation within the phylogeny of Aphredoderus.
3146: In central Texas (CTX), there is evidence of a potentially undescribed catostomid, the Llano River Carpsucker (Carpiodes cf. carpio). C. cf. carpio possess a more elongated body compared to sympatric River Carpsucker (C. carpio), with meristics and mouth morphology similar to C. cyprinus. While the U.S. Geological Survey suggests C. cyprinus were introduced to CTX, the earliest non-native record of C. cyprinus match the original collection of C. cf. carpio from the Llano River. Considering this, the relationship between C. cf. carpio with recognized species of Carpiodes is unknown along with its native status. The objective of this study was to assess genetic differences between C. cf. carpio and Carpiodes across their distribution using traditional molecular markers and phylogenetic techniques. Tissues collected from 260 Carpiodes specimens inhabiting Brazos, Colorado, and Guadalupe drainages of Texas were compiled with museum requested tissues representative of the distribution of Carpiodes. We extracted DNA from tissues, amplified the mitochondrial cytochrome b (CYTB) and nuclear IRBP2 genes, and sequenced data for each specimen. Our phylogenetic analyses revealed that potentially undescribed species of Carpiodes species exist within the southeastern United States which are currently listed as C. cyprinus. Furthermore, C. cf. carpio of CTX were closely related to C. cyprinus inhabiting Mississippi, Great Lakes, and Hudson Bay drainages yet possessed CYTB haplotypes that were unique among our sampled distribution. Our work suggests C. cf. carpio are native locally adapted C. cyprinus which has crucial implications for the conservation and management of native fishes in Texas.
3147: The macroevolutionary drivers of morphological diversification are varied, ranging from genetic mechanisms, developmental processes, and ecological and environmental pressures. Life history strategy, which optimizes growth, sexual maturation, and reproductive output, may also drive morphological evolution. Because morphological traits, such as body size, are linked to life history strategies, variation in life history may influence phenotypic diversity patterns. Lampreys have three remarkably different life history strategies: anadromous-parasitic, freshwater-parasitic, and freshwater-nonparasitic, each evolving repeatedly across the lamprey phylogeny. In this study, we explored the role of life history strategy in structuring morphological evolution in lampreys. We analyzed 14 traits that capture morphological variation across 35 lamprey species using a suite of phylogenetic comparative methods. Our preliminary results reveal patterns of phenotypic divergence among life history strategies, with the strongest divergences among traits linked to feeding. Additionally, we find that body size is the primary axis of divergence and is most strongly associated with migration. Our study emphasizes the importance of life history strategies in driving morphological diversification and adaptation.
3148: Spotted Gar (Lepisosteus oculatus, Winchell 1864) is widespread with a disjunct population in the Great Lakes Basin found from Michigan south to Louisiana, southwestern Texas, and the western Florida panhandle. The primary area of its range comprises the Mississippi River Basin and neighboring drainages. A disjunct northern and southern population sets L. oculatus apart from other gar species which have more contiguous ranges. Despite their external appearances being little changed since the Jurassic, there appears to be more diversity within gars than once expected. Here we compared differences in body shape using traditional and geometric morphometrics across the distribution of Spotted Gar. We also collected tissue samples from across the distribution for population genetic analyses using ddRADseq. Significant population structure was discovered in L. oculatus. Spotted gars from the northern disjunct population were not genetically distinct from neighboring populations in the Mississippi River Basin, likely due to the recency of their Great Lakes colonization after the Last Glacial Maximum. Sampled Florida gars (L. platyrhincus, DeKay 1842) were nested within a larger clade with samples of Spotted gars from their zone of sympatry in the Florida panhandle. These results have significant taxonomic implications given the prevalence and ease at which gars can hybridize.
3149: The behavioral displacement hypothesis posits that competition and behavioral interactions drive niche divergence, making these interactions potential determinants of invasive species success and distributions. House Geckos (Hemidactylus spp.) are widely distributed human-commensal invasive lizards. Over the past century, Mediterranean House Geckos (H. turcicus) have established populations in the southern USA, followed by Tropical House Geckos (H. mabouia) in southern Florida, and Sri Lankan House Geckos (H. parvimaculatus) in southern Louisiana and Texas. These species are ecologically similar, leading to speculation of competitive displacement of H. turcicus, which no longer occurs in southern Florida and is increasingly rare in southern Louisiana. Yet, no study has documented competition among these species. Our goal is to determine if the gradual disappearance of H. turcicus from previously occupied regions can be attributed to competition with congeners. Specifically, we are ascertaining the competitive dominance hierarchy among these three species. To determine this, individual H. turcicus were randomly paired with geckos of both competitor species (n = 3/species) and a conspecific control. Fasted pairs were introduced to arenas where behavioral interactions were night-vision video recorded for 45 mins. Predefined behaviors were quantified and categorized to assign dominance ranks that will be compared via GLM to determine the dominance order among species. Data indicate H. turcicus is submissive to H. mabouia yet evenly matched against H. parvimaculatus. Competitor sex did not matter, but body size may. Our findings will broaden our understanding of the role of behavior as a mechanism of competitive displacement among co-occurring invasive species.
3150: Habitat loss and fragmentation lead to the breakdown of important spatial processes that determine population and metapopulation persistence. For example, the decline of the longleaf pine-wiregrass ecosystem has led to the imperilment of many species, especially endemic amphibian species that breed in geographically isolated wetlands. In Georgia, Gopher frog (Rana capito) metapopulations and populations now exist on relatively small, isolated, and highly fragmented landscapes. Very few of these landscapes support more than one or two breeding wetlands. Thus, little is known about the factors that determine connectivity between breeding sites and how they affect Gopher frog population dynamics. I used an Individual-Based Model (IBM) to simulate how landscape features influence the patterns of breeding site occupancy and the genetic structure of Gopher frog populations on one of the few remaining landscapes that support multiple breeding wetlands in Georgia. Based on field and experimental studies, the model integrates frog behavior and breeding site population projection models. This technique creates a realistic, mechanistic model to evaluate how natural and human-driven variation in soil and land cover type affects metapopulation processes and persistence. The model can be used to evaluate management scenarios, including spatially explicit habitat management and translocation decisions, to maximize Gopher frog persistence in this and other managed landscapes.
3151: Invasive species are one of the largest contributors to global biodiversity loss, especially on islands. Novel interactions from introduced taxa including predation, competition, habitat loss, dietary shifts, and hybridization often cause population decline and extinction in native species. Despite the potential severity of threats, little research has focused on large scale impacts of invasive species on native lizards. Our goals are to identify the relative impact of invasive species as a threat to native lizards, the major species and threat types (e.g., predator, competitor) affecting native lizards, and the geographic patterns in invasive species occurrence and native lizard decline. We compiled data for over 600 lizard species with invasive species identified as a major threat. For each lizard species, we identified their invasive threat, their invasive threat type (e.g., mammal predator), other threats to the species, range type (island, continent, both), range midpoint, habitat, lizard body traits (e.g., average mass, length), and lizard extinction status (e.g., least concern, endangered, etc.). We used these data to assess which threats and conditions may be linked to high lizard extinction risk and which may be most conducive to native-invasive coexistence. The results of this research will be the first cohesive review of the threat of invasive species on native lizard species. Our work will provide valuable information that is immediately applicable to conservation strategies for lizard species across the globe.
3152: The niche concept has been widely reviewed by ecologists since its introduction by Grinnell in 1924 and by Elton in 1927, who described the spatial niche and functional role niche, respectively. In Florida, the impact of invasive species on the niches of native species remains uncertain. The vacant niche hypothesis states that nonnative species, upon arrival to a new area, will occupy a niche which is “unused” by native species, whereas the niche competition hypothesis states that nonnative species will occupy an overlapping niche, resulting in a shift or alteration of the niche composition of native species over time. We use δ15N and δ13C stable isotope analyses to test the vacant niche hypothesis and the niche competition hypothesis within the aquatic vertebrate community of Rainey Slough in Glades County, Florida. In the 1970s, Rainey Slough hosted high amphibian and reptile biodiversity and biomass, but drastic herpetofaunal declines have occurred over the past 50 years, likely driven by competition and predation from nonnative fish species, Cuban treefrogs (Osteopilus septentrionalis), and island apple snails (Pomacea maculata). Preliminary data from museum specimens collected in 1969-1979 and samples collected in 2024-2025 may determine if nonnative species occupy a niche space which either (1) is unused by native species, or (2) displaces native species. It is important to determine how community structure and diversity affects invasibility (susceptibility to invasion) in relatively undisturbed habitats as nonnative species continue to spread throughout Florida.
3153: Many lizards, like most other herpetofauna, are vastly understudied, and some of Southwest Florida’s invasive lizards are no exception. Understanding the ecology of invasive lizards and how they use their new environment is essential to not only determining their impact on our ecosystems but can give us a better idea about their ecology in their native range. This study sought to assess the habitat characteristics of vegetation used by Chamalaeo calyptratus (veiled chameleons) and Anolis equestris (knight anoles) in Southwest Florida. Nocturnal visual surveys were conducted to locate lizards, and all trees in which lizards were found were tagged to be measured later. Vegetation surveys were then conducted on all transects during daylight hours, where both trees used by individual lizards and randomly selected trees were identified to the species-level and measured for height, diameter at breast height, canopy cover, and stem number. Both C. calyptratus and A. equestris were found more often in taller trees and A. equestris was found more often in trees with higher canopy cover. Lizards were found using six of the seven most common woody vegetation species available (cypress, pine, colicwood, dahoon holly, wax myrtle, and cabbage palm), but were not found in the fifth most common species (silverling), suggesting that overall, these lizards may not have strong preferences for vegetation type. These data can support further research on the ecology of these lizards and inform potential management implications in the future.
3154: Raillietiella orientalis is an invasive pentastome parasite introduced to southern Florida by the Burmese python. This parasite poses a conservation threat for native snakes in the southeastern United States, as infections are associated with morbidity and mortality. Little is known about its life history, impacts on native snake species, or the extent of its spread. To address this, the Snake Lungworm Alliance and Monitoring (SLAM) organization was established to conduct opportunistic surveillance of infection. We performed dissections on collected roadkill and snakes found dead in habitat, examining the respiratory tract and viscera for R. orientalis adults. We assessed infection prevalence across Florida, comparing natural and anthropogenic land cover types, and analyzed infection rates among 30 native snake species. A generalized linear model with snake genus as a random effect found no significant difference in infection odds between natural and anthropogenic areas (OR = 1.24, p = 0.61, 33% vs. 28% probability). Compared to central Florida, odds were 91% lower in northeast Florida (OR = 0.09, p = 0.002, 3% probability) and 97% lower in northwest Florida (OR = 0.03, p < 0.0001, 1% probability). Southern Florida showed a non-significant trend toward higher infection probability (OR = 2.13, p = 0.1), with a predicted probability of 45%. Region was a significant predictor of infection likelihood. Chi-square analysis showed significant variation in prevalence among species. Several areas of Florida remain underrepresented in surveillance, highlighting the need for more data to fully understand the spread and impact of R. orientalis.
ASIH Stoye - Ecology & Ethology I / Conservation
3155: Prairie Rattlesnakes (Crotalus viridis) can gather by the hundreds to hibernate and give birth, making them an exceptional candidate for studying reptile social behavior. Why do snakes gather in these impressive aggregations and how are their social relationships maintained? Much of our historical knowledge of wild rattlesnake behavior has been confounded by the disturbance caused by human presence, leaving many unobserved behaviors and unanswered questions about social groupings among these mysterious and feared animals. Through the umbrella organization Project RattleCam, we used camera trap photos processed through the community science platform Zooniverse and the first 24-7 live-streaming camera on a den of wild reptiles to monitor interactions among snakes throughout the active seasons of two populations. While painted rattles identified individual snakes in the camera trap photos, community scientists named and tracked snakes based on unique scale patterns in the livestream. Our project has revealed group-level trends in activity as well as individual personalities among rattlesnakes. Social networks reveal that females are highly connected, and some males remain at rookeries throughout the summer. We continue to investigate the social dynamics of communicative head twitching behavior and drinking behavior from the livestream footage. Community scientists have been instrumental to this project’s success through the processing of photos, identification of individual snakes, and reviewing video footage. From dozens of dedicated volunteers to our growing YouTube subscriptions, this project has fostered a global community to deepen our understanding of snake behavior that could ultimately change how people perceive and interact with snakes.
ASIH Stoye - Ecology & Ethology I / Conservation
3156: Non-native species can pose significant threats to native biodiversity, especially once established in novel areas. We evaluated the effectiveness of ten years of removal effort in a recently established population of invasive non-native Common Watersnakes, Nerodia sipedon, introduced to Roseville, California. We used aquatic minnow traps to capture and remove snakes from 2015–2024. We estimated annual abundance using the Leslie depletion method and examined relative mass of snakes annually. We removed 110 snakes from 2015–2019, with none captured after 2019. Estimates from Leslie depletion models showed abundance declined annually during removal, with initial estimates of 55 snakes in 2015 and 41 snakes in 2016, followed by a decrease to 4 snakes in 2017, 7 snakes in 2018, and 8 snakes in 2019. Estimated abundance and relative mass of snakes were decreasing before removal began, possibly due to a drought, but relative mass increased after removal began, suggesting possible competitive release. Our results suggest the population was successfully eradicated, with no snakes seen since 2019. Drought conditions likely aided eradication, but the increase in relative mass of snakes as abundance declined highlights possible risk of compensatory growth and population rebound if removal effort had ended earlier. Our analysis highlights the value of targeting removal effort to coincide with environmental conditions that are challenging to non-native species, while revealing the risk of populations recovering from density-dependent releases if removal effort ends before successful eradication.
ASIH Stoye - Ecology & Ethology I / Conservation
3157: Blackside Dace (Chrosomus cumberlandensis; BSD) is a federally threatened leuciscid endemic to the upper Cumberland River system in Kentucky and Tennessee. BSD have been extirpated from numerous streams within their home range due to anthropogenic disturbances such as agriculture, logging, and surface coal mining. Streams within this system are characterized by low levels of background conductivity (<100 uS/cm); however, these anthropogenic activities are linked to elevated conductivity levels with impacted streams often exceeding 1000 uS/cm. BSD populations do not persist in streams over 340 uS/cm but the direct impacts of elevated conductivity to their physiology is unknown. Prolonged physiological stress from abiotic factors such as alterations in water chemistry can impact growth, feeding, and behavior of fishes. Elevated conductivity does negatively impact growth rate on the more widely distributed congener Southern Redbelly Dace (Chrosomus erythrogaster). Therefore, we hypothesize elevated conductivity directly impacts growth, feeding response, position in water column, and recovery to disturbance. We subjected shoals of three adult BSD to either the control treatment (<250 uS/cm) or high treatment (700 uS/cm) for four weeks. To test impact on growth, we measured total shoal weight before and after exposure. We assessed latency to feed, position in water column for a five-minute observation period twice per week during the trial period, and on the final day, we assessed time of recovery from disturbance. Impacts on growth and behavior are non-lethal, but likely contribute to reduced fitness of individuals when exposed to chronic levels of elevated conductivity.
ASIH Stoye - Ecology & Ethology I / Conservation
3158: In 2011, the IRL underwent a regime shift because of an intense harmful algae bloom (HAB) that fundamentally changed ecosystem conditions to favor phytoplankton over seagrass. We wanted to determine if this regime shift is reflected in fish community dynamics, including mass mortality events, in the IRL. We analyzed long-term data sets of fish kills and of population fluctuations of 10 fish species of interest. HAB events correlate with the frequency of fish mortality events, perhaps caused by hypoxia and exposure to toxins produced by certain algal species. It is conceivable that the 2011 regime shift may coincide with a decline in young-of-the-year (YOY) abundance and distribution for the fish species of interest, perhaps due to the loss of essential nursery habitat because of the regime shift. This situation underscores the impacts of human activity on the IRL and the importance of proactive environmental management to protect this vital ecosystem.
ASIH Stoye - Ecology & Ethology I / Conservation
3159: Ocean warming poses an ongoing threat to many species. To anticipate how populations will respond over multiple generations, we need to understand the genetic capacity of thermal responses to evolve and the processes that promote genetic variation. One potential source of such variation is local adaptation to environmental conditions. For example, if individuals inhabiting cooler waters tend to have cold-tolerant genotypes and individuals inhabiting warmer waters have warm-tolerant genotypes, then local adaptation could promote genetic variation in the population as a whole. We tested for local adaptation of thermal sensitivity in populations of California Grunion. We collected the gametes of Northern, Central, and Southern populations of Grunion and reared their embryos and larvae in a common laboratory environment. Larvae were reared across temperatures reflecting their natural range and we measured growth and mortality. The Central population exhibited a higher capacity for growth under higher temperatures than the Northern and Southern populations. Mortality was lowest at intermediate temperatures, but the Southern population exhibited peak survival at a significantly higher temperature than the Northern and Central populations. When examining the effects of temperature on biomass production (combination of survival and growth), we found that Southern populations indeed have a higher thermal optimum than northern populations. Grunion experience gene flow at large spatial scales and our results suggest that adaptation to local temperature conditions can increase overall heritability in thermal sensitivity by 25 to 75%. Local adaptation may thus increase the population-wide capacity for evolutionary adaptation to climate change.
ASIH Stoye - Ecology & Ethology I / Conservation
3160: Climate models predict that environmental conditions will change, exposing long-lived freshwater fish to novel climate patterns.
