To determine how the vital rates of long-lived freshwater fish species respond to climate change, we modified the environmental variation in a previous stochastic matrix model on June suckers (Chasmistes liorus) and used that model for comparison. We evaluated the demographic responses to four likely climate scenarios over a 200-year period: (1) increased stochasticity in river flow, (2) a 0.5 m decline in lake level due to a megadrought, (3) increased lake level amplitude from 1 m to 1.5 m, and (4) shortened climate cycles from 30 years to 8 years. We also performed combinations of scenarios to assess the relative strength of effects. We found that increased stochasticity in river flow and declining lake level had negative effects, while greater amplitude in lake level and a 12-year climate cycle had positive effects. In addition, we observed that different combinations of scenarios had varying effects on population growth. These results suggest that stabilizing lake levels and maintaining a 12-year climate cycle could promote positive population growth in June suckers despite ongoing climate change.
ASIH Stoye - Ecology & Ethology I / Conservation
3161: The warming world may shape food webs in different ways. Rising temperatures may strengthen top-down effects by increasing consumption of prey by predators or may dampen top-down effects if temperatures exceed predator tolerance limits. We investigated the effects of predatory amphibians and temperature on three aspects of a forest floor community: plant survival, invertebrate abundance and leaf decomposition rate. We used outdoor pens that contained either four or zero wood frogs and were either warmed with a greenhouse chamber or experienced ambient temperatures. In each pen we planted two common blue violets and two eastern red columbines. The plant species exhibited different responses to the treatments. Greenhouses decreased survival of violets, but their effects on columbines were contingent on the presence of frogs. With greenhouses, survival of columbines was increased when frogs were present. At higher temperatures within tolerance limits, frogs may consume more herbivorous invertebrates that would otherwise consume more columbine tissue. Without greenhouses, survival of columbines was decreased when frogs were present. Frogs decreased the abundance of springtails, detritivores that enrich the soil with nutrients. Although greenhouses decreased leaf decomposition rate, there was no effect of frogs on decomposition, suggesting that frogs did not affect plant survival by consuming detritivores. Our results provide mixed support for the hypothesis that rising temperatures strengthen top-down effects of amphibian predators on forest floor communities: frogs increased survival for one plant species when warmed, but frogs and warming did not interact to affect the other plant species, invertebrate abundance, or leaf decomposition.
ASIH Stoye - Ecology & Ethology I / Conservation
3162: Seasonal changes manifest variation in environmental cues, such as dial period and temperature, that can signal physiological and behavioral changes. Most terrestrial ectotherms reduce activity and metabolic rates during the winter to conserve energy when resources are scarce, which can result in changes in body condition and blood metabolites. Reproduction can produce drastic changes in body condition and energetic state in many animals. As infrequent eaters and capital breeders, snakes provide a model for analysis of interseasonal energy storage and allocation. Our study quantified variation in body condition and blood metabolites in two species of natricine snakes, with the expectation that values for both variables would be lower following brumation. During 2011-2015, we collected Thamnophis sirtalis and Thamnophis elegans from three sites within a montane valley wetland habitat and measured parameters of body condition, blood metabolites, and steroids as a function of year, sex, and season. We conducted radioimmunoassays to determine the concentrations of corticosterone and testosterone. Glucose and triglyceride levels were determined using standard assays. We found that body condition, but not corticosterone level, varied by season. Additionally, we detected changes in blood metabolites between Spring and Autumn. These results provide insight into how snakes store and allocate energy at a molecular level during energetically demanding events.
SSAR Siebert - Ecology, Physiology and Morphology
3163: The lower jaw is toothless in all frogs, with the notable exception of Gastrotheca guentheri (Guenther’s marsupial frog), a species that re-evolved true mandibular teeth. Frogs evolved a spectrum of dietary preferences, with some species specializing in hunting small insects like ants and termites to larger species that are opportunistic predators of small mammals. Such vast dietary variation could possibly drive the morphology of lower jaws. Frogs also occupy diverse ecological niches. For example, tree frogs from South America spend their entire lives in the upper canopy of trees, species of African aquatic frogs spend the majority of their life underwater, and some desert frogs live entirely underground, only coming to the surface to breed. Microhabitat differences may also influence jaw shapes due to variability in the types of prey available. A few frogs have tooth-like bony projections on the lower jaw called odontoid fangs. Some of these fanged frogs are among the largest anuran species and known to prey on other vertebrates. Additionally, some fanged frogs take part in male-male combat during the mating season, using their odontoids to bite one another. Currently, it is unknown if the lower jaw morphology of frogs is influenced by diet, microhabitat variation, or presence of odontoid fangs. Our study uses micro-computed tomography data and three-dimensional geometric morphometrics to quantify shape diversity of the lower jaw from 150 frog species. Using phylogenetic comparative methods, we are testing if jaw shape is correlated with diet, microhabitat, fang presence, and body size to understand the factors driving lower jaw morphology across living frog diversity.
SSAR Siebert - Ecology, Physiology and Morphology
3164: The relationship between organisms and their climate is complex, and it is influenced by hydrothermal physiology, behavior and evolutionary history. Microclimatic variation at a local scale provides a variety of conditions that animals can select, influencing selective pressures that act on physiology, particularly for small ectotherms such as anurans. One of the major sources of microclimatic variation in forested environments is provided by trees because temperature and humidity vary vastly along the ground-to-canopy axis. Therefore, arboreal habits and microhabitat selection will influence the selective pressures that act on physiological traits. To investigate how vertical microhabitat use mediates the evolution of physiological traits, I have collected detailed eco-physiological data of frogs in five localities across four years in the Amazon and Atlantic Forest of Brazil. I obtained critical thermal limits, dehydration and rehydration rates for multiple species of frogs and used phylogenetic comparative methods to investigate how arboreality mediates the evolution of physiological traits to different climatic regimes.
SSAR Siebert - Ecology, Physiology and Morphology
3165: Organophosphorus pesticides were created with the intent to inhibit the nervous systems of insect pests, to decrease their numbers from impacting agriculture or spreading disease. Due to their widespread use, pesticides can be found in nature at varying concentrations including the habitats of many amphibians. Malathion is a common organophosphorus pesticide that causes seizures, nausea, and even death in non-target organisms exposed to acute concentrations. However, exposures to low and more environmentally realistic concentrations are less well studied. In this study, we wanted to better understand the impacts of environmentally realistic concentrations of organophosphates on amphibians after a chronic exposure. To do this, we exposed Northern Leopard Frog (Lithobates [Rana] pipiens) tadpoles to either a vehicle control. 1 μg/L of malathion, or 10 μg/L of malathion for approximately three weeks in a blind, controlled laboratory study. We found changes in behavior, brain morphology, and gut morphology in tadpoles exposed to the organophosphates. By gaining a better understanding of how environmental pollutants impact tadpole development, we may be more likely to improve how we apply pesticides and help conserve herpetofauna worldwide.
SSAR Siebert - Ecology, Physiology and Morphology
3166: An unexplored dimension of biological invasions is the impact of acoustic interference among invasive and native anurans. Vocalizations by invasive frogs may result in attraction by heterospecifics if there are acoustic similarities to their conspecific signals. To gain insights into consequences of interactions between native and invasive species’ calls, we conducted field experiments in playback arenas that focused on acoustical overlap between calls of invasive American Bullfrogs (Rana catesbeiana) and native Chiricahua Leopard Frogs (Rana chiricahuensis). We found both female and male R. chiricahuensis showed positive phonotaxis to calls of R. catesbeiana. When given a choice, both sexes of R. chiricahuensis chose their conspecific call over the heterospecific call. However, their frequency of positive phonotaxis towards their conspecific call decreased when exposed to both heterospecific and conspecific calls simultaneously rather than sequentially. Female R. catesbeiana expressed mostly random movements in the phonotactic arena. However, male R. catesbeiana did express a phonotactic response to vocalizations of R. chiricahuensis. The attraction to the invasive bullfrogs’ calls could increase encounters between R. chiricahuensis and R. catesbeiana. This may in turn increase the native frogs’ susceptibility to predation by the invasive species. Reproductive costs to R. chiricahuensis, such as wasted energy or changes in mate choice, are other potential consequences. Thus, our findings may be one mechanism behind the pattern of extirpation of R. chiricahuensis following the arrival of R. catesbeiana.
SSAR Siebert - Ecology, Physiology and Morphology
3167: Squamates show tremendous variation in precloacal vertebral number, ranging from just 14 in Brookesia chameleons to nearly 400 in some snakes. Some evidence suggests that both ecological and developmental-genetic factors might influence vertebral counts, but the relative importance of these and other drivers of this variation across squamates remains poorly known. We tested how body size and habitat may explain variation in vertebral number between and within squamate clades. We predicted that vertebral counts within elongate clades would largely be explained by body size. In contrast, we predicted that vertebral number would be largely conserved in non-elongate clades, with changes associated with ecological differences or drift. We counted vertebrae from radiographs of museum specimens and supplemented these data from the primary literature to compile vertebral numbers for 2,360 species spanning the squamate phylogeny. Phylogenetic history explained a large proportion of the variance in vertebral number within clades, more so in lizards than in snakes. Size and habitat also explained a small proportion of variance in elongate clades, although there was still considerable unexplained variance. Vertebral number in amphisbaenians and blind snakes differs from patterns observed in other elongate clades, showing little influence of body size or phylogenetic history. Miniaturization or greater reliance on tunnel concertina locomotion may explain the decoupling between vertebrae and body size in these groups. Taken together, our results indicate a surprising complexity to vertebral evolution and we find little evidence that any single factor affects vertebral variation consistently across all squamates.
SSAR Siebert - Ecology, Physiology and Morphology
3168: Introduced species often occur within habitats similar to those of their native range (i.e., niche conservatism), but invasive populations occasionally exploit novel portions of their fundamental multidimensional niche space. The plasticity of an organism’s realized niche (i.e., niche divergence) tends to be more common among aquatic and semi-aquatic invasive species, and seems to occur independent of an organism’s lifespan and time since introduction. Spectacled Caimans (Caiman crocodilus) are unique among crocodilians in that they have established populations outside of their native range, and can frequently be encountered in Cuba, Puerto Rico, and Florida. The objective of our research is to determine whether the climatic niche of Spectacled Caimans within their introduced range has diverged from that of their native populations. Incorporating long-term climatic data associated with verified localities of native and introduced Spectacled Caimans, we used multidimensional hypervolume analysis to determine the degree of overlap and/or divergence (a) between native and introduced populations of caimans and (b) among the three areas where Spectacled Caimans have established outside their native range. By identifying whether this plastic species exhibits climatic niche conservation or divergence within areas of establishment, we can validate habitat suitability models that predict areas within the southeastern USA that might be vulnerable to establishment of additional crocodilian species.
SSAR Siebert - Ecology, Physiology and Morphology
3169: Overfishing, coastal habitat degradation, and climate change are altering marine food webs and interfering with ecosystem function. The declining abundances of preferred prey species may force predators to adopt increasingly generalist consumption strategies and incorporate novel resources. Tiger sharks (Galeocerdo cuvier) are a circumtropical coastal apex predator with a reputation for being indiscriminate generalists despite morphological adaptations specialized for preying upon sea turtles. We investigated tiger shark diet around Biscayne Bay, Florida, USA—where sea turtles are afforded protection under the Endangered Species Act—using DNA metabarcoding of minimally invasive cloacal swabs and opportunistically sampled regurgitated stomach contents. We identified a diverse assemblage of prey species with high taxonomic resolution and confidence belonging to at least 7 teleost families (Scombridae, Carangidae, Sphyraenidae, Mugilidae, Tetraodontidae, Haemulidae, and Echeneidae) and one elasmobranch genus (Carcharhinus). We also identified one species of seabird, the double-crested cormorant (Phalacrocorax auritus). Cloacal swabs yielded fewer taxa than stomach contents but proved a successful minimally invasive method of collecting prey DNA from large-bodied sharks. Overall, these results support the classification of tiger sharks as generalist predators that feed across a range of trophic guilds and coastal habitats. This consumption strategy may initially have been driven by historic declines in sea turtle populations but potentially now confers an evolutionary advantage in the face of anthropogenically destabilized coastal food webs.
3170: The use of nursery habitat by many elasmobranch species improves the growth and survival of juveniles, including young-of-year (YOY) bull sharks (Carcharhinus leucas). Identification and proper management of nursery habitat are essential, as sharks support healthy marine ecosystems through top-down effects and nutrient transport. Systematic frameworks for defining shark nursery habitat have been established in the literature; however many areas suspected as nursery habitat remain unevaluated according to such frameworks. Further, studies demonstrate that increasing water temperatures have altered the habitat ranges of many shark species, including the locations of historical nursery sites. The Alabama Gulf coast is home to Mobile Bay, a suspected bull shark nursery experiencing increasing annual water temperatures. Here, we employed a long-term fisheries-independent dataset to assess the entire coastline of Alabama, which includes the eastern Mississippi Sound, Mobile Bay, and western Perdido Bay, as YOY bull shark nursery habitat across multiple timescales (i.e. from 2004-2023 and in 5-year-increments). From 2004-2023 and 2014-2018, the entire Mobile Bay region of the coastline satisfied nursery habitat criteria. However, only lower Mobile Bay satisfied all nursery habitat criteria in 2009-2013 and only upper Mobile Bay did so in 2019-2023. From 2004-2008, no portion of the Alabama coastline satisfied all criteria. As changing habitat conditions persist, these results showcase the spatiotemporally-dynamic nature of nearshore bull shark nurseries and may be useful for understanding distributions of future shark populations.
3171:
The diverse reproductive strategies of elasmobranchs pose an unknown cost to pregnant females from the 1) provisioning of nutrients and 2) physiological and physical changes throughout gestation. Matrotrophic elasmobranch species that secrete lipid histotroph invest greatly into the post-fertilization and pre-parturition period.

Seventeen mature female Hypanus sabinus (220-320 mm) were collected with seines the first week of April 2024 along the Florida State University Coastal and Marine Laboratory coastline (IACUC PROTO20230000004). Pregnancy was confirmed through ultrasonography (PAL HD3 Phased and Linear Array). Specimens were housed in Florida State University Coastal and Marine Laboratory facility tanks for five months at 26°C (±1) and trials conducted every three to four weeks (N = 13). Dissolved oxygen was recorded over a 24-hour trial period then converted to average standard metabolic rate (SMR). Preliminary analysis shows a rapid drop in SMR from late-stage gestation to parturition and significant differences in SMR between the late gestation and post-partum period. Full analysis will be presented in full to test for an energetic and physical cost to lipid histotrophic gestation and identify the most vulnerable gestational stages.

Gravid H. Sabinus were also collected between April and August 2023 and euthanized (IACUC PROTO20230000004). Histotroph samples (N = 43) were collected through the puncture of uterine cavities with a sterile scalpel and fluid removed using a 0.5 mL syringe and stored at -80°C. Total protein and total lipid content were quantified through Bradford Protein Assay and Folch Modified Protocol. Total Energetic Content was quantified through Chemical Oxygen Demand Assay Kits. Fatty Acid Species and Protein components were identified through LC-MS to identify key biochemicals that contribute to embryonic development in matrotrophic species. This comparative study will compare biochemical contents of intrauterine fluids that support embryonic development in species with various reproductive strategies and identify how biochemical content changes through gestion in one individual. Overall, both studies will assess the cost of supporting a successful pregnancy while identifying how this varies inter- and intra-specifically.
3172: Intertidal reef flats serve as communal nurseries for juvenile stingrays, where they perform important roles as mesopredators and ecosystem engineers; however, contributions to ecosystem processes can vary among species. We investigated the foraging behaviours of three stingrays: the cowtail stingray (Pastinachus ater), mangrove whipray (Urogymnus granulatus), and pink whipray (Pateobatis fai) at Pioneer Bay, Orpheus Island. Individual rays were followed using drones for 7-18 minutes (mean = 13.5) at heights of 3-5 m, and details were recorded for each feeding event. Analysis of 96 behavioural tracks revealed distinct foraging tactics among the three species. Cowtail stingrays and mangrove whiprays fed more frequently at low tides than high tides, which may reflect changes in prey availability across the tidal gradient or increased predation risk with depth. Cowtail stingrays and pink whiprays preferred foraging on smooth sand using nondisruptive feeding behaviours, although cowtail stingrays also used intense excavation feeding more often than other species. In contrast, mangrove whiprays showed greater preferences for coral rubble substrates and alternated between surface and suction feeding. Although findings support resource partitioning and species-specific functional roles, further works are needed to effectively link diets, prey distributions, and specific foraging behaviours, and to quantify functional outputs at the species level.
3173: Recently, there has been increasing use of baited remote underwater video (BRUV) surveys for assessing shark and fish populations in marine ecosystems. This approach may provide a non-destructive, non-extractive, and cost-effective alternative to traditional fishing-based methods. However, to date, most studies using BRUVs have focused on their use in high-visibility ecosystems, such as tropical reefs. Furthermore, few studies have compared results from BRUV surveys with those obtained using traditional methods to evaluate the efficacy of this approach. Therefore, the goal of this study was to evaluate the effectiveness of using BRUV surveys to assess shark and fish populations in low-visibility ecosystems. This goal was addressed by conducting BRUVs and bottom longline surveys in the Tolomato River, a northeast Florida estuary that has been shown to serve as a communal nursery habitat for juveniles from multiple coastal shark species including sandbar (Carcharhinus plumbeus) and scalloped hammerhead (Sphyrna lewini). Surveys were compared using metrics of both abundance and diversity. Results of this study found that BRUV and longline surveys sampled different portions of the community and BRUV surveys were able to detect a greater number of species, including some that are not sampled using a longline survey in this system. However, longline surveys produced greater sample sizes, greater abundance estimates, and provided more information on shark populations, compared to BRUV surveys. While BRUV surveys did not provide similar data to longline surveys, especially regarding abundance estimates, they may work as a useful tool to provide insight into community ecology.
3174: The Rainbow characin is a freshwater fish endemic to western Ecuador and northern Peru, comprising two species: Rhoadsia minor and R. altipinna. Due to their morphological similarity, these species are primarily distinguished by geography: R. minor in northwestern Ecuador and R. altipinna in central and southern Ecuador and Peru. Previous analyses revealed genetic distinctiveness corresponding to these distributions, along with evidence of admixture and within-species population structure using twelve microsatellites and two mitochondrial genes. While these markers have proven effective in population genetic studies, they represent only a small fraction of the genome, potentially introducing bias into the results. We used Restriction-site Associated DNA Sequencing (RADseq), which analyzes thousands of genomic markers, to reassess the species status and population structure of the Rainbow Characin in western Ecuador. Our results were largely consistent with earlier findings, including evidence of admixture at the species range boundaries. However, low phylogenetic resolution for separation from the inferred maximum likelihood tree casts doubts on the separation of the two species. Further exploration is needed to clarify their systematics, including ecological differences, breeding compatibility, and potential reproductive preferences.
3175: The relative contributions of spatial and temporal scales to ecosystem variation is an area of focus in ecology. Most stream fish monitoring programs rely on data from single snapshots (e.g., one year) taken during a single time of year. Whether or not these snapshots are reflective of broader temporal variation is rarely tested. We surveyed stream fish assemblages at longitudinally distributed locations in the San Saba River and the Llano River multiple times at two temporal scales. Surveys included annual samples of each site during the summers of 2021, 2023, and 2024 (i.e., annual scale), and season samples of each site during March, May, June, July, and November of 2024 (i.e., seasonal scale). We used standardized seining protocols during each survey, and we identified and counted all fishes collected. We used permuted multivariate analysis of similarity and square root-transformed abundance data to test for temporal differences in assemblage structure at the annual and seasonal scales. Results revealed no significant difference in assemblage structure among years or seasons for the six sites included in the analysis. These findings suggest that inference gained from a single survey is representative of broader seasonal and annual time scales. Our results support loose equilibrium theory that fish assemblages remain within some bounds around a central tendency with temporal fluxes in species abundances. However, we identify potential directional change which may eventually push assemblages outside of loose equilibrium. We suggest long-term monitoring programs be established in regions where future change is expected.
3176: The Polochic-Cahabón Area of Endemism (AoE) is located in northern Central America, and comprises seven river basins across eastern Guatemala and southern Belize. It includes a large lake system, and numerous rivers, showing environmental heterogeneity in habitats and freshwater connectivity. Notably, the assemblage of freshwater fishes is not homogeneously distributed across the AoE. To assess the relationship between distribution of freshwater fishes and environmental heterogeneity across the Polochic-Cahabón AoE, we took a comparative approach in which we focused on the families Cichlidae and Poeciliidae, which dominate the regional species pool. We hypothesized that beta-diversity is higher for poeciliids compared to cichlids, as the former has a higher number of endemics for this AoE. To test our hypothesis we used species distribution models to understand the patterns in distribution of species richness and turnover across the AoE. A total of 16 species of poeciliids, and 13 cichlids are recorded from the area. Our results highlight contrasting distributional patterns between the two families. For cichlids, the highest species richness was predicted in the lowest reaches of rivers and shoreline of Lago de Izabal. Conversely, the predicted distribution of the species richness of poeciliids recovered a widespread distribution in the area, tightly associated with riverine habitats. Beta-diversity shows that species turnover correlates to habitat transitions. However, we found a greater assemblage turnover when comparing headwaters to the lake shorelines, with a larger effect in Poeciliidae. Present-day distribution of freshwater fish diversity in the Lago de Izabal basin responds to environmental factors.
3177: The luring apparatus of anglerfishes and their allies (Acanthuriformes: Lophioidei) comprises the esca, illicium, and associated pterygiophore, all derived from modifications of the first dorsal fin spine. These structures, used for prey attraction and potentially interspecies communication, exhibit remarkable diversity in size, morphology, and function across the infraorder. Our phylogenetic character state reconstruction revealed that the common ancestor of the Lophioidei possessed a purely mechanical lure, with chemical lures evolving independently twice and bioluminescent lures evolving once. Taxa inhabiting pelagic environments and those with bioluminescent lures exhibited significantly larger luring structures and higher diversification rates compared to other luring types. Our results suggest that bioluminescent lures, which are widespread among deep-sea anglerfishes, may serve dual purposes: attracting prey and facilitating sexual communication with parasitic male counterparts. Additionally, we identified habitat-related variation in the rotational range of lures: taxa from shallower waters (≤200 m) and extreme depths (3000–6000 m) showed restricted rotational ranges, while midwater taxa (200–3000 m) displayed more diverse ranges. These patterns may reflect ecological adaptations, such as optimizing lure visibility in deep-sea environments or enabling species-specific communication among ceratioid anglerfishes. Despite limitations in directly observing luring behaviors in anglerfishes and their allies, this study demonstrates the utility of museum specimens in investigating evolutionary transitions and inferring behavior. Our findings highlight the need for further observational and experimental research, particularly on deep-sea taxa, to refine our understanding of the functional and evolutionary dynamics of anglerfish luring mechanisms.
3178: The Neotropics have been recovered as a single biogeographic unit for freshwater fishes in global studies. Several analyses have identified subregions of biogeographic significance within the northern Neotropics and the core Neotropical region in South America. In contrast, the Neotropical islands of the Greater Antilles (GA), have received less attention. Building on the assumption that the islands of the GA do not function as single independent biogeographic unit, we test whether: 1) each island do possess a unique fish assemblage, 2) biogeographic structure can be identified within the GA at the scale of river basins, and 3) if patterns of community assemblages and genetic structure are congruent within islands. Our analyses support our hypothesis that the region is not a single biogeographic unit. Instead, it consists of multiple subregions of biogeographic significance, where river basins from the same island are more similar to each other than to basins from other islands, with Hispaniola as the only exception. Additionally, our analyses identified various areas of endemism within Cuba, Hispaniola, and Jamaica. A tight interplay between the region’s geological history and a diverse array of life-history traits, colonization events, and in-situ speciation events likely contributed to the observed patterns. Our research provides the first fine-scale analysis to help understand GA freshwater fishes' biogeographical patterns in over three decades, compiling the largest dataset on the distribution of this group to date. Altogether, we aim for these efforts to inform conservation planning and management actions in these biologically rich yet vulnerable islands.
3179: Body shape is a fundamental metric of functional diversity among taxa across the tree of life. For aquatic animals, body shape and size strongly affect physiology and behavior, and are excellent predictors of many ecological and life history traits, evolutionary patterns, and conservation threats. Fishes represent excellent materials to study how whole-body phenotypes, like shape and size, affect ecological dynamics, spatial distributions, and conservation decisions. Here, we applied 3D photogrammetry, PCA, and geometric morphometrics to study shape variance in freshwater fishes. We created digital 3D models representing 645 (72%) species and 105 (92%) families from 26 river basins of North and Central America. We then created a 3D morphospace to quantify body-shape disparity across taxa, basins, and climate zones. All the top PCs are complex, including shape variables from several landmarks. The major trends are elongation and flatfish asymmetry on PC1, body depth on PC2, and body width across several top PCs. Shape differences due to preservation artifacts are minimal due to the effective unbending and preparation of digital models before PCA. The morphospace margins are delimited entirely by Marine-Derived Lineages (MDLs). The morphospace taxonomic composition at the species and genus level is dominated by Mississippi Basin Fauna (MBF), and peripheral basins have a higher proportion of endemic and MDL taxa. Species composition and morphospace occupation are correlated with geographic distance from the Mississippi Basin center of diversity.   These data support the concept of an “MBF vacuum,” contributing to the structure of body shape disparity among North American fishes.
3180: Family Alestidae constitutes the most species-rich clade of African Characiformes. Therefore, understanding the phylogenetic relationships within this family is critical for advancing our knowledge and the conservation of biodiversity in African freshwater ecosystems. This study describes a new genus in Alestidae and explores speciation in the Kouilou and Ogooué rivers, offering novel insights into the historical biogeography of West-Central Africa. Using 1,759 nuclear ultraconserved elements (UCEs) and complete mitochondrial genomes of 38 representatives from all alestid lineages, we conducted likelihood and species tree inferences, as well as Bayesian time-calibrated and parametric biogeographical analyses. Our molecular phylogenetic analyses support the polyphyly of Brachypetersius and Nannopetersius, revealing that certain species classified within these genera form a novel clade (genus): referred to here as the ‘Brachypetersius’ gabonensis clade. Morphometric, meristic, and microcomputed tomography (µCT) analyses of 139 museum specimens further distinguish it by having more outer dentary teeth than Brachypetersius and fewer predorsal scales than Nannopetersius. Additionally, molecular data and µCT scans identifying three novel morphological traits support the revalidation of subfamily Clupeocharacinae, comprising eight genera from West and Central Africa. Time-calibrated analyses reveal that the new genus diverged during the Early Miocene (23–15 mya), suggesting the influence of geological events and potential river captures between Lower Guinea and Lower Congo drainages. Ancestral range reconstruction further elucidates the biogeography of this genus, highlighting how the geological history of the Kouilou and Ogooué rivers has influenced speciation. These findings enhance our understanding of the evolutionary processes shaping alestid diversity in coastal West-Central Africa.
3181: Color polymorphic species, where multiple color morphs coexist within the same interbreeding population, are extremely common in nature. In the salamander genus Plethodon, at least ten species exhibit a striped/unstriped color polymorphism, while closely related species are fixed for either morph. In a single species, the Eastern Red-backed Salamander (Plethodon cinereus), previous work has indicated that morphs may diverge in climatic niche space. However, the magnitude and direction of color morph-climate associations has varied across studies. Further, little research has examined the relationship between climate and color morph in the nine other color polymorphic Plethodon. Here, I scored color phenotypes from >65,000 web-based georeferenced community science images of color polymorphic Plethodon. With this extensive color morph dataset, I quantified the climatic niche of each species and their color morphs when applicable and utilized a comparative approach to examine patterns of climatic niche overlap, niche breadth, and potential responses to future climate change.
3182: Biofluorescence has recently emerged as a widespread phenomenon in amphibians, including the most speciose family of salamanders (Plethodontidae). Modified granular glands (MGGs), a distinct type of skin gland, have been hypothesized to be the source of biofluorescence in woodland salamanders (genus Plethodon), but this has yet to be confirmed and the function of biofluorescence remains unknown. In this study, we used a variety of microscopy and behavioral techniques to evaluate the morphology and function of biofluorescent skin glands (BFGs) in the red-legged salamander Plethodon shermani. We found that BFGs are synonymous with MGGs and are concentrated mainly in the ventral trunk and tail. BFGs are sexually dimorphic in size, with males having larger glands than females, but not in number. Further, BFGs resemble antipredator granular glands in their morphology, possessing a continuous myoepithelial sheath surrounding syncytial secretory compartments. Confocal microscopy revealed that BFGs possess a histologically-distinct sub-compartment and that the intensity of emitted fluorescence is not sexually dimorphic. Finally, BFGs did not appear to play a visual role during courtship and did not secrete during scent-marking or in response to electrical stimulation. Our results provide the first dedicated morphological and functional evaluation of biofluorescent skin glands in salamanders and reveal that the function of BFGs may be elusive and nuanced. We propose that BFGs may no longer serve a secretory role, instead serving as an honest signal of individual quality or as nutrient-storage organs. Our results also establish BFGs as a complex glandular system in need of further study.
3183: Traditional mark-recapture methods, though valuable for estimating population size, survival rates, and movement patterns, often rely on invasive techniques that may harm the animals being studied or affect their natural behaviors. To address this, non-invasive alternatives such as photo-recognition software have been developed, particularly for large mammals. However, in recent years, its use for smaller more cryptic species has been investigated, though mostly in the lab. This study investigates the efficacy of photo-recognition on small cryptic species in a field setting using Hotspotter, a photo-recognition software, and the lesser siren (Siren intermedia) across three manmade ponds. Using Passive Integrated Transponder (PIT) tags as redundant marks, we analyzed the software’s ability to match individuals over two seasons (2023 and 2024). False Acceptance Rate (FAR) and False Rejection Rate (FRR) were calculated to assess the accuracy of HotSpotter across different ponds. Results demonstrated a strong matching ability, with overall FAR at 1.6% and FRR at 5.5% with the majority of the false rejections occurring in a single pond. However, matching accuracy decreased over time, particularly for individuals recaptured after extended periods. Our findings suggest that while HotSpotter is a promising tool for short-term studies, time between captures can impact its long-term reliability. The integration of redundant PIT-tag marking provided an effective solution to mitigate these limitations. This study highlights the potential of photo-recognition software as a non-invasive alternative for mark-recapture studies of small cryptic species, offering a cost-effective and ethical method for population monitoring.
3184:
Oviposition site selection plays a crucial role in offspring survival and, consequently, adult reproductive success. While this behavior has significant conservation implications, the specific factors influencing oviposition site selection in many amphibian species remain poorly understood. In this study, we examine the role of habitat and microhabitat characteristics in shaping oviposition site selection in Indosylvirana indica, a stream-dwelling ranid frog endemic to the central Western Ghats of India.

To assess whether site selection is non-random, we conducted field surveys across three streams in Sirsi Taluk, Uttara Kannada district, Karnataka. We compared habitat and microhabitat features between 64 plots containing egg clutches and 91 plots without clutches. Our findings indicate that I. indica shows a preference for oviposition sites in streams bordered by forested patches rather than those adjacent to plantations or agricultural areas. Among the environmental variables analyzed, water depth, distance from the stream edge, and water temperature significantly influenced site selection. However, factors such as water velocity and substrate composition did not have a notable impact.

Our results suggest that I. indica females exhibit selective oviposition behavior, preferring warm, shallow waters away from the stream margins, particularly in areas with intact forest cover. These findings provide valuable insights into the reproductive ecology of I. indica and highlight the importance of conserving riparian forest habitats to support amphibian populations. Understanding the environmental factors driving oviposition site selection can aid in the development of more effective conservation strategies.
3185: The southeastern Coastal Plain has experienced widespread loss of pine savanna habitats, including the degradation of seasonal geographically isolated wetlands (GIWs). While previous management efforts have primarily focused on restoring upland habitats, this approach may only partially benefit species that depend on wetlands to complete their lifecycles. GIWs are crucial habitat for the reproduction of many common and rare amphibians including the State-threatened Gopher frog (Rana capito). Recently, agencies are focusing resources on restoring the plant community composition and structure, hydrology, and disturbance regimes of GIWs for priority species. We used acoustic recording devices and dipnet surveys to conduct post-restoration amphibian monitoring of 53 restored and non-restored wetlands among four managed landscapes in Georgia. Vegetation monitoring data was used to characterize pre- and post-restoration conditions. We used an integrated Bayesian community occupancy model to estimate amphibian occupancy probability across varying wetland restoration conditions. We predicted that amphibian occupancy would generally increase with canopy openness and emergent herbaceous abundance but vary among species. Among restored wetlands, we predicted that those managed with canopy thinning and prescribed fire would have the lowest woody plant cover, highest herbaceous abundance, and highest amphibian occupancy and richness. Additionally, we expect occupancy to have a time lag after restoration depending on wetland isolation, terrestrial habitat abundance, and vegetation management intensity. Our results will highlight the importance of integrating species-specific management strategies into restoration efforts, informing the need for additional management actions like animal translocations, while emphasizing the application of adaptive management and monitoring principles.
3186: Antipredator traits are often the focus of studies of the impact of urbanization on wildlife, yet this global threat likely has impacts on other fitness-relevant traits, including those that may contribute to variation in escape behavior itself. We addressed these considerations using adult ornate tree lizard (Urosaurus ornatus) populations across six sites in Tucson, Arizona, representing low, mid, and high levels of urbanization. We measured escape behavior (flight-initiation and flight distances), sprint performance (maximum speed and speed variance), and morphology (body size, limb lengths, and toe lengths). On the surface, while urbanization appeared to affect morphology and performance, antipredator behavior remained unchanged across the gradient. To further explore the impact of urbanization on underlying trait relationships, we used path models for each urban level. At low-urban sites, morphology, performance, and behavior were all positively linked: effectively, larger lizards sprinted faster and exhibited greater escape distances. At mid-urban sites, however, morphology and performance were unlinked, and faster lizards exhibited shorter escape distances. And, at high-urban sites, only morphology and performance were positively associated, supporting that larger lizards were faster, but these relationships were not tied to their escape behavior. Collectively, our results suggest that urbanization alters how morphology, performance, and behavior interact, not just behavior (or the other traits) alone. Our findings contribute to growing evidence that urbanization produces complex, sometimes hidden effects on wildlife. They highlight the need for more integrative approaches to understand how urban environments shape organisms beyond antipredator responses alone.
3187: Floating aquatic vegetation and algal blooms are expected to increase with climate change, reducing UVB exposure and vitamin D synthesis in freshwater turtles. Vitamin D is crucial for calcium metabolism and reptile health, yet its response to floating vegetation remains unclear. We quantified vitamin D3 levels in the blood of adult female painted turtles (Chrysemys picta) exposed to either high vegetation or clear water outdoors for one month, followed by another month indoors under similar conditions during the Fall. A marginal reduction was observed in the vegetation treatment by day 60 but disappeared after multiple corrections, suggesting that adult females are robust to the effect of floating vegetation. However, further research across various seasons, sexes, and age groups is warranted to determine painted turtles’ resilience in their vitamin D levels affected by floating vegetation. We also examined how floating vegetation influences turtle habitat preferences. We hypothesized that turtles would avoid areas with vegetation cover, preferring clearer waters that maximize basking duration for vitamin D synthesis. To test this hypothesis, we assessed female habitat preferences exposed to an artificial pond partitioned into clear-water and high-vegetation sections and later in tanks indoors at two temperatures. Results revealed that turtles prefer vegetation-covered habitats, suggesting that the benefits of floating vegetation may outweigh the costs of reduced UVB exposure. These findings provide new insights into turtle habitat selection and highlight the complex interplay between habitat features and environmental change, offering valuable implications for conservation management.
3188: Cryptic polymorphism can bias tests of phenotypic variation across space and time. Because many colors exist outside the range of human perception, color variation is not always easily detected even when it plays an important role in organismal biology. In lizards, ultraviolet (UV) color is often associated with aggressiveness and resource acquisition, but its dynamics across space and time are less well known. To test among factors structuring UV color variation, we captured 771 wall lizards (Podarcis erhardii), a color polymorphic species, across 35 islands in the Greek Cyclades and examined how UV traits vary across habitats, predator communities, and lizard densities. We discovered new evidence for a cryptic, low-UV phenotype whose presence varies from absent to being fixed within several islands. We did not find any correlation among predator presence, island-wide environmental variables, and UV phenotype. However, we did find that on islands with mixed-UV phenotypes, higher-UV individuals are more likely to occupy greener, moister areas. Evidence for microhabitat partitioning in mixed-morph populations suggests that UV phenotypes may be under natural selection at the local scale. We also found that lizards on low-UV islands are significantly larger than in mixed- and high-UV populations. Our results suggest that the presence of a cryptic UV morph may have novel ecological implications for our understanding of wall lizard social dynamics and evolution.
3189: The mechanisms allowing the coexistence of cryptic species have long puzzled ecologists. Cryptic species have nearly identical morphology and, therefore, would be presumed to have high niche overlap and potential for interspecific competition and competitive exclusion when resources are limited. Lowland rivers in South America have hundreds of coexisting fish species, with certain congeneric species having nearly identical functional morphology. Here, we compare key niche dimensions of Cichla cataractae and C. ocellaris, piscivorous cichlids that have nearly identical morphology and coexist in the Essequibo River Basin in the Guiana Shield region of South America. Data were collected on spatial distribution, habitat use, and diet to estimate niche overlap. Field research was conducted during the dry season when habitat and food resources are most limited, and competition is predicted to be the greatest. The two species were found to have high dietary overlap but negligible overlap in habitat use. Cichla cataractae almost exclusively inhabited rocky shoals located in river channels, whereas C. ocellaris occurred mostly within lentic habitats in the floodplain and near-shore areas of channels. This high degree of niche segregation contrasts with the assumption that phenotypic similarity should yield similar niches.
3190: Human actions are one of the most prominent drivers of local and global ecological change. One of the biggest anthropogenic modifiers of freshwater environments are human-made dams. While dams are a ubiquitous part of human infrastructure, they also significantly alter stream ecology, disrupting lotic environments and imposing barriers to upstream breeding habitats for migrating fish. Studying fish populations in watersheds impacted by damming provides a unique opportunity to ascertain the effects of these ecological changes and understand how anthropogenic actions impact vulnerable populations. We conducted a morphological comparison of anadromous steelhead trout, Oncorhynchus mykiss, along the South Fork Eel River. Utilizing museum specimens, we used geometric morphometric analyses to quantify shape differences across temporal and spatial scales around a human-made barrier, Benbow Dam. We find that lateral body shape varies both temporally and spatially, though shape differences cannot be explained by dam presence alone. Overall trends reveal similar levels of morphological disparity before and during Benbow Dam’s presence (temporal comparison), and differences in head shape between specimens collected above and below the dam (spatial comparison). Current research leverages 3D geometric morphometrics of high resolution microCT data to further understand morphological variation across these comparisons, particularly within the cranial region. A focused 3D interrogation of skeletal regions containing prominent 2D variation—specifically the cranium, orbit, preoperculum, and cleithrum—will allow for a rigorous methodological comparison between a non-lethal, field-deployable method and a more data-rich lab method to quantify internal structure.
3191: The Blunt-nosed Leopard Lizard (Gambelia sila) is an endangered species found in the San Joaquin Desert of California, USA, where much of its habitat has historically been converted for human land use. Remaining desert habitat is often impacted by roads, oil and gas extraction, and non-native grasses, and will likely be threatened with further degradation by climate change. Here, we examined how space use and activity of lizards was associated with drought and non-drought years and differed between a site with ample perennial shrubs and one with no shrubs. We radio-tracked 154 lizards when they were most active from May–July over four years (2018–2021), during which annual precipitation and temperature varied. We calculated minimum convex polygons and autocorrelated kernel densities to estimate space use across all years and at both sites. Males consistently had greater estimates of space use than females, consistent with earlier explanations that mate searching contributes to greater space use in male lizards. Estimates of space use were also greater in non-drought years than drought years (95% MCP of 0.57 ha versus 2.0 ha), and in the shrubbed habitat than in the habitat with fewer shrubs (95% MCP of 1.82 ha versus 0.71 ha), irrespective of sex. We suspect that the need for lizards to manage body temperatures and minimize the risk of over-heating and desiccation likely resulted in reduced activity that led to the smaller estimates of space use.
3192: 30% of North American minnow species engage in nest association, and current hypotheses indicate it is mutualistic with reduced egg predation risk through a dilution effect. While the nests confer safety to the eggs, the conspicuous adults are also susceptible to predation while in mixed species spawning aggregations. The skin of all North American minnows contain club cells that release an alarm cue (Schreckstoff ) which induces anti-predator responses in fish that detect it. Schreckstoff’s composition is species-specific, and while individuals typically have the strongest response to conspecific Schreckstoff, they can respond to heterospecific Schreckstoff. Through interspecific responses to Schreckstoff, nest association may also serve as an alarm system to reduce the threat of predation on adults. To investigate if nest association also serves as predator avoidance mechanism, we exposed spawning aggregations containing nest building Largescale Stoneroller (Campostoma oligolepis) and nest associating Southern Redbelly Dace (Chrosomus erythrogaster) to Schreckstoff from Southern Redbelly Dace and non-native Zebrafish (Danio rerio). We predicted that the nest building and associating species would have similarly intense fear responses to associate Schreckstoff and limited responses to non-native Schreckstoff. However, in our initial trials, spawning fishes did not respond to Schreckstoff, which may indicate a tradeoff between predator avoidance and reproduction. We conducted additional trials in and out of the spawning season to investigate this potential seasonal sensitivity to Schreckstoff. Preliminary findings indicate that non-reproductive aggregations have variable responses to both associate and non-associate Schreckstoff extracts.
3193: Physical armor is among the most widespread, diverse, and successful defensive adaptations in the tree of life. In fishes, thick dermal armor has arisen repeatedly, but is relatively uncommon in extant species. Among the exceptions are the marine family Agonidae (Poachers), featuring heavy coats of modified bony scales. Beyond their armor, many Agonids have noteworthy cranial appendages such as cirri and unusual bony processes. The Rockhead, Bothragonus swanii, features a uniquely strange skull with a large depression in the dorsal surface. This cavity takes up approximately as much cranial volume as the fish’s brain, and contains complex internal structures. Through a combination of optical microscopy and micro/nanoCT, we discovered significant innervation of the Rockhead’s cranial pit. This suggests it may function as a sensory organ. We discuss the pit’s purpose and expand on its role countering the tradeoffs of heavy armor in fishes.
ASIH Stoye - Genetics, Development, & Morphology I
3194: Environmental DNA (eDNA) is a powerful tool proving useful in detecting and monitoring  rare, threatened, and endangered species in both aquatic and terrestrial environments. Developing non-invasive methods, such as eDNA, is crucial for studying sensitive species in environments often difficult to access. The Floridan Aquifer System is home to many vulnerable species, including the Georgia Blind Cave Salamander (Eurycea wallacei), the Dougherty Plain Cave Crayfish (Cambarus cryptodytes), and many other species of conservation concern. These animals are difficult to access due to the need for specialized cave-diving skills or simply the physical barriers of submerged groundwater systems. These barriers leave researchers to rely on citizen diver’s accounts alone regarding the biodiversity residing in these caves. Environmental DNA provides a cost-effective, safer, and more feasible alternative to unveiling broad-scale biodiversity in hard-to-get-to habitats. The goal of this study was to determine if eDNA is a feasible method to categorize metazoan biodiversity, as well as compare active and passive sampling techniques at various levels of cave accessibility. In this study, we performed an eDNA field survey using both active and passive sampling techniques from seven locations within a cave system near Marianna, Florida, sampling at various horizontal distances from the cave entrance, including inside the cave, at the cave vent, and above the vent at the surface. A fragment of the cytochrome c oxidase subunit 1 (COI) gene was amplified using a metazoan primer set and submitted for Illumina sequencing. Biodiversity estimates, across different cave microhabitats, will be presented.
ASIH Stoye - Genetics, Development, & Morphology I
3195: Asexual lineages face higher extinction rates than sexual species, suggesting that asexual reproduction incurs significant fitness costs. One hypothesis explaining why sexual species outlive their asexual counterparts is Muller’s ratchet, which posits that without recombination and segregation, harmful mutations accumulate more readily in the genomes of asexual lineages. In this study, we tested Muller’s ratchet by estimating mutation accumulation in the hybrid-origin parthenogenetic lineage, Aspidoscelis tesselatus. We utilized RNAseq data for the parthenogenetic lineages and IsoSeq data for the parental species. Using this data, we constructed subgenomes based on phased haplotypes in A. tesselatus. We then estimated mutation accumulation by calculating dN/dS ratios between the parental and phased subgenomes, along with analyzing structural variants. We observed higher dN/dS ratios in both A. tesselatus subgenomes, indicating that the parthenogenetic species accumulates more nonsynonymous mutations than the parental species. Although the subgenomes did not show significant differences, there was variation in the dN/dS ratios among the haplotypes, suggesting the potential for haplotype-specific divergence. We also identified several indels in the transcriptomes that likely affect protein structure and function. Through functional annotation and mutation effect analyses, we characterized specific biological functions impacted by mutation accumulation, including protein-DNA organization, regulation of apoptosis, and gene expression regulation. Consequently, we found evidence that mutations accumulate in the parthenogenetic lineage, adversely affecting its fitness. This study demonstrates that not only do mutations accumulate in the parthenogenetic lineage, but they also influence protein function and individual fitness.
ASIH Stoye - Genetics, Development, & Morphology I
3196: Vocal communication, characterized by species-specific advertisement calls, is the primary mechanism of mate attraction in frogs and relies on a complex integration of vocal and auditory systems. However, some species have lost key structures in these systems, raising the question of how they communicate in their absence. We hypothesize that frog species with losses in the auditory and/or vocalization systems will have compensated through enhanced visual systems, specifically through enlargement of the eyes. To investigate this, we analyzed relative investment in eye and corneal size across 253 anuran species spanning all 55 recognized families, testing for correlations with six ecological traits, including for the first time, the condition of the auditory and vocalization systems. Contrary to our expectation that sensory losses would favour larger eyes, we found that increased investment was specific to corneal size, which showed significant enlargement independent of overall eye size, body size, or weight. Enlarged corneas enhance light capture and visual acuity but are expected to have a lower metabolic cost than larger eyes. Larger corneas in frogs with auditory and/or vocalizations loss likely and allow these frogs to rely more on vision for communication, navigation, and social interactions, while at the same time a minimizing metabolic costs in small animals that are already metabolically constrained. Our findings suggest that the visual system may play an adaptive role in response to the loss of auditory or vocal communication and introduce the condition of sensory systems as an important ecological factor shaping anuran evolution.
ASIH Stoye - Genetics, Development, & Morphology I
3197: Oncorhynchus mykiss is a recreationally and ecologically important salmonid species found along the Pacific Northwest coast, consisting of many genetically distinct subpopulations that can be resident in freshwater or anadromous. Eleven anadromous populations have received endangered species listings under the California Endangered Species Act and hatcheries have made great efforts to increase O. mykiss ocean-going populations. Throughout all life stages, olfaction aids in navigation, feeding, detecting social cues, prey and predators; however, it is particularly implicated in homing, helping anadromous O. mykiss return to natal streams. These behaviors are controlled by a small suite of chemoreceptor cells: ciliated, microvillous and crypt cells, each of which appeared abnormal in our initial studies of hatchery individuals, potentially due to chemical treatments during ontogeny. To distinguish hatchery from wild individuals, the adipose fin is clipped, so it is common practice to anesthetize hatchery-released O. mykiss using tricaine methanesulfonate (MS-222). There is little research on how MS-222 treatments might affect the delicate microstructures and anatomy of the olfactory rosette. I compared gross anatomical and ultrastructural differences between wild and hatchery-reared residents using histological serial sectioning of the olfactory rosette, microCT scanning and Transmission and Scanning Electron Microscopy of the surface and the interior of the olfactory epithelial tissue. Through controlled dosage of MS-222, I also observed the effects of anaesthesia on rosette structures. Determining whether rosette atrophy and immune responses in hatchery fish are due to MS-222 exposure vs. genetic abnormalities may have downstream implications for management of this culturally and economically important species.
ASIH Stoye - Genetics, Development, & Morphology I
3198: Extreme structural adaptations serve as valuable models to help answer a central question in functional morphology and biomechanics: How do novel behaviors evolve from existing structures? Some organisms have evolved highly specialized anatomical structures which increase the performance of a specific behavior. However, these structures can be co-opted for additional purposes, providing benefits to the organism beyond their primary role. Chameleons have evolved a unique feeding mechanism which allows them to ballistically project their tongue up to 250 percent of their body length to capture prey. Despite this extreme specialization, some chameleon species have been documented directly capturing certain prey items using only their jaws. We compared the feeding kinematics of ballistic tongue projection and direct prey capture in two chameleon species to determine whether direct prey capture is a co-optation of the ballistic tongue projection feeding strategy or if distinct behaviors can be performed despite the extreme specialization of the feeding mechanism. Our results confirm that during direct prey capture in chameleons, the jaw is contacting the prey item before the tongue, however, direct prey capture kinematics varies across chameleon species and prey types. Understanding how highly specialized structures evolve novel behaviors provides insight into the evolutionary flexibility of extreme systems and may illuminate whether the extreme specialization of the chameleon feeding system has necessitated the evolution of a novel feeding mechanism or if the mechanisms underlying the direct prey capture feeding strategy are conserved across iguanian families.
ASIH Stoye - Genetics, Development, & Morphology I
3199: In fisheries, depredation is the partial or complete removal of a hooked species by a non-target species. Depredation of targeted fish by sharks affects myriad fisheries in the United States (US) and globally. Fishers in the US are demanding action, but shark depredation is not just a US problem. Understanding how shark depredation is impacting fisheries elsewhere can provide important insights into mitigating this interaction in US waters. Building on 10 years of research in Australia, an international team conducted a comprehensive review of methods to mitigate shark depredation via a semi-quantitative ranking process. Using seven criteria (effectiveness, suitability across fishing sectors, cost to implement, impacts on target species, impacts on depredating sharks, impacts on non-target animals and impacts on the environment), ninety mitigation methods were identified and ranked. These methods were then presented to fisheries stakeholders at ten workshops in Western Australia, the Northern Territory, Queensland and New South Wales. Additional feedback regarding fishers’ perceptions, attitudes, and beliefs towards shark depredation was gathered using participatory mapping exercises and a national online survey. Results from this project are an important first step for identifying the mitigation strategies that are most likely to effectively reduce shark depredation and be practically implemented in Australia and beyond.
3200: Despite their reputation for occasional bites and fatalities, California enacted protection for white sharks in State waters in 1994. Since that time, the population has shown considerable signs of recovery likely attributed to a mosaic of environmental and fisheries management regulations. As the population has increased, so have white shark sightings and aggregations along public beaches, raising human safety concerns. The California Shark Beach Safety Program was formed working closely with ocean lifeguards to understand the behavior of white sharks along southern and central CA beaches to assess risk. The research program has focused on understanding movements, habitat use, diet and foraging, as well as quantifying shark-human interactions. Social and economic research has focused on human perceptions (locals and tourists) of shark risk as well as costs associated with safety mitigation. Data from this on-going research is provided to lifeguards and water safety officials and is being used to inform adaptive beach safety management. These data are also used in a variety of public outreach vehicles including in-person informal beach safety education, infographics, PSAs, social media, and comic books. Results thus far indicated that science-based education and outreach is increasing public understanding of white sharks and fostering conservation stewardship and reducing preconceived fears, despite continued shark-human related incidents. This program is being considered as a non-lethal, cost-effective mitigation model for use in other locations where shark bites occur.
3201: Over the last decade, coastal New York has seen notable rises in human-shark interactions, which include both shark bites on water users and perceived increases in depredation in some fisheries. These patterns are often sensationalized by media outlets, resulting in growing cultural sensitivity and proposed causalities lacking in robust scientific evidence. Immediate mitigation measures include strategies that have proven useful elsewhere, such as drone surveillance. However, the paucity of local historical knowledge about shark behavior, coupled with the environmentally dynamic nature of temperate marine environments, risks a decoupling between current response efforts and positive outcomes. Here, we present a brief history of human-shark interactions occurring over the last ten years in coastal New York. We summarize current knowledge of shark assemblage composition and horizontal and vertical habitat use in coastal New York waters gathered by several longstanding research organizations. Growing data volumes highlight diverse shark assemblages, which routinely utilize nearshore beach environments under somewhat predictable oceanographic conditions. Importantly, vertical movement data and limited water clarity suggest that drone surveillance may be largely ineffective at mitigating risk for ocean users. As such, we discuss the need for a broader portfolio of management responses informed by science, placing particular emphasis on addressing human perceptions and expanding educational initiatives.
3202: Scientific and public concern about declining shark populations has prompted the implementation of management plans and protective legislation for many species in recent decades, and some populations are beginning to recover. However, the continued success of such measures depends on an ability to mitigate the potential for increases in negative shark-human encounters, which can undermine public support of conservation policies, as recovering populations return to regions where they have long been absent. Cape Cod, Massachusetts, is a popular tourist destination that has emerged as a seasonal aggregation site for the recovering northwest Atlantic white shark, Carcharodon carcharias, population over the past fifteen years, and negative interactions with humans have been on the rise. This has resulted in progressively dramatic media coverage that has skewed the public’s perception of risk and raised concerns that the presence of the species will negatively affect the region’s tourism-driven economy. In response to these issues, we have been using tagging and drone technologies to better understand the nearshore behavior of white sharks. To mitigate concerns regarding public safety, our scientific results are shared in a timely manner with educators, conservation groups, local officials, and the news media through multiple vectors. This kind of communication and collaboration outside of the scientific community is critical for navigating the complex societal conflicts that arise when and where white shark populations recover, which will likely present the next major conservation challenge for this iconic species.
3203: The Cornell University Museum of Vertebrates (CUMV) has several long-term sampling sites. Of these, Catatonk Creek is the most regularly and longest sampled locality. The first collection efforts concerned with the community of fishes occurred in 1930 and sampling has continued every other year up to and including 2022. This talk will explore an overview for several aspects of a near century of ichthyological sampling including changes in the faunal assemblage, and a look at preliminary results from stable isotopes (C, N, and S) in this community over time.
3204: Mortality and habitat fragmentation associated with roadways are leading threats for freshwater turtles. While road mitigation for wildlife is becoming more common, it is often expensive, and effectiveness for small animals remains understudied. The Minnesota Zoo, in partnership with the Minnesota Department of Transportation and Twin Cities metro counties, spent four years evaluating the effectiveness of barriers and warning signs in reducing turtle road mortality. Our goal was to redirect turtles away from roadways and to existing under-road infrastructure where practicable. We implemented a Before-After-Control-Impact (BACI) study at 25 sites from 2018 to 2021. Starting in 2019, modified chain-link fences, 8-inch corrugated pipe barriers, or wildlife warning signs were installed across 12 different treatment sites. Our results showed that chain-link fencing (with wrap-around end treatments) effectively reduced mortality of adult turtles, but not juveniles. After retrofitting fences with ½-inch wire mesh, we documented a significant reduction in mortality of all age classes at treatment sites (up to 91% over pre-treatment) when comparing treatment with control sites. Although our sample size was limited, 8-inch diameter drainage pipe also appears to be an effective barrier, with mortality reductions of over 50%. The value of wildlife warning signs, however, remains less clear, as preliminary data suggest significant variability in effectiveness among sites. This study provides a framework for measures that can be implemented to mitigate road mortality of turtles, thereby benefitting wildlife conservation and improving safety for drivers.
3205: Will County is the most herpetologically rich county in northeastern Illinois, with 18 amphibian and 25 reptile species known to occur in the county. Will County is also home to the extensive Will County Forest Preserve system, which has grown to cover over 23,000 acres of land since 1927. Between 2022 to 2025, we conducted resurveys of these forest preserves to learn how the herpetofauna of Will County survived, thrived, or were displaced since the last comprehensive compilation was published in 2015.  We have collected tissue and/or vouchers of 14 amphibian and all 25 reptile species, thus contributing hundreds of modern voucher and genetic materials to the collection of the Field Museum of Natural History in Chicago for use in research on midwestern herpetofaunal diversity. We present here the results of these surveys, summarizing our observations of the relative abundance and distribution of amphibians and reptiles in comparison to historical datasets. We also discuss the relevance of these updated records to informing land management efforts on their effect on local herpetofauna.
3206: Invading novel habitats can increase ecological opportunity, promoting rapid phenotypic evolution as species adapt to new niches. Conversely, invading homogenous habitats can limit phenotypic adaptation to only a few niches, reducing ecological opportunity and leading to slower rates of morphological change. However, invasion of a novel habitat can limit phenotypic diversity without changing the rate of evolution, if the transition is recent and selection favors only a few highly adaptive phenotypes. We examine body shape diversity in neotropical characiforms across flow regimes and explore the role of time, evolutionary rate, and functional constraints in explaining patterns of morphological diversity. High-flow habitat invasion was rare until the last 60 million years, after which it steadily increased.  Low-flow fishes exhibit greater body shape disparity than high-flow species, though evolutionary rates are similar. Low body shape diversity in high-flow habitats results from a combination of two factors. First, characiforms have occupied high-flow habitats for less time, having recently transitioned from low-flow environments. Second, the body shapes of high-flow lineages are not a random subset of low-flow lineages. Instead, they are restricted to intermediate body shapes and some unusually dorsally flattened and elongated forms, apparently as a response to the mechanical demands of living in fast-flowing water. Higher body shape diversity in low-flow habitats reflects longer occupation, fewer flow-related constraints, and environmental stability over 100 million years. Our study highlights how patterns of phenotypic diversity emerge on broad landscapes through the interplay between habitat-specific environmental factors and evolutionary time.
3207: Terrestrial salamanders function as dominant predators in forest floor communities because of their large population densities and voracious appetites. The impact they have on the community structure of their prey (leaf litter invertebrates) is appreciable. I investigated these relationships in a bottomland hardwood forest where Plethodon mississippi was the prevailing salamander species. An unrestricted field experiment using coverboard arrays and leaf litter collection was used to accomplish this. In light of an unprecedented drought resulting in mass salamander mortality, leaf litter samples were paired with gut content analysis for further comparison.
3208: Urbanization is hypothesized to promote greater overlap in resource use among persisting species. Florida green watersnakes (Nerodia floridana) and brown watersnakes (Nerodia taxispilota) are abundant in freshwater habitats in southern Florida and appear to exhibit distinct dietary preferences, with the former feeding on a variety of fishes and amphibians, and the latter feeding almost exclusively on fishes. The two species are further known to occupy canals in the region which traverse urbanized habitat matrices. Based on previously reported reductions in native amphibian abundance along urban-rural gradients, we hypothesized that populations of N. floridana and N. taxispilota from urban habitats would exhibit greater trophic overlap compared to those from more natural habitat following their exploitation of the remaining prey resources (i.e., fishes). To test our hypothesis, we used stable isotopes to assess trophic overlap by comparing carbon and nitrogen isotope signatures from individuals sampled across three urban transects, with those of museum specimens collected from a more natural habitat in the region. We found significant enrichment of nitrogen in both species for individuals sampled from urban habitats relative to the natural habitat, and significant differences in carbon signatures in N. floridana collected in natural habitat relative to those sampled from the urban habitat, where urban habitat N. floridana exhibited no significant difference relative to natural and urban habitat N. taxispilota. The greater isotopic overlap observed in urban populations of the two snake species indicates a more similar diet, suggesting a prey community constrained by urbanization.
3209: The syntopic coexistence of species with overlapping life-history traits suggests that resources in shared habitats are either partitioned among species or sufficiently abundant to minimize competition.   Resource availability is not static, however, and shifts in the diversity, abundance, and spatial distribution of prey likely influence patterns of dietary overlap among predators.   In wetland ecosystems, both predictable (seasonal) and stochastic fluctuations in hydrology impact prey availability, altering access to key resources and influencing predator foraging dynamics.  Using stable isotope analyses, we examined the diets of five semi-aquatic snake species from three distinct clades that co-occur near the northwestern extent of the Gulf Coast Plain.  By comparing plasma and scale tissues, which differ in isotopic turnover rates, we assessed dietary integration and examined temporal shifts in dietary overlap.  We classified the prey community into seven guilds based on carbon and nitrogen isotope profiles and used Bayesian mixing models to estimate their relative contributions to the diet of each snake species.  Plasma tissue analyses revealed greater resource partitioning among snake species than scale tissue analyses, which reflect a longer dietary history.  This pattern is indicative of seasonal fluctuations in prey availability, particularly the increase in dietary overlap when certain prey resources, such as anuran larvae, become widely available.   As these resources decline, dietary partitioning among snake species becomes more pronounced.  Our findings highlight the role of seasonal prey pulses in shaping niche utilization and the importance of equitable sampling in assessing predator-prey interactions in dynamic ecosystems.
3210: Snubnose Darters compose much of subgenus Simpoperca within the speciose genus Etheostoma.
