When threatened, this species curls up ventrally and bites their tails, turning them into a spiky, difficult-to-swallow torus. We constructed a comprehensively sampled Computed Tomography dataset for cordylids and their close relatives, isolated all presacral vertebrae, and then used GMM to quantify and analyze sequential vertebral variation. To test the effects of landmark type, position and number on the output shape scores, we ran analyses using several different landmarking strategies and compared these with the output from a neural network approach that utilizes a signed-distance-function (SDF) to capture and quantify 3D shape Information. In all cases, the vertebrae of each species shows a stereotyped progression through morphospace from the cervicals to the sacrum. The vertebrae of Ouroborus appear similar to other cordylids but displayed some notable differences in the cervical region, suggesting that critical adaptations to the tail-biting behavior occur in the anterior axial skeleton.
3263: John Hutchison Garnier (1823–1898) was a pioneering herpetologist based in the town of Lucknow, Ontario. Some mystery surrounds his birthplace as well as his birthname. Garnier was a physician but spent much of his time hunting and observing wildlife. He built a huge private natural history collection by exchanging specimens with correspondents all over the world. Among his papers on amphibians and reptiles was the first list of the herpetofauna of Ontario published in 1881 and augmented in 1882 and 1894. Although his species list was inflated with misidentifications and synonyms, he appears to have recognized 39 of the 50 species of amphibians and reptiles currently recognized as present in the province or recently extirpated. Garnier’s publications included several novel nomina. He described two species of Necturus from Ontario. While one is generally acknowledged and included in the synonymy of N. maculosus, the other has only been cited once in 144 years. Additional new varieties named by Garnier have likewise escaped notice. He also published on the two rattlesnake species in Ontario, including the now extirpated Crotalus horridus, and on treatments for snakebite. Most of Garnier’s work is now forgotten and only 50 Ontario specimens are extant from his collection, now housed in the Royal Ontario Museum and the U.S. National Museum of Natural History. His activities as a frontier naturalist in the mid-19th century represent a starting point for herpetological studies in Ontario.
3264: As the primary repositories of source material, publicly held collections that include genetic resources enable foundational research in biology; each sample is a critical snapshot in time of a population, held safe for current and future investigation. A major consumer of these resources is phylogeography, where productive studies are only feasible in the presence of adequate sampling, with key sampling gaps or lack of representation in putative contact zones sometimes disrupting the ability to distinguish biogeographic pattern and process as well as confound downstream interpretation such as taxonomic revisions to a system. We examined records of snake tissues deposited in North American herpetology collections as well as tissue use in modern molecular phylogeographic studies for signs of phylogenetic, ecological and other biases. While demand for larger, more inclusive datasets increases, deposition of materials into collections peaked during the early stages of phylogeography and museums are receiving very little contemporary material. In the face of the Anthropocene biodiversity crisis, it is more important than ever to deposit tissues and vouchers in museums, particularly from incidental or salvage occurrences. We highlight some key cases where just a few pieces of reference material could make all the difference in an investigation and share tools we’ve developed to demystify the process of collection to allow non-specialists, citizen scientists and avocational herpetologists to contribute.
3265: Natural history collections are invaluable resources that scientists have used to describe the biodiversity, ecology and evolutionary biology of organisms. Museum specimens also serve as a set of permanent records that scientists can employ to infer historical distribution, occupancy/abundance and demography of declining or even relict populations of species. The University of Alabama Herpetological Collection (UAHC) was created in the late 1940s by Ralph L. Chermock. Previous efforts to ensure the security of specimens and digitize their associated collection data have fallen short meaning obscure or erroneous collection data, misidentifications and outdated taxonomy were still common issues. Moreover, UAHC specimen data are not publicly available meaning it is difficult for researchers and educators to access this information. The UAHC received a collections improvement grant in 2023 to completely re-curate the collection as well as digitize and upload all collection data to biodiversity data aggregators (i.e., GBIF, iDigBio, VertNet). To date, we have quality checked and labeled >17,000 physical specimens (~98% of all holdings), georeferenced all collection localities and updated taxonomy. The UAHC and other herpetological collections will be essential to future studies regarding the natural history of these organisms as well as efforts to effectively manage populations of vulnerable and rare taxa in an era of rapid environmental change. Although not always considered a priority, it is important to continue to support natural history collections (e.g., time, expertise, funding) as we continue to expand our knowledge of the natural world.
3266: Development of a non-lethal liver sampling method could reduce the need for animal sacrifice while furthering research in various fields of study. However, a tradeoff exists between the amount of tissue that can safely be sampled to maximize animal survivability and the minimum volume of tissue necessary to conduct the laboratory analysis to meet the goals of the study. With regards to toxicological studies, 1 gram of tissue is traditionally used, but since elasmobranch livers can accumulate high contaminant levels, a non-lethal liver biopsy method using less tissue could potentially be employed. The objectives of the study were to 1) determine the minimum amount of tissue we could extract before analytes of interest were lost and 2) determine if a non-lethal biopsy method could be used in a field setting while demonstrating animal survivability post-procedure. In the laboratory, liver samples of varying quantities were taken from the same source sample, solvent extracted, and a suite of POPs were quantified by GCMS. Results show that 0.2g-samples reflected >85% of the 1g-samples, and 0.5g-samples were all >91% of the 1g-samples. In the field, liver biopsies were taken from three species of elasmobranchs that were also outfitted with internal acoustic tags to track their movements post-procedure. Movements were species-specific, with bat rays traveling long distances compared to angel sharks and leopard sharks. We demonstrate here that liver biopsies can be sampled in field settings that reduce animal sacrifice while meeting the objectives of the study.
3267: In the Yucatan Peninsula (Gulf of Mexico and Mexican Caribbean), the Whitespotted Eagle Ray (WSER) is traditionally fished and consumed by local communities as a primary source of fish protein. This study aims to evaluate the concentrations of heavy metals in muscle samples of WSER collected from artisanal fisheries in Campeche and Quintana Roo. The predominant metal distribution observed was As > Ni > Cr > Pb > Cd. Statistical analysis revealed significant differences in Pb, Ni, Cr, and Cd concentrations between the two locations, with Campeche exhibiting the highest levels. Our findings indicate that WSER can accumulate substantial amounts of heavy metals, particularly arsenic. The elevated concentrations of heavy metals not only pose serious health risks to individuals consuming WSER—known to adversely affect hormonal functions and the nervous system in marine species—but also raise significant conservation concerns. These health risks to human consumers highlight the urgent need for public awareness regarding the potential contamination of local seafood. Furthermore, the impact of heavy metal accumulation on WSER populations threatens their sustainability, underscoring the dual significance of our findings for both public health and conservation efforts. Addressing these issues is crucial for protecting marine biodiversity and safeguarding the health of local communities.
3268: Stable isotope analysis of individual molecules, such as amino acids (AAs), is an emergent technique that continues to provide novel insights into the trophic behavior and energetic resource use of elasmobranchs. However, recent work has suggested that changes to physiological status associated with processes such as starvation or gestation, can elicit substantial variation in AA carbon (δ13C), nitrogen (δ15N), and hydrogen (δ2H) stable isotope values in wild populations. Here, we illustrate the potential of AA isotope analysis to discern changes in physiological status using a case study taxon, the bonnethead shark (Sphyrna tiburo). Amino acid δ13C, δ15N, and δ2H values were measured in liver and muscle tissues obtained from wild females spanning a full gestational cycle (~5 months). We hypothesized that shifting energetic demands at different gestational stages would elicit unique patterns of AA isotope fractionation. Significant differences in δ13C, δ15N, and δ2H values were observed between individuals associated with earlier and later term gestational stages. These differences were consistent across essential and non-essential AAs and most pronounced in δ15N and δ2H values of liver tissue, which were substantially lower in individuals at later gestational stages. Given the central role of the liver in AA biosynthesis, these findings imply potential changes to nitrogen and water balance as females proceed through gestation. More generally, these results underscore the role of physiology in promoting isotopic variation in wild elasmobranch populations.
3269: The individual effects of high temperature and low oxygen have been assessed in a model species of elasmobranch, the little skate (Leucoraja erinacea). These abiotic environmental variables often co-occur in nature, however, and the potentially synergistic impacts of these stressors are unknown. This study aims to fill this knowledge gap by exposing little skate embryos to a factorial combination of temperatures (15°C, 18°C, 20°C) and dissolved oxygen levels (> 85%, 45%) for the entire embryonic stage. We will measure embryonic standard metabolic rate (SMR) using intermittent flow respirometry every month, and will determine yolk sac consumption rate and eye growth rate via imaging every week. We will also measure days until hatch and overall survival rates of the embryos. Following hatch, we will measure maximum metabolic rate (MMR), SMR, blood-oxygen binding (Hb-O2 % saturation), hematocrit (Hct), and hemoglobin concentration ([Hb]). We will use MMR and SMR to calculate aerobic scope (AS), use Hct and [Hb] to calculate mean corpuscular hemoglobin content (MCHC), and use Hb-O2 % saturation to identify the and partial pressure of O2 at which Hb is 50% saturated (P50). Blood samples from the parent population of skates will be compared to blood analysis metrics from the offspring to analyze phenotypic plasticity in oxygen transport mechanisms. This work has implications for understanding population health of species with a long reproductive cycle in a rapidly changing marine environment.
3270: Species that thrive across diverse environmental conditions typically consist of populations occupying only a subset of these conditions, frequently exhibiting population-specific traits that enhance fitness. The mechanisms underlying these traits fall along a spectrum. At one extreme, phenotypic plasticity allows individuals to modify their traits in response to new environments, facilitating survival and performance across different conditions. At the other extreme, strong local adaptation results in populations so specialized for their native environments that they struggle to persist elsewhere. Our study aims to disentangle the contributions of plasticity and genomic adaptation that enable populations of the Desert Horned Lizard (Phrynosoma platyrhinos) to inhabit an exceptionally wide climatic range—from some of the hottest, driest places on Earth (e.g., Death Valley) to cold deserts where freezing temperatures persist for six months of the year. We integrate population genomics, transcriptomics, acclimation experiments, and thermal biology to assess these mechanisms. Our findings reveal a combination of plastic and adaptive responses, varying across populations, detectable at the genomic level, and linked to fitness-related traits. This research provides key insights into how organisms persist across extreme environmental gradients.
3271: Many have found the vast literature on discovering species and species concepts frustrating and trying to stay current on methods. Species in nature are known as Individuals in a Natural Class.   Natural Classes include things that participate in natural processes. You cannot define an Individual.  Individuals have a beginning and an end and are temporospatially bounded. They are always “slippery,” and humans feel uncomfortable with them. On the other hand, there are things that humans feel more comfortable with, and these entities are part of an Artificial Class.  They do not have a beginning or an ending – they are timeless.  They have definitions and are not temporospatially bounded. They have operational definitions and instructions to follow to find things that fit the definition. This difference stands at the root of decades of controversy.  Why? Most of us, unfortunately, are not skilled in the philosophy of science, an essential grounding for scientists to observe and describe the world. Rarely are there opportunities to learn about the philosophy of science. However, species in nature are Individuals that cannot be defined. Still, the species category is an Artificial Class that can and requires a definition that does not intentionally exclude things we would agree are species as lineages. Any concept of species that is easy to use and operational is inappropriate as the definition of the Artificial Class Species and can have disastrous downstream impacts.  The pure lineage concepts best serve us for this Artificial Class. All other concepts are operational and simply exclude some biodiversity.
3272: Female mimicry in vertebrates is a rare and valuable phenomenon, particularly given that it informs our understanding of suites of traits and/or genes that explain the mechanisms of alternative reproductive strategies. Despite the age and diversity of snakes as a group of vertebrates, female mimicry has been robustly documented in only one species (Thamnophis sirtalis). Female garter snake mimics have testes, produce sperm, court and mate with females, and even have significantly elevated circulating androgens compared to normal males during the spring breeding season. However, mimics are also significantly attractive to other males and produce substantial amounts of female sex pheromone but are not as attractive as even the smallest females in the population. For the past 10 years, we have been studying female mimicry in wild red-sided garter snakes (T. s. parietalis) to determine how mimics differ from both male and female snakes at multiple biological levels: sex pheromones, steroid hormones, gene expression, and mating behavior. We recently discovered two key attributes of mimics that explain the activation and/or maintenance of mimicry. First, mimics are heavier per unit length than males, but are smaller than females, and this may be a result of differential investment in body fat. Second, in their skin, mimics exhibit female-typical gene expression of a network of enzymes central to skin lipid synthesis. Unlike males, mimics have a gene network that ultimately produces significant amounts of long-chain, modified lipids that comprise the female sex pheromone blend. Our results reveal that female mimicry is complex because the combination of body composition and specific expression of key genes permit or activate the mimic phenotype without disrupting normal male reproductive physiology. How the mimic phenotype is initially established, whether mimicry is obligate, and if sexual size dimorphism is a prerequisite for mimicry are all open questions. Our studies have demonstrated for the first time that female mimics exemplify biological intermediacy between female- and male-typical biology and at multiple scales.
3273: Chemical communication, facilitated by the secretion and recognition of pheromones, plays a vital role in the behavior of squamate reptiles. These chemical signals are linked to various intraspecific and interspecific interactions, such as kin recognition, mate choice, and aggression. Whiptail lizards of the genus Aspidoscelis possess femoral glands, which likely play a key role in their chemical communication. However, the composition of the pheromones and the genetic mechanisms regulating expression of the glandular content are not well understood. In this study, we compared the expression of pheromone-related genes between parthenogenetic and sexually reproducing whiptail lizards, anticipating minimal differences due to the presence of pseudocopulatory behavior in all-female parthenogens. We collected lizards in the field, extracted gland chemicals, and excised femoral gland and forelimb tissues for transcriptomic analysis. We used gene ontology and combined pathway analyses to investigate the diversity of proteins associated with glandular tissue and infer potential biochemical pathways. Finally, we performed differential gene expression analyses to compare glandular gene expression between male and female A. gularis. Our findings shed light of the genetic machinery that maintains the evolutionarily ubiquitous femoral glands and contribute to our understanding of chemical communication in reptiles, paving the way for future research in this field.
3274: Hybridization is a prominent evolutionary force throughout the animal kingdom, generating numerous evolutionary outcomes driven by the dynamic of genomic consequences introduced in hybrid populations.  The smooth greensnake (Opheodrys vernalis) is widely distributed across the United States that consist of two lineages that likely experienced allopatric divergence during the Last Glacial Maximum (LGM) and recent secondary contact following post-LGM northward advancement. Although known to hybridize in Ohio, the specific selective forces driving hybridization and any potentially associated genomic consequences remain unknown. I used ddRADSeq to generate a single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) dataset to assess the genomic composition between both O. vernalis clades and hybrids. I located an isolated hybrid population in Killdeer, Ohio composed of only late generation hybrids (F2 and later) with low inbreeding, abundance of private alleles, and a near uniform ancestral proportion biased towards western ancestry. Hierarchical Bayesian genomic cline analysis identified a collection of predominately freely introgressing outlier SNPs with shallower clines than genome average. Of the few SNPs that were resisting introgression, most indicated evidence of directional selection against eastern ancestry. Outlier SNPs identified from genotype-environment analyses using WorldClim bioclimatic variables indicated minor but significant environmental associations with O. vernalis genetic variation. Altogether, Killdeer hybrids show evidence of heterosis, and directional selection may be characterized by factors not limited to climate such as transitional habitat between the primarily agricultural western and deciduous eastern regions. However, genetic drift likely exaggerates and obscures true selection signals as most western populations are small, isolated, and highly inbred.
3275: Color polymorphism, the occurrence of multiple discrete color morphs with co-adapted sets of traits within the same population, may provide the raw materials for rapid species formation. It has been hypothesized that fixation of a single morph can result in character release, whereby the monomorphic form evolves without the constraint of accommodating multiple adaptive peaks. However, the rates of evolution between populations fixed for different morphs likely depend on the specific adaptive zones occupied by each morph. We studied the evolution of dorsal color polymorphism (striped and unstriped morphs) in woodland salamanders (Plethodon), a North American radiation in which the polymorphism can be found in even the most distantly related species (~44 Ma divergence). We estimated a phylogenomic tree of Plethodon, representing all extant taxa with multiple samples for most species. Morphometric data suggest that between-species variation exists predominantly along an axis of relative body elongation, likely corresponding to a terrestrial–fossorial continuum. Polymorphic species occupy an intermediate phenotypic space between the evolutionary optima of striped and unstriped species, although polymorphic species did not have elevated speciation rates. Faster rates of body shape evolution were observed in unstriped species, suggesting that body elongation, which is co-adapted with the unstriped morph, is constrained by the polymorphism. Striped species had slower rates of evolution than polymorphic species, despite lacking the genetic constraints often associated with polymorphism. Our results demonstrate that rates of phenotypic evolution and speciation following character release can be asymmetric and idiosyncratic depending on the alternative adaptations of each morph.
3276: Population monitoring is an essential tool for wildlife conservation. Protocols based on individual identification, such as mark–recapture, allow for the modelling of population sizes and dynamics. In this context, the viability of studies depends on the available technologies for reliable identification of individual animals. Studies focused on squamate populations have used methods such as scale and toe-clipping, heat-branding or internal emitters, which are invasive and can induce stress and pain for the individuals. Photo-identification is another potential method that uses long lasting natural patterns such as spots or scales to recognize individuals without applying a mark or an emitter. However, it can be time-consuming if pictures are analyzed manually. To overcome this, several photo-recognition programs have been developed. But which should you use for your focus species? And what part of the animal should be photographed? To answer these questions, this study tested efficiency of three commonly used programs (I3S Pattern, WildID and HotSpotter) for individual recognition of squamates using pictures of the head, jaws and chest. At the time of writing this abstract, species from 15 families spanning the squamate phylogenetic tree have been studied, with more being analyzed. The results will allow to provide recommendations on area of interest to photograph and software choice for the different groups, from geckos to colubrids and more.
3277: Camera traps are becoming increasingly popular in wildlife research because they can be deployed for long periods with little maintenance and are less invasive than traditional trapping methods. We tested the efficacy of the Adapted-Hunt Drift Fence Technique (AHDriFT) for surveying eastern diamondback rattlesnakes (Crotalus adamanteus; EDBs), which are imperiled and declining across their range. Because EDBs are cryptic and difficult to detect visually, passive sampling techniques have the potential to assist in surveys. We deployed 20 AHDriFT arrays across our study site in South Carolina where we are concurrently conducting a long-term mark-recapture and radio-telemetry study on EDBs. Between August 2022 and May 2024, we collected 79 independent EDB observations (images) from camera traps. We used mixed effects logistic regression to evaluate covariate effects (e.g., weather, changes in day length, and EDB behavioral season) on the probability of detecting EDBs in camera traps and evaluated candidate models using AICc model selection. The probability of detecting EDBs was low and associated with interactive effects of air temperature and photoperiod, with detection increasing in the fall as photoperiod shortened and temperatures decreased. In the spring, as photoperiod increased, detection increased when temperature was above average. Stationary camera traps are inefficient at surveying for EDBs, likely reflecting the species’ sit-and-wait ambush foraging strategy that limits movement activity.
3278: Describing the space use and activity patterns of small animals is important to evaluating reintroduction projects. The development of miniaturized tracking devices, such as UHF (ultra-high frequency) transmitters, has provided opportunities to better understand the ecology of many smaller-bodied species and assess conservation efforts using automated radio telemetry systems (ARTS). The blunt-nosed leopard lizard (BNLL; Gambelia sila) is an endangered species endemic to the San Joaquin Desert of Central California. We are releasing captive-produced BNLL to bolster an almost-extirpated population in Fresno County, CA where we installed an ARTS of >300 nodes. Stationary tag calibration tests indicated a median location error (true - estimated) of 29.5 meters. We also performed moving tag calibration tests: home ranges were similar between those generated with known and estimated locations. In June 2024, we released 10 captive-reared BNLL equipped with UHF backpacks and later equipped four wild lizards, and plan to release more in 2025. We monitored lizards with a combination of hand and automated tracking, using multilateration methods to estimate >200,000 lizard locations. The use of ARTS data resulted in better home range estimates than hand-tracking alone, provided insight into post-release movements, and confirmed that both released and wild lizards selected habitat near dirt roads. Additionally, we used data from the ARTS to predict when lizards are below ground, detect late season activity, and determine likely mortality events. Our results confirm ARTS can be a powerful and cost-effective tool for monitoring small-bodied terrestrial vertebrates at high resolution.
3279: We need accurate data about species occurrence for recovery plans to be effective. Turtles are a highly imperiled group. Baited, aquatic traps are often used to monitor freshwater turtles. Recent studies show that trail cameras can detect turtles, but we lack comparative studies contrasting these approaches. We ask which method is more effective at detecting turtles in Minnesota. In summer 2022 and 2023, we pointed trail cameras at basking platforms at 15 sites in two state parks. We also used aquatic traps at 12 sites. Aquatic traps captured four species, including the Painted (Chrysemys picta), Blanding’s (Emydoidea blandingii), Snapping (Chelydra serpentina), and Spiny Softshell Turtles (Apalone spinifera). Camera traps documented these same species as well as map turtles (Graptemys spp.). Daily detection probabilities for Painted (aquatic = 0.653 vs. camera = 0.691) and Blanding’s Turtles (aquatic = 0.104 vs. camera = 0.100)  are similar between methods. Snapping and Spiny Softshell Turtles are more likely encountered via aquatic traps. Map turtles were only detected at one site where we did not trap. We further explore these data using hierarchical occupancy models to investigate covariates that impact detection of and site use by these species. Trail cameras require less personnel time and have lower equipment costs compared to aquatic traps. Additionally, for some species, such as the rare Blanding’s Turtle, trail cameras are just as effective. For these reasons, we recommend incorporating trail cameras into survey efforts for freshwater turtles aimed at documenting species use.
3280: Frogs are one of the most threatened groups of animals on the planet, yet our current understanding of global frog species diversity, distributions and population trends remains poor. Professional biologists are working hard to gather the information needed to conserve frogs but cannot do it alone. In 2017, the Australian Museum launched FrogID, a national citizen science project based upon a smartphone app used to record calling frogs. The project has now engaged almost 100,000 people to collect over 1.2 million records of frogs across the continent, revolutionising revolutionised both our understanding of Australian frogs and public engagement in frog conservation. The dataset is growing rapidly, with a peak of over 6,200 frog records in a single day. These occurrence records and audio recordings have helped uncover the true diversity and distributions of Australia’s frogs, along with the impact of threats such as fires, drought, climate change and habitat modification. People across Australia have clearly demonstrated the power of community engagement in frog conservation.
3281: A combination of visualization techniques provides a multidimensional assessment of gross and microscopic anatomy. The olfactory organs and associated tissues in larval, aquatic adult, and terrestrial adult phase rough-skinned newts, Taricha granulosa, were examined by Diffusible Iodine-based Contrast-Enhanced Computed Tomography (diceCT), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), and traditional histology. DiceCT enabled comparison of the overall morphology of larval and adult main olfactory cavity (MOC) and vomeronasal organ (VNO). Histology and SEM provide detailed information about the sensory and supporting cells of the MOC and VNO. In both aquatic and terrestrial individuals, the olfactory epithelium of the MOC has strips of sensory and supporting cells set between ridges of respiratory epithelium. In aquatic adults, the respiratory epithelium is covered with long, presumably motile cilia; the olfactory epithelium has much shorter cilia. In contrast, terrestrial animals largely lack cilia on the ridges of non-sensory epithelium of the MOC, and the respiratory ridges are much more pronounced. The respiratory epithelium of the lateral nasal groove is ciliated in both aquatic and terrestrial forms, with long, thick, presumably motile cilia, while the vomeronasal epithelium has short, slender cilia. Changes in epithelial characteristics between aquatic and terrestrial forms have also been reported in European newts (Lissotriton, Triturus) and in Asian newts (Cynops), though differing in detail from those in Taricha. This morphological transition between media likely indicates a change in both olfactory mechanism and in sensitivity to chemical cues from conspecifics, as T. granulosa move between water and land as part of their annual reproductive cycle.
3282: The Non-Clinical Tomography Users Research Network (NoCTURN) is an international community of students, educators, and engineers dedicated to advancing the use of CT scanning technology in research and education. We promote resources available in online repositories, like Morphosource, and 3D models published by the open Vertebrate project (oVert). Although tomography data are becoming increasinlgy accessible to researchers, educators, and natural history enthusiasts, with some freely available for download, adoption and integration of open-access 3D data into K–12 education remains poor. Addressing limited classroom integration is a major interest area for the NoCTURN. Through its Education and Outreach (E&O) initiative, NoCTURN aims to cultivate the use of outputs from cutting-edge scientific tools in K-12 classrooms by providing accessible, CT-based educational resources. One approach we have taken is the development of education kits (Ed-Kits) geared towards specific age groups alongside learning objectives to support teachers in accessing, using, and instructing with freely available tomographic data. Examples include exploring homology and an introduction to Morphosource. These kits are published to QUBESHub (BioQUEST Curriculum Consortium), which allows assignment of persistent identifiers to track usage metrics and versioning to adapt content for evolving education and technological needs. Here we discuss our recent Ed-Kits, their deployment, reception by the community, and use them to provide an overview of the process of developing and publishing broadly accessible Ed-Kits using non-clinical tomography resources. We plan to continue expanding our Ed-Kit topics and add content designed specifically for different age groups within the broader K-12 range.
3283: Newer methods of scientific research have led to the increased use of 3D data when examining morphologies of organisms. I’ll be the first to admit that I jumped on that train when starting my own independent research. What started as CT-scanning neotropical electric fishes to examine craniofacial morphologies transitioned to identifying possible structural similarities across taxa with elongated faces. This brought me to the idea of “convergent evolution.” What started as CT-scanning afro-tropical electric fishes to examine craniofacial morphologies transitioned into a closer examination of the secondary sets of jaws in these species (the tongue-bite-apparatus). This brought me to the idea of “ecomorphology.” And what started as examining the diverse body shapes of minnows and shiners native to Minnesota transitioned into an interest in the tuberculation patterns on their faces. This brought me to the idea of “secondary sexual characteristics.” In all these projects, old and new, incorporating 3D data into my investigations has allowed me to expand my visual examinations of fishes, but also allowed me to expand into new fields as I attempt to connect shape to the vast number of factors influencing organismal evolution and ecology.
3284: Over the past decade, diffusible iodine-based contrast-enhanced Computed Tomography (diceCT) has commonly been used to create 3D representations of the soft tissue anatomy of vertebrate specimens preserved in natural history collections. It has been successfully used to uncover a treasure trove of anatomical characters and natural history records hidden within these specimens. While the technique has been widely applied, there has not been systematic documentation of protocols that can be adapted to a diverse range of vertebrates. Here, we apply diceCT to the most taxonomically and morphologically broad sampling of vertebrates, 3D imaged for the open Vertebrate (oVert) Thematic Collections network. We document our methods, adaptations, outcomes, and observations throughout all stages of the process: preparation, staining, scanning, and data processing.  As expected, larger specimens take a longer time to stain, but the final staining time depends on the taxon, whether there is dermal and/or bony armor present, and whether any internal structures (e.g., eggs, embryos, large fat deposits) require large amounts of iodine to become fully saturated. We establish a scoring system for diceCT-imaged soft tissues that reflects the usefulness of the data for research. As well as high-quality CT scans, we also provide examples of specimens that exhibit severe soft tissue damages, incomplete preservation, permanent specimen alteration, and understaining. All datasets produced have been made freely available for download via the data repository MorphoSource, and we hope that our work can serve as a resource for scientists and the public to explore and study vertebrate anatomy.
3285: The adhesive toes of geckos and other lizards are an amazing example of naturally occurring nanotech, comprised of complex micro and nano-scale structures called setae. A basic step in understanding their structure, function, and variation is the ability to accurately measure their dimensions. This can be a difficult endeavor. Electron microscopy is a common high-resolution imaging approach, yet electron microscopy can suffer from optical distortions. To address this challenge, we used high resolution laser confocal microscopy to generate 3D scans. Geckos (and other pad bearing lizards) use a wide variety of surfaces in the wild. We focused on four sympatric species of Phelsuma geckos from the island of Mauritius suspected of using different surface textures. Our scans allowed us to measure setal length, diameter, and density across the rear toes of our focal species. These measurements will allow for comparisons to surface texture to infer how these species may be adapted to specific scansorial microhabitats. Gaining a better understanding of their adhesive morphology is an exciting first step to better understanding patterns of niche partitioning and character displacement.
3286: Many current methods for assessment of the brain are destructive, which can compromise the relative positions of various structures and can be impractical for the study of rare and/or valuable specimens. Bioimaging techniques, including computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), are unique in their ability to non-invasively acquire high-resolution, digital, 3D data in situ. These techniques facilitate highly accurate and efficient visualization and analysis of internal anatomy that have been applied to both extant and even extinct chondrichthyans. Although many of these cutting-edge technologies and methods are more extensively developed for applications in human brain research, their utility in comparative neurobiology in other taxa has been comparatively underexplored. This talk will focus on the application of MRI as an investigative tool for neuroanatomy in cartilaginous fishes, including optimization and advances in instrumentation, contrast and resolution, and applicability of MRI to understand peripheral (olfactory rosette, eye, inner ear) and central (brain) anatomy in sharks and batoids. These techniques have greatly broadened our understanding of brain evolution in this group by expanding our capacity to include rare and/or endangered specimens into comparative datasets (e.g. the Greenland shark, Somniosus microcephalous; whale shark, Rhincodon typus; sawfishes, Pristis spp.), where dissection is sub-optimal. Further, digitization of specimens serves a critical role in preserving biological material in perpetuity, enabling worldwide access to specimens, development of new teaching tools, and allowing for new questions of the same tissue by future generations of scientists.
3287: As natural habitats change rapidly, understanding how wildlife responds to environmental shifts is crucial for assessing population health and stability. Glucocorticoids (GCs), primarily corticosterone (cort) in amphibians, regulate the vertebrate stress response and play a key role in maintaining homeostasis, reproduction, energy allocation, and behavior. Changes in GCs, from baseline to stress response and negative feedback to recovery, can indicate an organism's coping capacity in a given environment. We measured waterborne cort in lesser sirens (Siren intermedia) over 2 years and across life stages. Our goal was to gain a better understanding of the environmental pressures sirens face and how they are coping with environmental change. We also wanted to understand if there are vulnerable periods across a sirens life when coping may be limited. We measured GCs across 3 time points (baseline, stressed, and recovery) to assess coping capacity in 3 populations of lesser sirens. We repeatedly captured and sampled individuals to assess endocrine responses through time. We found that larval sirens exhibited strong stress responses and efficient negative feedback, characteristic of a ‘healthy’ endocrine profile. Cort levels peaked in spring, coinciding with the onset of the breeding season, and was higher in smaller individuals. Temperature was positively correlated with cort levels, but only in stressed and recovery samples, suggesting heightened sensitivity to environmental factors under stress. These findings indicate that S. intermedia are currently coping well but are vulnerable to increasing temperatures. Given high larval mortality, understanding stress responses during early life stages is critical for conservation.
Stress and Welfare in Organisms throughout Lifetime (HL)
3288: Temperature affects organisms across all ontogenetic life stages, but the embryonic stage, in particular, is often sensitive to changes in temperature. For ectotherms that inhabit large latitudinal ranges, environmental factors, such as temperature, create gradients to which local populations must adapt. These gradients thus result in phenotypic variation across populations spanning the species range. For embryos, traits such as developmental time and metabolic rate can interact in response to the shifting environmental conditions, resulting in shifts in associated costs and benefits. This study investigates adaptations associated with embryonic development in Prairie Lizards (Sceloporus consobrinus) across a latitudinal thermal gradient. Gravid adult females were collected from two latitudinally distinct populations. Eggs from each clutch were randomly assigned to two temperature treatments (25°C and 31°C) in a split-clutch design and checked daily for hatchlings to determine developmental time. Embryonic metabolism was measured as both whole organism respiration and heart rate at respective incubation temperatures. Results show the expected response of warmer temperatures decreasing development time with general increases in respiration and heart rates. Populations differed, however, in how developmental time, heart rate, and respiration rate collectively responded to temperature treatments, suggesting evolution in plasticity has occurred in these traits. As temperatures become more variable, understanding how temperature influences embryonic physiology will be important for determining whether developmental pathways of ectotherms will respond to changing temperatures in adaptive or maladaptive ways.
Stress and Welfare in Organisms throughout Lifetime (HL)
3289: Environmental heterogeneity can present a challenge for many organisms. Overcoming this challenge can be difficult, especially for embryos of oviparous species who are subject to the stochasticity of the environment unable to behavioral change their circumstance. Adaptive developmental plasticity is one route by which embryos can cope with environmental heterogeneity. The environmental matching hypothesis (EMH) predicts that organisms will develop phenotypes suited to their environment when the developmental environment matches the post-developmental environment. We collected eggs (n = 2,296) from a wild-caught colony of brown anoles (Anolis sagrei) and subjected them to incubation profiles that mimicked the shaded and open environments in the field. Hatchlings (n = 1,535) were released on one of two islands that corresponded with the incubation conditions in the lab: an open island that has very little structure or a shaded island that was mostly covered with trees. Our reciprocal transplant design ensured that the developmental environment either matched or mismatched the post hatching environment on the island. We recaptured hatchlings over a 5-month period to access growth and survival. Preliminary results show that hatchlings from the open incubation treatment have increased survival on the open island compared to those from the shaded incubation environment regardless of post developmental environment. These results provide evidence that the fitness consequences of the developmental environment may depend on the post-hatching environment.
Stress and Welfare in Organisms throughout Lifetime (HL)
3290: Suites of coevolved traits related to reproduction and demography enable species to persist in the face of environmental change. In the case of biological invasions, the suite of life history traits, “life history strategies”, can be linked to successful establishment after an introduction. Conservation translocations share many similarities with biological invasions, yet studies examining the relationship between life history and translocation outcome are scarce. We collected data on key life history traits for all herpetofauna profiled in the IUCN Global Conservation Translocation Perspectives series to examine how life history can predict outcomes and difficulties of conservation translocations. For reptiles, our model showed that age at maturity showed a significant positive association with higher probabilities of more successful outcomes, while increased clutch/litter size and lifespan predicted less successful outcomes. We found no relationship between any life history trait and translocation outcome for amphibians. Our results showed that difficulties with conservation translocations are related more to phylogeny than life history. Amphibian translocations faced more difficulties due to the physical environment of release sites, but reptile translocations experienced more socio-political difficulties. These relationships provide important insights for conservation practitioners that can be used in the feasibility and planning stages of translocations to anticipate and avoid challenges facing this complex and increasingly common form of conservation intervention.
Stress and Welfare in Organisms throughout Lifetime (HL)
3291: Endocrine-disrupting chemicals like bisphenol A (BPA) are widespread in aquatic environments and can impact organisms’ health, especially when exposure happens during critical developmental stages. We examined the effects of pre and postnatal exposure to BPA on two live-bearing fish species: Heterandria formosa and Gambusia affinis which differ notoriously in the level of matrotrophy. Gravid H. formosa females (highly matrotrophic) were exposed to 200 µg/L BPA, and BPA’s effects were assessed in ~3-week-old offspring. Subsequently, gravid females G. affinis (lecithotrophic) and 1-week-old offspring were exposed to 1 µg/L BPA (environmentally relevant concentration) for 1 month, with consequences evaluated between pre and post-natal exposed fries, and between 1 month-old BPA-exposed offspring and their control. Differentially Expressed Genes (DEGs) were obtained for the three comparisons. Although we found no DEGs between 1-month-old BPA-exposed offspring of G. afinnis and their controls, most DEGs were downregulated in the other two comparisons. Interestingly, in 3-week-old fries of H. formosa, those downregulated genes in BPA-exposed fry were mainly involved in immunity and development. In 1-month-old fry of G. afinnis, despite many downregulated genes may reflect the silencing of embryonic pathways in postnatal fish, others are involved in immunity, detoxification, cancer, cognition, and metabolic disruption, potentially due to BPA toxicity. Our findings suggest that prenatal BPA exposure can cause long-term effects in fish and that even environmentally relevant BPA concentrations can potentially impair the immune function and cognition, highlighting risks of BPA exposure during key stages of development in aquatic viviparous organisms possibly independently of matrotrophy.
Stress and Welfare in Organisms throughout Lifetime (HL)
3292: Landfall of hurricanes that form in the Atlantic Ocean has shifted earlier into the year over recent decades, and these early-season hurricanes will coincide with the reproductive season of many organisms. Due to flooding associated with these storms, species that rely on ground habitats for reproduction are particularly vulnerable, such as ground-nesting reptiles whose developing embryos would experience periods of seawater inundation and/or highly saline soils. For example, the brown anole (Anolis sagrei) inhabits coastal and island habitats prone to these disturbances, and their nests are often in areas inundated by seawater. Unfortunately, relatively few studies have considered the consequences of inundation or substrate salinity despite their potential impacts on embryo survival. The primary aim of this study was to test the hypothesis that saltwater submersion and subsequent development in saline substrate would negatively affect embryonic development because of the desiccating effect of the hypoosmotic condition of the eggs. We conducted a full factorial experiment with three submersion treatments (no submersion, freshwater submersion, and saltwater submersion) and two egg incubation treatments (sand mixed with freshwater or saltwater). Our results provide evidence that eggs rapidly lose mass when exposed to saltwater, and embryos cannot survive either saltwater submersion or incubation in a substrate mixed with saltwater. These findings have important implications for understanding how major storms associated with global change can impact reptile populations that inhabit coastal or island ecosystems.
Stress and Welfare in Organisms throughout Lifetime (HL)
3293: In 2010, the Deepwater Horizon oil spill had a devastating immediate impact on the DeSoto Canyon and adjacent areas. As the spill occurred at 1500 m, deep-sea communities were among the first to be affected, followed by those in shallower habitats. Extensive research on the effects of the spill has been conducted on surface-dwelling megafauna such as sea turtles and marine mammals, in addition to coastal fisheries.  Deep sea benthic communities were studied following the oil spill, however elasmobranchs and teleosts, or the benthopelagic organisms, living at depths greater than 200 m, have been understudied. To address this gap, we investigated ecosystem-wide changes to deep sea elasmobranch and large teleost communities post-oil spill residing across a depth gradient from 200-2000 m. Through bottom longline surveys coupled with sediment sampling, community structure and any relative changes over time are described from multiple lenses spanning across an eight-year period. The overall community structure of deep-sea elasmobranchs and teleost did not deviate over the sampling period: however, there were variances on a species-specific basis influenced by depth and region sampled, indicative of unique community gradients. Whole community diversity trends follow similar studies of the deep sea, with a variable distribution of diversity (H’), catch-per-unit-effort, and species richness at shallower depths that stabilizes as depth increases. Sediment data support previous findings related to organic carbon flux following the oil spill and indicate the system is nutrient-dense enough to support biodiversity regardless of year and depth. Further sampling effort is recommended to identify small-scale spatial trends, especially as deep-sea ecosystems experience increased exposure to anthropogenic efforts.
3294: Fisheries independent surveys can be used to identify long term abundance trends in sharks and rays. For many species globally abundance data is lacking. Long-term ecosystem sampling regimes, using unbaited gear, allow analysis of species populations, identifying species-specific interactions, and determining environmental impacts upon study species over extended periods of time. The north-western Cape York region is a unique environment, and its elasmobranch species composition is not well understood. From 2016 to 2024, gillnet surveys for sharks and rays were conducted in the waterways of Mapoon (Port Musgrave, Ducie River, Wenlock River) and Weipa (Albatross Bay, Hey River, Embley River), in the Gulf of Carpentaria, north-western Cape York, Queensland.  A total of 916 elasmobranchs belonging to 37 species were captured. Factors that affect capture rates and distributions of elasmobranchs were analysed for the five most abundant species in the data set; ocellate eagle ray Aetobatus ocellatus, bullshark Carcharhinus leucas, winghead shark Eusphyra blochii, sicklefin lemon shark Negaprion acudentis and graceful shark Carcharhinus amblyrhynchoides). Environmental (depth, visibility, salinity, temperature, tidal state, time of day) and geographic factors’ influence upon species capture rates are examined using generalized linear mixed models, along with yearly abundance estimates based on CPUE, sampling methods and juvenile-to-adult ratios examined for the five study species. The implications of using these methods to examine the influence of the Queensland gillnet ban in 2027 are presented.
3295: The giant manta ray (Mobula birostris) was listed on the U.S. Endangered Species Act as a “Threatened” species.  In 2020, the Florida Manta Project was the first to describe the highly-developed coastline of southeastern Florida as a potential manta ray nursery habitat. Here, we provide updated results on the demographics of the nursery habitat, and attempt to define its boundaries using acoustic and satellite telemetry data. Since 2016, we have identified 212 individuals (52% resighted) in south Florida using in-water photo identification. Aerial surveys revealed that most (89%) manta sightings occurred between July and January across years. Additionally, acoustic (n=27) and satellite (n=40) tag deployments on both juvenile and adult mantas along the eastern coast of Florida highlighted both long distance movements and site fidelity. Taxonomic and genetic evidence suggests that manta rays in the Western Atlantic are a separate species (M. cf. birostris) and little is understood about the ecology and life history of this putative species. Understanding the spatial extent of this manta ray nursery habitat will facilitate management decisions of this threatened species in an area where juvenile manta rays are frequently harmed by vessel strikes and fishing gear entanglement.
3296: Species distribution modeling is often used to predict species’ habitats and how these may shift under climate change. However, these models commonly assume that all members of a species have the same environmental niche, which is problematic when applied over a broad environmental range, since local adaptation can lead subpopulations to have different optimal conditions. Here, we use a simulated dataset to develop a hierarchical modeling framework that can predict optimal habitat for locally-adapted populations of a widely distributed species. We apply this framework to occurrences of juvenile tiger sharks (Galeocerdo cuvier), large marine predators with evidence for genetic differentiation between subpopulations. Our approach relies on generalized additive mixed modeling built on a joint likelihood framework that allows information-sharing between adaptive groups, unlike previous methods that either split data from each population into separate distribution models or pool into one without accounting for local adaptation. Using the simulated dataset, we test different model parameterizations, identify the optimal use of predictors, explore implications of inconsistent sampling across space, and assess the model’s specificity when inferring differences between adaptive groups. We find that models that include a variable representing adaptive subpopulation have better predictive power than models that do not. Model results for tiger sharks include population-specific predictions under climate change that account for local adaptation to different optimal oceanographic conditions. This model framework serves as a valuable first step toward accounting for local adaptation in species distribution modeling, representing important advances to fishery research and management in a changing ocean.
3297: Genomic variation within species is key for adaptation and survival in changing environments. Determining what factors influence that variation is thus an important goal for managing wildlife populations and conserving biodiversity. Amphibians are lacking from many comparative studies of genomic variation because they have large, complex genomes, and few studies have characterized genomic diversity across geographic space in a comparative framework. In this study, we generated new genome-wide sequence data for 46 frog species sampled across eastern North America to investigate the influence of historical processes and contemporary landscape on within-species variation. For two years (2022–2023), we launched a large-scale fieldwork effort across 30 states in the USA, producing >1,900 holistic specimens from >40 species, which are searchable via the Arctos collection management system and available for loan from the Museum of Southwestern Biology, University of New Mexico. We supplemented these samples with >900 frozen tissues through loans from 23 other natural history collections to fill in geographic sampling gaps. We used a double-digest Restriction Associated DNA (ddRAD) sequencing approach to generate genome-scale data for >2,600 frogs, with an average of 48 individuals per species. We use these data to map genomic diversity within species, identify potential ‘hot spots’ of diversity across species, and test predictions about the role of historical climate stability on current patterns of genomic variation. This resource will help address pressing questions about the determinants of genomic diversity, a fundamental component of biodiversity needed to ensure population persistence.
3298: Temperature is a critical environmental factor that profoundly influences the life histories of organisms, particularly ectothermic animals that rely on external heat sources for thermal homeostasis. This study explores the molecular evolution of temperature-sensitive ion channels, specifically TRPA1, on Neotropical frogs, a group of organisms facing the imminent threat of accelerated climate change. We generated RNA-seq data for 50 Neotropical frog species. We then isolated TRPA1 sequences and used Bayesian and maximum likelihood models to detect positive selection at different amino acids. We spatially visualized those sites under selection by performing 3D modeling of the protein. Finally, we compared our results with results obtained in other vertebrate groups. Preliminary findings show a novel insertion of approximately 15 amino acids in TRPA1 upstream of the transmembrane domain in poison frogs, suggesting possible adaptations to deleterious temperature changes. Furthermore, distinctive modifications in pre-S1 and linker, ARD, and pore regions are identified in poison frogs, suggesting possible behavioral consequences linked to temperature-sensitive pore opening. Further examination of TRPA1 sequences from different families reveals considerable variation in the ARK regions, which is important in temperature activation. Comparative analyses between TRPA1 pore-forming regions reveal conserved amino acid changes (I905L, I906M, S910T, R919H, E920D) in hTRPA1. These changes likely underlie the observed differences in temperature activation, as humans show sensitivity to cold temperatures and frogs respond to higher temperatures. This research provides an understanding of molecular adaptations in temperature-sensitive ion channels in Neotropical frogs, shedding light on their resilience strategies amidst the challenges of climate change.
3299: Fish, amphibians, and squamate reptiles are distinctive among vertebrates for possessing unisexual lineages. While the mechanisms of reproduction among these lineages vary, two unifying characteristics that set them apart from other vertebrate species: (1) they asexually pass on all of their genetic material to descendants (clonal reproduction), (2) they are of hybrid origin and maintain high heterozygosity via infrequent recombination ("frozen genome"). These characteristics (clonality and hybridity) establish a unique genetic environment that contributes to the evolution of these lineages, resulting in differences in mitonuclear dynamics in unisexual lineages compared to sexual lineages. Here we provide a perspective on the intra-parental and inter-parental genomic interactions experienced by unisexual vertebrate organisms and the implications of these interactions on mitochondrial function and resulting organismal performance and fitness. We incorporate our organismal, physiological, and genomic findings that we’ve collected from whiptail lizards (genus Aspidoscelis), and discuss how approaches can be expanded to other study systems. Building upon the hypothesis that sexual reproduction arose as a means to cope with the consequences of maintaining two independently-evolving genomes in a cell (nuclear and mitochondrial), we pose that the predominantly young ages of unisexual lineages may be due to incompatibilities that are a consequence of either clonality or hybridity. We discuss approaches fish, amphibian, and reptile researchers can take to disentangle the effects of clonality and hybridity to understand the degree to which these characteristics contribute to differences in mitochondrial function, organismal performance, and fitness.
3300: Exploring the evolution of chromatin conformation among species is fundamental to decipher the mechanism(s) responsible for the origin and plasticity of genome architecture. Distant loci within the genome interact non-randomly during the cell cycle to regulate gene function, in patterns that vary among species and may dictate the evolutionary dynamics of genome function. Indeed, 3D chromatin structure responds to environmental stimuli in ways that remain obscure, particularly in non-model organisms such as turtles, whose 3D-CS is understudied. This gap hinders our understanding of the full epigenetic machinery underlying adaptation to changing environments beyond chemical changes to the linear genome. In an attempt to capture the diversity and evolution of vertebrate chromatin conformation, here we generate de novo genome assemblies for two cryptodiran (hide-neck) turtles combining Illumina sequencing with chromosome conformation capture and RNA-seq. This included the spiny soft-shell turtle Apalone spinifera (ZZ/ZW, 2n = 66) and the Mexican musk turtle Staurotypus triporcatus (XX/XY, 2n = 54), who possess contrasting sex chromosomal systems and diploid chromosome numbers. Whole-genome comparisons revealed distinct trends of chromosome rearrangements in turtles: i) low rate of genome reshuffling in Apalone whose karyotype is highly conserved when compared to chicken (likely ancestral for turtles), and ii) moderate rate of fusions/fissions in Staurotypus (Kinosternidae) and Trachemys scripta (Emydidae). Moreover, we identified chromosome folding patterns previously undetected in turtles, namely centromere-telomere interactions. This pattern differs from chromosomal territories commonly present in eutherian mammals and centromere clustering (previously reported in sauropsids and marsupials). This combined turtle pattern (centromere-telomere interactions plus centromere-clustering) is novel for amniotes. We hypothesize that the divergent pattern found in turtles originated from a vertebrate ancestral state defined by a nuclear configuration with extensive associations among micro-chromosomes that were preserved upon genome reshuffling. Our findings open interesting questions about the way that the epigenome might respond adaptively to environmental changes.
3301: Early exposure to STEM experiences is widely recognized as a method to increase interest and retention in undergraduate and graduate programs, but there are several barriers limiting high school students from participating in STEM internship experiences, especially those from underrepresented minority groups. Using a long-term mark-recapture study on Blanding’s Turtles (Emydoidea blandingii), we developed the T.U.R.T.L.E. (Teens Understanding Research Techniques and Learning Ecology) program to provide high school students with hands-on, authentic field experiences that foster inclusion and belonging. Interns were given pre- and post-experience surveys to assess changes in confidence applying for or obtaining a job in conservation, knowledge of field equipment and transferrable skills, perceived inclusion in the field, and feelings of belongingness/support. We also instituted a returning cohort to assist with training new recruits and provide peer-to-peer role models. Participants reported that they gained field conservation skills, felt like they belonged in the field, built a community among their cohort, and enjoyed their experience.
Panel Discussion: DEI in Ecology and Resource Management
3302: Ongoing discussions around diversity, equity, inclusion, accessibility, justice, and safety have heightened awareness of the systemic barriers faced by marginalized individuals in STEM. Research consistently highlights high rates of harassment, discrimination, isolation, and institutional inaction, particularly affecting women and racial and ethnic minorities. This presentation examines these challenges within conservation, ecology, and natural resource fields, focusing on harassment, accountability, reporting measures, and a case study in herpetology. We analyzed survey responses from over 900 individuals across these disciplines, emphasizing the experiences of women and racial and ethnic minorities. Our findings show that women, gender-nonconforming/non-binary individuals, and racial and ethnic minorities reported discrimination at significantly higher rates than white cisgender men. Additionally, two-thirds of men in our studies reported witnessing discrimination against women or minorities. Aligning with previous research in marine sciences, these high rates of harassment, dissatisfaction with reporting outcomes, and institutional inaction contribute to decreased career efficacy and retention. Our findings underscore the urgent need for stronger accountability mechanisms and structural reforms to address harassment and foster more inclusive professional environments. Implementing protocols established by organizations such as Field Inclusive can help create safer spaces for future scientists. Additionally, evaluating both effective and harmful reporting mechanisms is crucial to ensuring meaningful institutional responses to these pervasive issues.
Panel Discussion: DEI in Ecology and Resource Management
3303: Aquifers and springs serve as critical freshwater sources for humans as well as being habitats for numerous imperiled species. However, due to anthropogenic modifications including impoundments and other infrastructure, there are many challenges to conserving species within these habitats. The Barton Springs complex within the Edwards Aquifer of central Texas illustrates these challenges because it is situated in the middle of a large metropolitan area and is home to two endangered spring-dwelling salamanders in the genus Eurycea. This study discusses the results of expanding habitat for the endangered Barton Springs salamander (E. sosorum) by restoring a 21 meter spring-run that had been buried for almost 100 years. We evaluated salamander colonization and quantified biological and physical characteristics of the spring-run to assess the project’s effectiveness. We documented salamander colonization within the first 8 months after construction. A distinct macroinvertebrate community also colonized the spring-run, including a hyperendemic spring snail Elimia comalensis, groundwater isopod Lirceolus hardeni, and a microcaddisfly common to fast-flowing streams Leucotrichia sarita. Salamander abundance dramatically improved after we reduced the substrate size class found within the spring-run habitat. Comparing periods before and after the spring-run restoration, average salamander density increased from 4.8 to 10.6 ind./m2 and average abundance (N) increased from 354 to 1051. Our results demonstrate the benefits of habitat restoration projects and how a relatively small habitat expansion can have a large impact on an endangered species.
3304: The intensity and frequency of forest fires are increasing, with serious consequences for animal populations. The effects of fire are both immediate (death from heat, smoke, etc.) and delayed, through injury and habitat degradation. In burnt landscapes, survivors are largely deprived of shelter (to protect them from extreme weather conditions and predators), food resources and their usual geographical landmarks. However, these survivors represent the greatest hope for repopulation. In the summer of 2021, a forest fire in south-eastern France devastated several thousand hectares of Mediterranean habitats, causing high mortality rates (40% to 60%) and numerous injuries in one of the last populations of Hermann's tortoises (Testudo hermanni hermanni). Survivors were immediately monitored by radio tracking for two years. Other individuals were monitored before and after the fire on a nearby unburned control site, allowing a reliable assessment of delayed fire effects. Surprisingly, the survivors did not leave the devastated landscapes and exhibited movements similar to those of the control tortoises. They were able to select high quality residual microhabitats and maintain their body condition. The image of devastated landscapes with survivors apparently wandering over scorched earth is misleading; it is preferable not to rescue them by moving them to intact areas. It might even be beneficial to support repopulation through population reinforcement. Preventive measures should also be tested to limit immediate mortality, for example by building many small stone shelters, which protect tortoises from fire much better than bushes.
3305: In snakes, male-to-male fights are much more common in species where the males are larger than the females. This relationship is not systematic. Sexual competition can be expressed in other ways, such as territoriality without physical fighting. This seems to be the case in the Montpellier snake (Malpolon monspessulanus), a fast species in which the males are much larger and more powerful than the females. In the French Mediterranean region, urban development and infrastructure projects are threatening the populations of this species. Assessing possible territorial interactions, in terms of habitat occupation and spatial distribution, has become important to address the ecological needs of the species in the context of declining populations and consequent conservation measures. Observations based on radio tracking and CMR monitoring clearly indicate that males can coexist peacefully even in the presence of adult females, with individuals of different sizes using the same shelter at the same time during the mating season. However, possible spatial exclusion or avoidance between individuals of similar size has been suggested when shelter resources are abundant. Despite regular radio tracking and numerous field observations, no signs of fighting were observed. Habitat restoration could therefore take into account access to shelter (e.g. through the construction of a network of artificial shelters) and the maintenance of sufficiently large protected areas with heterogeneous microhabitats. Where appropriate, we recommend a comprehensive approach to the translocation of individuals into host populations to avoid disrupting what appears to be a complex social balance.
3306: Automated image analysis can enable rapid and consistent measurements from visual data, reducing manual effort and error. We developed a software workflow to measure salamander size from thousands of standardized digital photographs. Photographs were taken of every individual of Eurycea sosorum (Barton Springs salamanders) captured as part of a long-term capture-recapture study. Individual data on size are important for understanding population demographic trends, recruitment, and survival. However, with thousands of images captured on an annual basis, manually measuring salamanders from photographs is time-consuming and tedious. To automate measurements from these data, we first segmented each image by thresholding (transformed into a binary black/white) in Photoshop. We then used ImageJ to calculate the dorsal salamander area, length (skeletonize) and diameter of the largest inscribed circle (max feret) for 1851 images that we had manually measured. With half of the data, we fit a linear model to predict body length. We then evaluated the performance of our automated measurements versus the “known” body length with the test data. The adjusted R-squared was 0.98 for the fitted model. Comparing the predicted values versus the “known” values from the test data, the mean absolute error was 0.61 mm (2.8%); root mean square error was 0.89 mm. Size classification of adult versus juveniles with a body length cutoff of 22.5 mm resulted in a test error rate of 1.6%. For studies that have access to many standardized images of animals, automated measurements may save time without significant loss of accuracy.
3307: The Wood Turtle, Glyptemys insculpta, is a candidate for federal listing as threatened. Like many species, they are imperiled by a multitude of factors, including habitat loss and fragmentation. Consequently, it is imperative that we understand their patterns of movement and habitat use. Wood Turtles can often be seen making large movements across both terrestrial and aquatic habitats, exposing them to potential barriers and bottlenecks. We attached GPS units to turtles to gather data on preferred habitats and movement patterns. Monitored individuals made use of a variety of terrestrial habitats types, especially forest. However, they remained within 500m of suitable rivers and streams. With this identification of patterns of movement and habitat use, Circuitscape was then used to identify the connectivity patterns for the turtles across the landscape. Our findings will inform land managers as they develop management strategies for both the species and the landscape.
3308: Anabantarian fishes (labyrinth fishes, snakeheads, swamp and spiny eels, etc.) are tropical freshwater fishes that inhabit Afrotropical and Indomalayan freshwaters. Anabantarians are notable for their ability to breathe air through the use of air-breathing organs (ABOs). Also notable for its broad phenotypic diversity, with body shapes ranging from eel-like to perch-like or scale-less to armored. The evolution of an air-breathing organ may be correlated with the evolution of such diverse body shapes in this group. Within Anabantaria, the ABOs of Anabantiformes (labyrinth fishes, snakeheads, and leaf fishes) are reported to be derived from the gill skeleton, located between the neurocranium and the pectoral girdle. Given the large space the ABO occupies in the post-cranial region, we hypothesize there has been re-patterning of the skull, particularly with respect to anterior-posterior coordination, in anabantiforms with ABOs compared to those without. Here, we use 3D landmarking and geometric morphometrics in a phylogenetic context to compare the degree of phenotypic integration of the skull between closely-related lineages with and without air-breathing organs, as well as describe shape disparity of the cranium across anabantiforms. We predict that lineages with ABOs will exhibit greater shape disparity in the posterior neurocranium, as well as a deepening or elongation of the body relative to aquatic-respiring sister taxa. This work was supported by the National Science Foundation awards DEB-2333683 and DEB-2333684.
3309: Forests are three-dimensional ecosystems where species occupy habitat across both horizontal and vertical space, creating a complex web of interactions shaped by food web dynamics, climate variability, and species-specific behaviours, among other factors. However, due to the logistical challenges of accessing the canopy, vertical niche data remains extremely limited. To address this gap, we applied a novel microphone array and audio triangulation technique to map the vertical distribution of calling amphibians in a tropical rainforest. From August to November 2024, we deployed fourteen GPS-synchronized Audiomoth microphones between ground and canopy (0 - 25 meters) at a vernal pond in southern Gabon, and recorded acoustic data with microsecond precision. Using a newly-developed algorithm, we extracted call localities with unprecedented vertical accuracy and analysed a four-day subset of data to assess species-specific vertical stratification and seasonal shifts in community composition. Preliminary results reveal significant vertical niche differentiation, with some species specializing in the canopy while others exhibit flexible vertical habitat use. Importantly, these findings demonstrate the power of acoustic triangulation for studying canopy biodiversity, offering a scalable and non-invasive method applicable to a wide range of sound-producing taxa, including crickets, bats, and birds. By improving our understanding of how species use vertical space, this approach has the potential to enhance conservation strategies, particularly in the face of habitat modification and climate change.
3310: Genetic, environmental, and functional constraints can limit morphological diversification. Integration between separate morphological units may require coordinated evolution to maintain function, constraining morphological diversity, but when parts of a system in an organism become decoupled, these limitations can be lifted, resulting in accelerated morphological divergence. The feeding apparatus in ray-finned fishes is a classic example of a functionally decoupled system. Ray-finned fishes have an oral jaw derived from the anterior bones of the gill arches and a second set of jaws derived from the posterior bones of the gill arches (pharyngeal jaws), separating the prey capture and prey processing mechanisms. This morphological and functional separation of the jaws allows fishes to bypass the mechanical constraints of a single jaw system, which is confined to the typical force/velocity trade-offs. Additionally, extrinsic factors, like diet type and microhabitat, can influence the form and function of the jaws, where the food processing pharyngeal jaws may be correlated with prey type, whereas the oral jaws may be associated with prey capture mechanisms. The leuciscids provide an ideal model to test for decoupling of the two-jaw system and determine how ecological transitions may influence decoupling. Leuciscids are ecomorphologically diverse, inhabiting a wide range of freshwater environments and displaying variation in morphology that their ecologies may influence. In this study, we use 3D geometric morphometrics and phylogenetic comparative methods to test for decoupling of the two-jaw system and how ecology may influence decoupling in the North American leuciscids.
3311: Biomechanical systems can be inherently complex, comprised of several traits that function and operate together to perform specific tasks. Today these systems are widespread across the tree of life and present across a broad diversity of organisms. How do these complex systems organize and evolve? Modularity-the compartmentalization of traits into semi-autonomous units has been hypothesized to play an important role in the evolution of complexity.
