Here we examine the role of modularity in the evolution of one of the most complex biomechanical structures on the planet; the fish skull across three different clades of fishes and show that modularity has played a central role in the organization of the fish skull. We also find that evolutionary modularity has strongly impacted the evolutionary trajectories of different regions of the skull. Our results suggest that modularity is critically important for the organization of complex systems by allowing them to evolve and adapt semi-independently.
3312: Pricklebacks (Stichaeidae) are a model for studying nutritional adaptations to diet in fishes. Several species integrate increasing amounts of plant material into their diets as they grow, and these ontogenetic dietary shifts are matched by digestive adaptations to better process and assimilate plant material. Since the mechanical demands of eating plants vary considerably from the demands of a carnivorous diet, we hypothesized that oral and pharyngeal jaw morphology and shape would reflect the differing demands of diet over ontogeny. We captured the fine morphology of these fishes using high resolution microCT across four species of pricklebacks and over ontogeny. We first explored oral jaw morphology, dental characteristics, and tooth biomechanics. We then compared jaw and dental traits between species and quantified the scaling of these traits over ontogeny. We used linear discriminant analyses to identify traits that drive differences between dietary groups. Lastly, we quantified functional variation within dentitions using a functional homodonty model. Pricklebacks span jaw and tooth morphotypes from fast-moving jaws with many needle-like teeth, to stronger jaws with large, rounded teeth. While there is trait overlap between groups, we found several jaw and dental traits differentiate dietary groups and exhibit allometry over ontogeny. We then used 3D geometric morphometrics to characterize the shape trajectory of the oral and pharyngeal jaws and their covariance. Preliminary results show herbivorous and omnivorous fishes to exhibit isometry in oral jaw shape but they develop robust pharyngeal jaws for prey processing, while carnivorous fishes develop large oral jaws with little pharyngeal changes
3313: The growing availability of computed tomography (CT) data enables biologists to compare complex morphologies across larger macroevolutionary scales. However, the challenge with large data sets is processing it in a timely fashion, which calls for the development of new analytical softwares. Recently, 3D Slicer has gained a lot of traction among organismal biologists as an open-source platform for analyzing 3D morphology due to the development of new extensions, tutorials, and user community. To facilitate the ease and speed of collecting biomechanical data from CT scans, we developed SlicerBiomech, a 3D Slicer extension that currently includes tools for modelling tooth and bite mechanics as well as calculating cross-sectional properties of skeletal structures. With SlicerBiomech, data collection procedures that previously took hours and multiple software, can be accomplished semi-automatically in seconds using a single platform. Here, we demonstrate how SlicerBiomech can aid studies on evolutionary morphology. Specifically, we investigated the hypothesis that adaptive feeding traits are associated with arboreality in Aneides. We quantified the function of 780 teeth across 20 salamander species, and compared stiffness of the jaws based on their cross-sectional morphologies. We did not find support that changes in Aneides dentitions are accompanied by functional shifts, nor are there similarities among different arboreal lineages. Nevertheless, this study leverages new tools to generate an integrative data set that provides a more comprehensive understanding of the salamander feeding apparatus. Developing new tools to rapidly quantify 3D morphology is essential for increasing the number and diversity of evolutionary questions that can be answered.
3314: The field of ecology inherently encompasses a wide range of interactions among organisms, populations, species, systems, and environments, extending from individual to global scales. Three-dimensional approaches to ecological studies are equally varied, ranging from microhabitat use in forests to the geographic structure of biodiversity in the open ocean. In this talk, I present a brief overview of the background and current advancements in 3D ecological studies of fishes and herpetofauna. By synthesizing these studies, I demonstrate that incorporating the third dimension into ecological research, much like in morphological studies, enhances accuracy and precision. However, these opportunities often require approaches that demand more extensive and higher- quality data compared to traditional 2D methods. Continued collaboration in 3D ecology holds the promise of overcoming these challenges, deepening our understanding of ecological processes, and improving conservation and management strategies.
3315: Imaging sonar offers new opportunities to study aquatic organisms in three dimensions, enabling volumetric measurements and species identification without traditional capture-based biases. Operating at frequencies up to 3 MHz, beyond the hearing threshold of most aquatic fauna, this technology allows in situ data collection independent of turbidity or ambient light. We are using adaptive-resolution imaging sonar to develop methods for (1) obtaining volumetric measurements of aquatic fauna and (2) building a database of species-specific shape, movement patterns, and acoustic signatures to inform machine learning models for automated species identification. For volumetric measurements, we conducted pilot experiments on free-ranging Alligator Gar (Atractosteus spatula), Alligator Snapping Turtle (Macrochelys temminckii), and Diamondback Terrapin (Malaclemys terrapin), comparing acoustically derived measurements to those taken upon capture. Preliminary results are promising, particularly for A. spatula, though challenges remain in resolving carapace height for M. temminckii and M. terrapin. To advance species recognition, we supplemented field data with controlled imaging of captive paddlefish (Polyodon spathula), lake sturgeon (Acipenser fulvescens), buffalo spp. (Ictiobus), and longnose gar (Lepisosteus osseus) at the Audubon Aquarium of the Americas. These data will inform machine learning models designed to differentiate species based on sonar-derived morphology and movement signatures. This work aims to refine imaging sonar as a non-invasive tool for species identification, improving biodiversity assessments across diverse aquatic systems. Further collaborations are essential to expand its potential with advanced post-processing tools.
3316: Continuing discoveries of coelacanth populations off the East African coast and in the Indo-Pacific suggest our knowledge of their distributions is far from complete. Current species distribution modelling tools were designed for use in 2D terrestrial environments, and when deployed in marine ecosystems, the influence of depth as an axis is often neglected. Here, we introduce infrastructure to model and project coelacanth distributions in 3 dimensions. Using occurrence records for the West Indian Ocean coelacanth, Latimeria chalumnae, we produced 3D and 2D maximum entropy ecological niche models and projected them into the habitat of the Indonesian coelacanth, Latimeria menadoensis. We gauged each model’s success by how well it could predict L. menadoensis presences recorded from submersible observations. While the 2D model omitted 33% of occurrences at the most forgiving threshold, the 3D model successfully predicted all occurrences, regardless of threshold level while still limiting commission errors. The 3D model predicted coelacanth suitable habitat off the coast of the Philippines, the Northern coasts of Papua and Papua New Guinea, the islands of the Banda Sea, and the Lesser Sunda islands between 100 and 250 m. Incorporating depth resulted in improved model accuracy when predicting coelacanth habitat, and projecting into 3 dimensions provides insight for targeted future sampling. This 3D modelling framework can help improve our understanding of how marine species are distributed by depth, allowing for more targeted conservation management.
3317: Sea turtles are some of many wildlife species adversely affected by Florida red tide, Karenia brevis. This marine dinoflagellate blooms almost annually along Florida’s southwest coast and produces brevetoxins, a suite of potent neurotoxins. These brevetoxins can be transferred through the marine food web to reach carnivorous loggerhead and Kemp’s ridley sea turtles to then cause significant impacts on various physiological systems. Sea turtles stranded during red tide can be rescued, transported to rehabilitation facilities, and given palliative care with the goal of release. However, there are no definitive diagnostic criteria for brevetoxicosis other than stranding association with red tide, but often sea turtles experience delayed exposure because of the long temporal scale of trophic transfer of toxins. Our hypothesis is that brevetoxicosis can cause alterations in sea turtle plasma protein abundance, and those with significant differences in abundance can be used as diagnostic biomarkers. Plasma samples that were taken from red-tide exposed and healthy sea turtles were analyzed via bottom-up labelled quantitative liquid chromatography tandem mass spectrometry-based proteomics to identify such biomarkers. We were able to conclude that the abundances of multiple sea turtle plasma proteins were significantly altered when exposed to the red tide. With predicted increases in severity and duration of red tide blooms due to climate change, the threatened and critically endangered status of the loggerhead and Kemp’s ridley sea turtles, and demonstration of plasma protein alterations after red tide exposure, this study can inform more accurate diagnoses and mechanism-based treatments for wildlife with brevetoxicosis.
3318: The fully aquatic, neotenic Barton Springs salamander (BSS; Eurycea sosorum) and Austin blind salamander (Eurycea waterlooensis) inhabit the Barton Springs segment of the Edwards Aquifer in Austin, Texas. The City of Austin has monitored wild populations and maintained captive assurance colonies of these endangered species for decades as part of a Habitat Conservation Plan. The BSS is normally found in the cobble and gravel near springs, but we found individuals floating in the water column and at the water’s surface exhibiting gas bubble trauma (GBT). GBT is caused by harmful gas bubbles in an animal’s body and can be due to uncompensated, supersaturated total dissolved gas (TDG) pressure in the animal’s aquatic environment. There is little information in the scientific literature on GBT in amphibians in the wild. In this presentation, we discuss our observations and related data on GBT in these salamanders. We documented 33 observations of GBT in BSS in the wild. In extreme instances, we found salamanders like balloons with gas bubbles that resulted in skin ruptures, hemorrhaging, secondary infections, and death. From 2,383 unique days of daily average measurements of TDG, we found that the groundwater was supersaturated 99% of the time and above 110% saturation 49% of the time. We also observed GBT and mild GBT/gas-bloat in both species in captive environments. This interesting phenomenon warrants more research so we can better understand how these species survive supersaturated TDG in the groundwater to which they are endemic.
3319: Metabolic rate (MR) is a metric that summarizes an organism’s energy expenditure over a given period. While many factors influence MR, body size is a primary determinant. Therefore, considerable research has focused on the allometric scaling relationship between MR and body mass in adult animals. However, much less is known about the relationship between MR and body mass in neonates and juveniles, which is an important distinction given that growth represents a significant energetic cost that is not present in adult animals. Additionally, little work has investigated the metabolic differences between juveniles from the same clutch, although body size can vary between littermates and often impacts neonate survival. Such research could shed light on the characteristics of a successful neonate in species, such as chameleons, in which many neonates do not survive to adulthood. The present study examined the scaling relationships of resting metabolic rates in ten juvenile Southern dwarf chameleons (Bradypodion ventrale) over the first five months of life. Resting metabolic rate was measured using stop-flow respirometry in postabsorptive animals. There was significant variation in growth rate and metabolic scaling among individuals; scaling exponents ranged from 0.62 to 0.95. However, there was no correlation between scaling exponent and individual survival, suggesting that MR is not a reliable predictor of individual survival in neonate B. ventrale. This work will help to characterize the most energetically costly stages of growth, which can be applied towards increasing survival outcomes of neonates and juveniles in other chameleon species and other reptile taxa.
3320: Common Garter Snakes (Thamnophis sirtalis) are abundant and widespread semiaquatic colubrid snakes in North America. However, Southern California populations are rare and declining amid climate change and urbanization. Habitat suitability may have declined because of changes in microniches that affect the physiological water requirements of T. sirtalis. To determine if this has occurred, we are (1) characterizing remaining habitats (2) comparing microclimates between current (n = 6) and historic (n = 6) sites, and (3) comparing rates of temperature-dependent (20, 25, 30, and 35 ºC) evaporative water loss (EWL) for T. sirtalis (n = 6) and five other local snake species (Arizona elegans, Lampropeltis californiae, Masticophis flagellum, Pituophis catenifer, and Thamnophis hammondii, n = 8 per species).  We standardized EWL rates by snake body mass and controlled for water vapor associated with the testing apparatus. We predicted historic habitats have become drier than those with current populations, and that the water dependence of T. sirtalis, inferred by EWL rates, will be higher than those of other snakes. Neither temperature nor humidity of historic snake localities were different from extant localities, yet T. sirtalis had elevated EWL rates compared to regionally abundant species. Our findings will inform conservation efforts for this snake, which is listed as a California Species of Special Concern.
3321: Amphibians are the most endangered vertebrates in the current global scenario, with emerging pathogens being one of the leading causes of population declines. However, amidst a changing environment and exposure to stressors, the amphibian immune response is understudied. The initial hours following pathogen exposure are critical for mounting an effective immune response, with the liver playing a pivotal role in producing acute-phase proteins. We tracked the gene expression of cytokines and acute-phase proteins during the early stage of the inflammatory response in immune-stimulated toads (Rhinella diptycha). Toads were injected with lipopolysaccharide (LPS) or saline and tissue samples were collected 1-, 3-, 6- and 18-hours post-injection to measure mRNA levels of pro- and anti-inflammatory cytokines and acute-phase proteins. The toads upregulated all cytokines in spleen and liver, but complement protein C1s showed a time- and organ-dependent effect, being upregulated only in the liver at early time-points. Further investigations in the liver showed upregulation of complement proteins C4 and C5, and acute-phase protein SAA in response to LPS. C4 and C5 exhibited a significant interaction between treatment and time. C4 showed upregulation in the LPS-stimulated toads specifically at 3h and 18h post-injection, while C5 showed upregulation at 6h post-injection that persisted through 18h. These results indicate a coordinated activation of cytokines and specific complement components, highlighting the liver as an immune organ in amphibians and the critical involvement of acute-phase proteins during early inflammation. Such responses are likely crucial for controlling initial pathogen proliferation and directing subsequent immune responses in amphibians.
3322: Miniaturization is a phenomenon seen across clades which has profound effects on organismal body plans and ecologies. Miniaturized species experience different selective pressures than their non-miniaturized congeners including prey availability and acquisition capacity, and increased mass-specific metabolic rates (MR), likely influencing their feeding ecologies. We sought to better understand how miniaturization may influence feeding frequency in Brookesia chameleons using comparative Specific Dynamic Action (SDA). SDA, broadly defined as the overall energetic “cost” of processing prey, has been shown to vary by species feeding frequency where infrequently feeding species display greater SDA-induced peak MRs, elevated MR durations, and overall energetic cost. Following this pattern, miniaturized Brookesia species are predicted to show high cost of SDA relative to non-miniaturized chameleon species, reflecting a comparatively infrequent feeding frequency. To set the basis to test this hypothesis, Brookesia brygooi and Brookesia thieli individuals were fed cricket meals measuring 3.5 ± 0.5% of the chameleon’s body mass after a 72-hour fasting period. Changes in MR post feeding were measured overnight to avoid effects of circadian rhythm at 12-hour intervals until MR returned to basal rates (Standard Metabolic Rate). Our results suggest variability in the effect of SDA even within the Brookesia genus with significantly longer duration, higher mass-corrected peak MR, and greater SDA cost in B. thieli than in B. brygooi. Such a finding between closely related species would suggest stronger comparative power of SDA than previously believed and will lay the foundation for future work seeking to compare to non-miniaturized species.
3323: Lead (Pb) is an extremely toxic heavy metal pollutant pervasive in many environments with serious health consequences for humans and wildlife. Identifying organisms that can serve as models to understand mechanisms of lead tolerance is therefore an important goal. We found that Cuban brown anole lizards (Anolis sagrei) in New Orleans, USA, have the highest mean and individual blood lead levels of any free-living vertebrate reported to date, with values over two times higher than the next highest published levels. Unexpectedly, this extreme field lead exposure did not decrease performance in whole-organism traits commonly affected by lead (balance, sprint speed, endurance). We next employed a 60-day lead dosing experiment and found that the brown anole blood lead threshold for decreased whole-organism performance is over an order of magnitude higher than the already extreme mean field concentration. Transcriptomic analysis of brain and liver from lizards in high and low lead sites revealed relatively minor effects of lead exposure. However, several of the differentially expressed genes function in metal ion homeostasis and oxygen carrying capacity, pointing to cellular mechanisms that may contribute to high lead tolerance in these animals. The brown anole may be the most lead-tolerant vertebrate known to date and has the potential to be a powerful model system to help us better understand how organisms cope with heavy metal exposure.
3324: Emerging fungal diseases caused by dermatophytes, or dermatomycoses, have become especially prevalent in reptiles. One such emerging disease is ophidiomycosis in snakes, caused by the fungus Ophidiomyces ophidiicola (Oo). To predict susceptibility to fungal infections and prioritize populations for conservation and management, we need to better characterize immune responses associated with fungal infections and examine variation between species and populations. In the present study, we characterized immune function in snakes in Arkansas by conducting microbial killing assays on blood serum (serum and buffy layer) collected from multiple snake species and populations. To identify the contribution of specific innate immune components (e.g., live cells, complement, and heat-resistant proteins) to microbial killing ability, we used fresh, frozen, and heat-treated serum. To further build a baseline and quantify variability of live immune cells, we quantified relative heterophil, lymphocyte, and azurophil population proportions at baseline using flow cytometry. We then examined whether relative leukocyte proportions and killing ability of each serum manipulation could inform predictions of lesion presence, lesion severity, and ophidiomycosis presence (confirmed using quantitative PCR). This research provides insight into the functional immune responses in wild snakes and further informs which immune metrics are useful for assessing disease risk in snake species and populations.
3325: Novel challenges from the external environment can evoke physiological and behavioral changes in an organism. Ambient light at night (ALAN) is an environmental challenge that can disrupt physiological and behavioral rhythms. An organism may also use behavior to ameliorate the effects of ALAN and to maintain natural rhythms (behavioral or physiological). It was the objective of this project to determine how ALAN affected physiological and behavioral norms in Green Anoles (Anolis carolinensis). Specifically, we measured metabolic rates and glucocorticoid concentrations of anoles (n=18) at noon and midnight following a prolonged exposure to ALAN and compared these results to anoles kept under a natural light:dark cycle (Control Treatment; n=18). We measured food intake for all anoles and behavior of anoles. Half of the anoles in each treatment were provided a shelter box that they could use as refugia from ambient light at any time during the day. ALAN affected food consumption and glucocorticoid concentrations, but this was dependent on time of day and the presence of a shelter. Anoles in the ALAN Treatment without a shelter had disrupted glucocorticoid cycles and consumed more food. Anoles spent more time in shelters in the ALAN treatment compared to the Control Treatment. Results suggest that ALAN may disrupt glucocorticoid physiological processes; ultimately, mobilizing more energy within the body. Anoles may try to compensate by consuming more energy and using refugia to ameliorate the effects of ALAN. Environmental challenges may not only affect physiological processes, but may increase energy demand from the organism’s environment.
3326: Pacific newts (Taricha spp.) are poisonous salamanders common to the west coast of North America. Taricha are chemically defended against predation by tetrodotoxin (TTX), a paralytic neurotoxin which is synthesized by bacteria living on the skin of the newts and which is most concentrated in cutaneous granular glands. The existing literature shows a predictable pattern in toxicity across rough-skinned newt (Taricha granulosa) development, wherein TTX is present in eggs, declines after hatching and during larval development, reaches its lowest point in newly metamorphosed newts, and then dramatically increases in the first three years of adulthood. Granular glands develop during metamorphosis, and amphibian skin microbiomes typically change dramatically at this time as well, suggesting a relationship between morphological and microbial developmental changes and TTX acquisition. We seek to investigate the role and timing of microbial symbiosis and granular gland development in Taricha toxicity. We collected skin biopsies from larval, metamorphic, and adult T. granulosa and T. torosa (California newts) found together in a breeding pond in Santa Cruz County, California in September 2023 and 2024. Our results narrow the developmental window in which TTX accumulation is known to start in T. torosa. We will subsequently investigate changes in microbiome composition, host and microbiome gene expression, and skin morphology and TTX distribution across sampled age stages.
3327: Female Lemon Sharks, Negaprion brevirostris, have been documented to exhibit natal philopatry to the island of Bimini, The Bahamas, where the return to nursery habitats for pupping has been observed to follow a biannual cycle. However, the timing and drivers of their return to nursery grounds have yet to be determined. Mature females (n=16) were tagged with passive acoustic transmitters (Innovasea-V16) and tracked from 2014-2020 using a passive acoustic array of 80 receivers (Innovasea-Vr2w), 21 of these receivers were located near nursery habitats. We ensured that all sharks included in this study were around the island to pup by using the genetic lineage of pups collected for a concurrent mark-recapture project. Detections were analyzed to determine relationships involving arrival and movements within the nursery lagoon and abiotic factors such as tidal cycles, month, lunar phases, and environmental temperature. Further, Kernel density estimations were used to determine space use within the shallow water Bimini lagoon during the pupping phase. Despite being biannual reproducers, we have observed that certain individuals enter the nursery grounds every year. With these detections, it was found that more time spent in the lagoon occurred at night, in between tidal peaks, and during waning lunar phases. This study adds to the knowledge of the environmental cues that trigger return and pupping in a philopatric shark. Such information has great management implications as it can help with implementing informed seasonal protection measures and protecting critical habitats to boost species resilience in the Anthropocene.
3328: The Lemon Shark (Negaprion brevirostris) is a member of the large coastal shark complex found throughout the Atlantic Ocean and Gulf of Mexico, as well as the Gulf of California. The species is currently listed as vulnerable under the IUCN due to an apparent decrease in their populations, but their distribution is not well known throughout their entire range. We aim to understand the extent of Lemon Shark use of Mississippi Coastal Waters and identify trends in habitat association to better define characteristics of nursery habitat for the species. We used catch data from long-term gillnet monitoring in conjunction with a focused gillnet study in shallow water habitat around Cat Island, MS. Captured elasmobranch species were identified, sexed, measured, weighed, and surgically implanted with acoustic transmitters. In total, 29 Lemon sharks were implanted with acoustic transmitters between July 2023 and September 2024. Individuals were monitored through an acoustic array surrounding the tagging location and throughout the barrier island region. Captures and detections of Lemon sharks were concentrated mostly in shallow water, but in close proximity to deep water slopes. Preliminary temperature analyses demonstrate higher temperatures within the partially enclosed cove on the southern face of Cat Island and a wider temperature distribution than previously described for nursery areas (3.39 – 34.34˚C). Lemon Shark detections continued within our array even during extreme low temperatures. Information from this study will help to inform the designation of Lemon Shark nursery habitat in hopes to better describe available habitat for the species within their range.
3329: Sexual segregation is common in elasmobranchs and since females bear the energetic burden of reproduction, they may require different habitats and prey items than males, which may lead to different migratory patterns. Off the U.S. East Coast, male blacktip sharks overwinter off southeastern Florida and migrate as far north as Long Island, NY during summer months. Female blacktip sharks exhibit a synchronous, biennial reproductive cycle in which one year of reproduction is followed by a year of rest. The resting year is required for the female to recover fat stores that are depleted from nourishing its developing embryos during its gravid year. As a result of this greater energetic demand, migratory patterns may differ between males and females. We instrumented 36 female blacktip sharks with acoustic transmitters in South Carolina and tracked them along the U.S. East Coast and modeled their migratory movements using sea surface temperature (SST), chlorophyll-a, and photoperiod. We found that female blacktip sharks do not travel as far north as the males, where their migratory pattern ranged from Palm Beach, FL to mid-New Jersey. The shorter migratory range of females may be due to the lower energetic budget they exhibit because of reproduction. Females traveled northward as chlorophyll-a decreased in spring and SST and photoperiod increased during summer, and southward as photoperiod decreased during autumn and winter. Photoperiod may be a zeitgeber that facilitates preemption of upcoming changes in prey availability and temperature, which enables an individual to abandon deteriorating habitat before conditions become too poor.
3330: Juvenile white shark (Carcharodon carcharias) populations throughout the Southern California Bight are growing, yet our understanding of their movement and behavior within coastal nurseries remains limited. Particularly sparse is quantitative information detailing fine-scale shark-environment interactions, which ultimately underpin the dynamics of nursery site selection. These knowledge gaps impede our ability to identify critical juvenile white shark habitat resources, prevent negative fisheries interactions, and assess potential risks to coastal beach communities. In this study, we used fine-scale acoustic telemetry to investigate juvenile white shark nursery behaviors at a prominent aggregation site in San Diego, CA. We first used a Vemco Positioning System to estimate precise geolocations of 30 acoustically tagged individuals from July – December 2023. We are now using shark movement data in concert with high-resolution nearshore habitat data to fit time-discrete Hidden Markov Models (HMMs), which allow for estimation of latent states of shark behavior from telemetry-derived movement metrics (e.g., swimming speed, turning angle, depth occupied). This enables us to identify the timing and location of key nursery behaviors, as well as establish linkages between environmental conditions and the patterns of behavior they modulate.
3331: Nurse sharks (Ginglymostoma cirratum) are an abundant elasmobranch species found in shallow, coastal waters throughout the Atlantic Ocean. Previously listed as ‘data deficient’ by the IUCN, their status was updated to ‘vulnerable’ in 2021. Nurse sharks have historically been considered a benthic and sedentary species with strong side fidelity, but studies have found they can make long movements of over 500 km. New research has also determined they are slower-growing and longer-lived than previously documented, indicating additional work on this species is critical. In this study, 20 adult nurse sharks (11 M:9 F) from Bimini, The Bahamas, were tagged using 10-year passive acoustic transmitters from March 2015 to December 2017. Using acoustic telemetry data from these individuals, we describe their overall movement patterns, sex and seasonality-based variation, and presence of philopatry and/or site fidelity. Our findings show that Bimini nurse sharks move throughout The Bahamas, and occasionally cross international waters to the east coast of the USA. We even observe one female making a minimum distance migration of 773.5 km from Bimini to Charleston, South Carolina, USA. This movement behavior is not ubiquitous in the local population, as 11 individuals (6 M:5 F) were only detected in Bimini, making partial migration a plausible movement strategy for Bimini nurse sharks. Identifying the degree of movement and philopatry in these areas will help determine critical habitats, including overlap with areas at risk of anthropogenic disturbances, allowing conservation biologists to more appropriately assign protections for this species.
3332: Recovery of some shark populations due to conservation success along with rising popularity in ocean recreational activities has resulted in higher likelihoods of shark-human encounters, raising concerns for beach safety. However, little is known about how sharks might detect and respond to human activities in coastal beach habitats. Aerial observations of juvenile white sharks (Carcharodon carcharias; JWS) show orientation toward beach goers from distances exceeding 16-m in low visibility waters, which suggests strong directional acoustic-lateralis stimuli. We recorded swimmers, surfers, and kayakers at two standardized periodicities using a hydrophone, and described the differences of soundscapes, power spectra, and particle acceleration for each activity which were all found to be detectable above ambient levels as far as 16-m. We then compiled soundtracks from recordings into playback experiments at a JWS aggregation site where we compared response behavior between each activity treatment using aerial observations.
3333: Sandbar sharks (Carcharhinus plumbeus) primarily use the coastal waters of the New York Bight (NYB) from late spring through fall. Though sandbar sharks are a prohibited species in federal and state waters, including the NYB, habitat and dietary resource use in the NYB remains relatively unexplored. This study aims to address the gap in information on their habitat and forage preferences in the region in three ways: 1) acquire a better understanding of sandbar shark residency in the coastal NYB (within 25 kilometers from shore), 2) illuminate dietary resource use in the coastal NYB, and 3) quantify individual variation in sandbar shark dietary resource use in the NYB. We calculated a continuous residency index for each individual using acoustic telemetry data from 2018 – 2024. We then implemented carbon and nitrogen Bayesian isotope mixing models to estimate the contribution of key prey groups to individual dietary resource use. Using mixing model outputs, we calculated a diet similarity index by comparing each individual to the sampling population. The average duration of a residence event ranged from 0.25 – 27.5 (SE = 0.07 – 11.7) hours. Stable isotopes and the diet similarity indices revealed high diet similarity across individuals, with a strong preference for pelagic forage fish (77.1%), moderate preference for carnivorous fishes (19.4%), and low preference for benthivores (3.5%). Our results indicate that sandbar sharks exhibit temporal variance in resident behavior in the coastal waters of the NYB but are highly dependent on pelagic forage fish and, to a lesser extent, larger teleost fishes.
3334: The degree of connectivity between populations influences gene flow, which affects genetic diversity and the long-term adaptability of a species.  An understanding of connectivity and migration patterns is fundamental to guiding proper conservation and management decisions for protected species. Satellite-linked tags have revolutionized our understanding of population connectivity by providing unprecedented insights into animal movements, behaviors, habitat utilization, and transoceanic migrations.  In May 2024, a fisher from Indonesia with a satellite tag in their possession contacted a local conservation group (Project Hiu).  Subsequent contact with the tag manufacturer led to the tag owner (Ocearch).  Remarkably, the tag was identified as having been attached to a 390 cm TL subadult female white shark (Carcharodon carcharias) in May 2012 off South Africa.  Through subsequent investigations, it was determined the tag came off a 473 cm TL female shark (misidentified at the time as a longfin mako, Isurus paucus) captured in longline gear in November 2016 off the Indonesian coast.  This recapture marks the first documented movement and connectivity of a white shark between South Africa and Southeast Asia.  Over the 4.5 years at liberty, the shark grew in length an estimated 83 cm (18.4 cm per year).  This record of events highlights both the potential for misidentification and trade of protected shark species and the increasing benefits of close collaboration with local fishers.  This newly discovered link expands our understanding of the connectivity between remote regions and underscores the importance of ongoing international research and conservation efforts to protect these apex predators.
3335: Offshore wind farms are an expanding source of renewable energy in the Northwest Atlantic Ocean. Subsea export cables that induce electromagnetic fields (EMFs) pose potential risks to electro-sensitive species such as elasmobranchs. However, the degree to which anthropogenic EMFs impact elasmobranch behavior is not well understood in natural settings. As an already vulnerable group due to life history constraints, it is critical to understand the impacts of EMFs on a broader array of elasmobranchs in an era of offshore wind development. We monitored habitat use of clearnose skates (Raja eglanteria) before and after the activation of a subsea cable associated with the Ørsted South Fork Wind Farm (East Hampton, NY). Acoustically derived fine scale positions were collected from 32 individuals from 2021-2022 (pre-EMF) and 2024 (post-EMF); four individuals were detected before and after cable activation. Kernal density estimates suggested partitioning of individual space use across all years. Core habitat areas overlapped with the subsea cable in all years, and did not change in size after cable activation. Combined, these findings suggest that the activation of the subsea cable had minimal impacts on clearnose skate space use. Future work will implement network analysis to determine movement connectivity relative to the subsea cable as well as Hidden Markov Models to assess potential changes in activity states through time. These findings provide novel insight into the spatial and behavioral effects of EMFs on elasmobranchs, which may have broader implications for fitness and survival.
3336: The Galapagos shark (Carcharhinus galapagensis) is a large, primarily inshore species, found in the Pacific, Atlantic and Indian oceans, characterized by a patchy distribution, typically found in waters around islands in tropical and warm-temperate regions and is often confused with the very similar dusky shark (Carcharhinus obscurus).  There is concern about population declines of Galapagos sharks due to fishing pressure although particularly in the Eastern Tropical Pacific and in continental waters, knowledge of the biology of these sharks is limited.  To investigate movements of Galapagos sharks along the Pacific coast of Panama, we tagged four individuals with satellite transmitters and tracked their movements over the span of 244-518 days.  Tracked sharks concentrated their movements within inshore areas near the Panama/Colombia border, but were distributed over a span of coastline greater than 450 km.  Detections of sharks were predominantly in water less than 50 m deep and within 40 km from shore.  Our study expands understanding of movements of Galapagos sharks along continental coastlines and in the Eastern Tropical Pacific region.
3337:
Cichlids of the tribe Lamprologini form an exceptionally diverse clade in the Congo Basin, yet their evolutionary history has been notoriously difficult to resolve—particularly the river-dwelling lineages within the genus Lamprologus. This group notably includes L. lethops, the only known blind and depigmented cichlid.

In this study, we reconstruct the evolutionary, population, and biogeographic history of a Lamprologus clade from the Congo River using genomic data from ultraconserved elements (UCEs) and a broad taxonomic sampling from the Lake Tanganyika radiation.

Our findings suggest that in the mid-to-late Pliocene, two distinct lineages from Lake Tanganyika independently colonized the Congo River, where they hybridized and diversified, eventually forming the monophyletic group of riverine Lamprologus seen today. The timing of these events aligns with major geological changes in the region, indicating that rapids-driven vicariance, fluctuating water levels, and repeated episodes of secondary contact were key drivers of rapid speciation.

This group’s complex evolutionary history—shaped by hybridization, isolation, and reconnection—illustrates the intricate processes underlying species diversification in the Congo River. Our results provide new insights into how river systems can act as both barriers and conduits for diversification, contributing to the remarkable freshwater biodiversity of this region.
3338: The genus Conopsis is a group of endemic colubrids with a wide distribution in northwestern, central, and southern Mexico. It consists of six currently recognized species (C. acuta, C. amphisticha, C. biserialis, C. lineata, C. megalodon, and C. nasus), distributed from 1500–3200 masl in pine-oak forests, xerophilous forests, and disturbed areas. Despite being very common, little is known about their evolutionary histories. In this work, we establish the first phylogenetic hypothesis based on genetic data (ND4, C-mos, and CytB) and recreate the biogeographic history of the group. The results suggest that Conopsis is a monophyletic group consisting of a larger number of lineages than currently recognized. Some taxa are composed by two lineages, such as C. acuta, C. megalodon, and C. nasus; C. lineata, by three; and it is proposed the synonymy of C. amphisticha within one of the C. acuta clades. The ancestral area of the genus is estimated to have been the Trans-Mexican Volcanic Belt, with an age of ~17 Ma. Multiple dispersal events occurred toward the Sierra Madre Occidental, the Central Mexican Highlands, and the Sierra Madre del Sur, in addition to vicariance and duplication processes in the Sierra Madre del Sur. Clearly, the diversity reported previously does not reflect the genetic diversity of the group; therefore, it could be a phenomenon of cryptic diversity. Finally, we propose exploring new sources of variation to complete the picture of the evolutionary history of this genus endemic to Mexico.
3339: Heroine cichlids are one of the most diverse groups of freshwater fishes in the northern Neotropics. Despite this diversity, our understanding of species boundaries, phylogenetic relationships, and morphological variation within this tribe remain poorly understood, particularly at the intrageneric level. One of the most species-rich genera of Heroini is Thorichthys, which includes nine valid species distributed from northern Honduras to southern Mexico. Its widespread distribution, polymorphism and cryptic diversity, and sympatric ocurrence among different species makes Thorichthys a compelling system for studying the patterns and processes driving diversification in northern Neotropical cichlids. Here, we present a novel phylogenomic hypothesis for Thorichthys based on ultraconserved elements, which we use as a template to test if species of Thorichthys exhibits low intraspecific morphological variation, suggesting niche conservatism. To assess morphological variation across the distribution of each species we examined cranial morphology using skeletal traits, particularly associated with the pharyngeal jaws, which are hypothesized to play a key role in trophic adaptation in cichlids. We performed geometric morphometric analyses of body and skull shape, and meristic analyses of the lower pharyngeal jaw using cleared and stained specimens. Our results uncovered the presence of at least two distinct cranial morphologies within Thorichthys, which match with two well-supported clades in our phylogenomic hypothesis. Additionally, we found significant inter- and intraspecific variation in pharyngeal jaw morphology rejecting the hypothesis of conserved intrageneric morphology in structures associated with adaptive diversification in northern Neotropical cichlids.
3340: Biological collections serve as primary sources for understanding biodiversity. They document diversity through time and provide a baseline for tracking geographical and temporal changes, as well as extinctions at local and global scales. As a regional center, the Marine Vertebrate Collection (MVC) at the Scripps Institution of Oceanography (SIO) has integrated numerous smaller collections, including the University of California Los Angeles Ichthyology Collection and the Pitman Epipelagic Collection, providing accessibility to this valuable material. In 2022, the National Science Foundation awarded funds to rescue and facilitate the transfer of the University of Puerto Rico Fish Collection (UPR-M). The UPR-M was one the largest biorepositories of marine fish biodiversity in the Caribbean, encompassing historical data from 13,000 specimens, comprising 805 species, 392 genera, and 123 families. This collection was formalized and grew significantly with the arrival of Jack Randall in 1961, and grew steadily under Danny Hensley to the final Curator, Matt Craig. Factors leading to the deteriorating conditions included severe budget cuts at many levels, a permanent fish curatorship hiring freeze, and insufficient curatorial resources. This collection enhances SIO by bolstering collections of nearshore Caribbean fishes as well as deep-sea fishes from the Puerto Rico Trench, adding species not or poorly represented as well as numerous type specimens. We are in the process of digitizing records and integrating over 2,500 lots into the MVC and subsequent data repositories for better public access. Additionally, we are training undergraduates in systematics and collection management via continued digitization and curation efforts.
3341: Fishes of the order †Redfieldiiformes (~23 genera, 27 spp.) are an extinct group of lower ray-finned fishes found globally in geologic deposits from the Early Mesozoic. Redfieldiiforms possessed a fusiform body shape, thick enameled (ganoid) scales covering the entire body, fixed maxilla, more upright jaw suspensorium, prominent and often tuberculated snout, and reduction in the dorsal lobe of the caudal fin. Redfieldiiforms represent one of the last remnants of a once-dominant lineage of fishes during the Paleozoic (†Palaeoniscimorpha), but the evolutionary relationships within the †Redfieldiiformes have not been fully ascertained via a quantitative phylogenetic analysis. Redfieldiiform fishes are reexamined, with updates to the anatomical and morphological descriptions of certain taxa, and the inclusion of new taxa described within the last eight years. Parsimony and maximum-likelihood analyses support a monophyletic †Redfieldiiformes with two families, †Brookvaliidae and †Redfieldiidae. A new classification of the †Redfieldiiformes is presented, with comments on the relationship of the order to other stem actinopterygian lineages.
3342: DNA sequencing has revolutionized our understanding of biodiversity, ecology, and evolution. While analyzing DNA sequence data allows us to address countless questions, vertebrate DNA is predominantly obtained from recently collected samples. Most of the world’s vertebrate specimens remain inaccessible for molecular sampling due to the absence of modern tissue samples and/or the degradation of DNA from formalin preservation. Recent studies have focused on extracting DNA from historic specimens, and advancements in extraction and sequencing technologies are enhancing the possibility of capturing genomic information from holotypes, characterizing genetic diversity within species complexes, and incorporating rare samples into phylogenetic analyses. In this study, I present the successful extraction and sequencing of DNA from historic museum specimens representing enigmatic threadfin fishes in the genus Polydactylus (Teleostei: Polynemidae). These specimens represent rare, genetically uncharacterized taxa that have yet to be included in a phylogenetic analysis. I analyze the data captured from these specimens, combined with a newly generated mitochondrial dataset and a previously published UCE dataset, to construct a phylogenetic framework. I then use this framework to explore new and previously described morphological variation within threadfins, identifying several shared characters that warrant the description of a new genus. These findings demonstrate that sequencing historical DNA from specimens and analyzing these data with complementary datasets of molecular markers from modern tissue samples can provide accurate and comprehensive phylogenetic assessments across fishes and other vertebrates.
3343: The goby genera Eviota and Sueviota (family Gobiidae) are commonly known as dwarfgobies, and collectively the two genera are among the most abundant and diverse groups of fishes on coral reefs. Despite the diversity, abundance, and ecological importance of this group, and the large and growing number of species described to date (133 Eviota, 9 Sueviota), there is a lack of understanding of: (i) the phylogenetic relationships among the major clades of dwarfgobies; (ii) relationships between dwarfgobies and other Gobiidae species; (iii) taxonomically informative phenotypic characters. We inferred a time-calibrated phylogeny of the 99 specimens of Eviota and Sueviota and 66 specimens of related gobies using genome-wide data from 440 ddRADseq loci. We also assessed the distribution of 14 morphological characters across the tree to assess which may be useful for diagnosing clades. Our results robustly established the non-monophyly of the genus Eviota, which was resolved into two separate clades, with one of them (which will be elevated to its own genus) nested within a lineage of other coral-associated genera. Additionally, Sueviota is deeply nested within one of the clades of Eviota, thus Sueviota will be synonymized with Eviota. We also found strong phylogenetic signal for 12 out of the 14 phenotypic traits examined, providing strong complementary support for the clades in our tree. This stablished validity of phenotypic traits corresponding with genetic groupings will aid in future taxonomic studies for this group.
3344: Within the genus Ilisha (Clupeiformes: Pristigasteridae), species having asymmetric swimbladder and 28–34 abdominal scutes, have been regarded as synonyms of Ilisha megaloptera (Swainson, 1839), a species widely distributed in the Indo-west Pacific region. However, morphological examination of specimens identified as I. megaloptera obtained throughout the distribution revealed the presence of three species, Ilisha motius (Hamilton, 1822) (distributed in the Hooghly River, India), Ilisha megaloptera (eastern Indian Ocean from Bangladesh to Sri Lanka), and Ilisha russelli (Bleeker, 1852) (Gulf of Thailand to Borneo, Penang region, Java). Ilisha motius can be distinguished from the other two by having more gill rakers (35–37 total gill rakers on first gill arch vs. <34 in other two), fewer ventral scutes (28 or less vs. 28 or more) and pectoral-fin rays (14 or 15 vs. 15–19), more elongated body (<30.8% of SL vs. >31.1%), and a shorter maxilla (<12.2% of SL vs. >13.0%). Furthermore, I. megaloptera differs from I. russelli in having more anal-fin rays (43–51 in I. megaloptera vs. 38–45 in I. russelli), longer anal-fin base (>37.6% of SL vs. <36.7%), shorter dorsal-fin base (<10.9% of SL vs. >11.1%) and more vertebrae (47–50 vs. 44–46). Current available information on these three species suggests they are allopatrically distributed, with I. motius preferring freshwaters whereas the other two are marine. It is, however, essential to better understand the biology and genetics of each species for future conservation.
3345: Dibamid lizards (family Dibamidae) are one of the most poorly-studied families of squamates. Their fossorial habits make these nearly-eyeless, nearly-limbless lizards difficult to find and observe, resulting in an almost complete lack of literature on their ecology and severe under-representation in museum collections. Yet these lizards are crucial to understanding the evolutionary history of reptiles; they are perhaps sister to all other squamates, and appear to have experienced profound morphological stasis over the past 60+ million years, even as they have spread between continents to their current disjunct distribution.  Here, we present the preliminary results of a multilocus phylogenetic study of Dibamidae using more than 300 genes, including RELEC (Rapidly-Evolving Long Exon Capture) and traditional markers. Using data from more than 70 modern specimens, including 18 named species, this is by far the best-sampled phylogenetic study of Dibamidae ever undertaken, and its scope will be expanded by the addition of more than 30 formalin-fixed tissue samples. Our results clarify dibamids’ foggy biogeographic history and indicate the existence of many cryptic species of Dibamus. We better constrain the timing of Anelytropsis’s dispersal from Asia to North America (via the Beringian route) and track the complex routes of Dibamus dispersal from mainland Southeast Asia East to New Guinea. Furthermore, we find several new species-level lineages of Dibamus in Wallacea, with their diversity centered around the tectonically complex island of Sulawesi.
3346: The Atherinomorpha includes over 30 families of ovalentarian fishes distributed throughout the world in fresh, brackish, and marine waters. With an incredible breadth of morphological diversity, reproductive strategies, and habitats, atherinomorphs are a diverse and ecologically important lineage of teleost fishes. Three orders of fishes constitute the Atherinomorpha, including Atheriniformes (silversides and their allies), Beloniformes (needlefishes and their allies), and Cyprinodontiformes (killifishes and their allies). In this study we use a combination of ultraconserved elements (UCEs) and mitochondrial genomes to investigate the evolutionary relationships across the atherinomorph radiation and discuss their diversification across the globe.
3347: Shifts in the timing of life history events (i.e., phenological shifts) from climate change are expected to alter species interactions, in part by affecting size variation among individuals that would modify interaction strengths. However, predicting how such changes may manifest are difficult due to an inability of most systems to explore potential climate changes scenarios. The goal of this project was to test how advanced breeding by spotted salamanders (Ambystoma maculatum) would impact interactions with predatory larval ringed salamanders (A. annulatum) We manipulated the hatching of spotted salamanders to simulate earlier-than-typical breeding phenology and then reared larvae in outdoor mesocosms with predatory larval ringed salamanders. However, we found that even several weeks of advanced breeding did not alter the outcome of their interactions: spotted salamanders had very low survival with ringed salamanders, regardless of timing of breeding. To understand a potential mechanism behind this surprising result, we re-analyzed 8 previous experiments on ringed salamanders to understand how winter severity affected their growth and development. We found that warmer winters, like the one experienced by larvae in the current experiment, resulted in larger body sizes and faster development in ringed salamanders. This indicates that advantages of earlier breeding by spotted salamanders could be offset decreasing winter severity. Overall, our results demonstrate that at least in this system, wholesale changes to ecosystems across multiple seasons because of climate change (e.g., warmer temperatures alongside phenological shifts) may interact in unexpected ways to alter or maintain species interactions.
3348: We collected larvae of the Patch-nosed Salamander, Urspelerpes brucei, and analyzed size-frequency distributions throughout a 12-mo cycle to determine the length of the larval period and size at metamorphosis. The hatchling-size class entered the population across a wide time window, from early winter to late summer, and at a minimal size of 6 mm snout–girdle length (SGL). Examination of both pooled total sample and the samples across six seasonal periods strongly show that the typical larval period is approximately 24 mo with metamorphosis occurring during late summer to early fall at 18–19 mm SGL. Because oviposition and hatching are extended across several months, it is possible that some animals metamorphose up to 30 mo after hatching. Larval growth in Urspelerpes is 0.5 mm/mo, which is comparable—and even slower—to the slow larval growth seen in all other stream-dwelling plethodontid larvae. Our samples of recently metamorphosed animals and mature adults indicate that males are sexually mature at metamorphosis. This is more difficult to know for females, and we suggest that females may be a mixed group that contains individuals that mature at metamorphosis and individuals that delay maturation for an additional 12 mo. There is no difference in either sex between body size at metamorphosis and at sexual maturation. As in other species in the Spelerpini, the timing of metamorphosis and the timing of sexual maturation appear to be able to evolve independently, with the remarkable result that the early sexual maturation in Urspelerpes results in a tiny adult size despite having a multiyear larval period.
3349: Considerable attention has been devoted to studying the ecological impacts of climate change on fisheries. An overlooked component of climate change impacts on fisheries is shifting behavior of fishers in response to warming trends. The extent to which fishers respond to declines in productivity of cold-adapted fish species by either moving to new fishing locations or targeting growing populations of warm-adapted competitors may alter the trajectories of these declining populations. To understand the potential outcomes of fisheries threatened by climate change, we construct an integrated social-ecological model of a fishery along a latitudinal spatial gradient that includes feedbacks between ecological and social dynamics. The model tracks the dynamics of a cold-adapted species and a warm-adapted competitor as well as specialist and generalist fishing communities comprised of individuals that will only fish the cold-adapted species and individuals that fish whichever species is most abundant respectively. We show that specialist fishing exacerbates climate-driven declines, as initial declines in the most equatorward population displace and concentrate harvest pressure poleward. However, generalist fishers willing to switch target species can slow the pace of extinction. By increasing the harvest rates of a warm-adapted competitor, a generalist fishery can facilitate coexistence and therefore sustainability. Our research sheds light on the critical role that fisher behavior can play in determining the climate resiliency of harvested populations.
3350: Since ectotherms use their environment to thermoregulate, they are highly susceptible to rapid changes in climate and ongoing climate change. While the majority of salamander species practice both cutaneous respiration and pulmonary respiration, lungless salamanders (Plethodontidae) only respire through their skin. As a result, plethodontids are especially vulnerable to changes in climate, as respiration through skin limits the temperatures and moisture levels at which individuals can be successful. Due to a particularly high biomass in the northeastern United States, Plethodon cinereus (Red-Backed Salamander) has been extensively studied for decades and is often used as a model system for how plethodontid populations may be changing. To examine how plethodontid populations are impacted by climate change, we compare P. cinereus populations across a ten-year span. We use six coverboard arrays (50 boards each) of different ages in the same forest in Ithaca, NY for spatial capture-recapture (SCR) surveys. Four sites were established in 2014 and we established two additional arrays in 2023. Because many of these boards were degraded, we replaced approximately 50% of boards at 2014 arrays in 2024. Using these sets of sites we examine coverboard preference, salamander life span, and changing population structure. We predict that salamanders will prefer older boards in the 2014 arrays, and that different demographics of salamanders will be found under the old and new boards. We also expect to find a significant population of salamanders that have remained in the old arrays for the last ten years. Lastly, while we do not expect to observe a change in salamander density, we predict a difference in salamander surface activity between 2014 and 2024. Preliminary data supports that P. cinereus prefers older coverboards, and shows that approximately 7% of salamanders caught in 2024 were initially caught and tagged in the 2014 CMR surveys. We also observe a shift detection probability, indicating a shift in peak surface activity, between 2014 and 2024. Additional work will examine how range size and movement patterns have changed since 2014.
3351: A population of the blue spotted salamanders (Ambystoma laterale) and their hybrid has been protected by a road closure in Marquette, MI since 2020 as a result of prior documented vehicle mortality. The population has been studied by students at Northern Michigan University as a community service project with the scientific goals of understanding migration timing and its association with environmental variables. Annual counts at a standardized time as well as hourly through the day night cycle were made. Results show that the migration typically occurs over about two weeks, but that outliers can be found moving as much as two weeks in advance or following the main migration, depending on environmental conditions. Movements are tightly tied to dark hours with salamander activities starting at just after sunset (about 21:00) and concluding at sunrise, with relatively consistent movements throughout the night. As expected, highest counts occur on rainy nights, but we have seen movements in warm and dry weather in recent years. Ongoing work seeks to characterize the different timing of movements of sexes and genetic morphs.
3352: Many woodland salamanders have narrow ranges restricted to higher elevations, whereas related species are widespread across both elevational and latitudinal gradients. Despite many decades of research, the processes that determine range sizes in woodland salamanders are poorly understood. Because higher temperatures should lead to increased metabolic rates, range limits could occur where endemic species are unable to meet their caloric requirement for growth and fat deposition. If this is the case, widespread species should be better able to grow and store fat in warmer environments as compared to related high-elevation species. I studied a high-elevation endemic salamander (Plethodon sherando) and its widespread congener (Plethodon cinereus) across elevational gradients in a region of Virginia where both species occur. I hypothesized that body size and condition would decline more steeply with decreasing elevation for the endemic species than for the widespread species. As is typically the case, my hypothesis was entirely incorrect. I did find some evidence that salamanders had reduced body size and condition at lower elevations, but this was more apparent with the widespread species than with the endemic species. Furthermore, for both species, body size and condition varied more among sites at similar elevations than it varied across elevations. Body condition tended to be correlated with soil temperature at the time of the survey (rather than elevation), suggesting that body condition may change over relatively short time intervals in response to seasonal changes in temperatures. I conclude that woodland salamanders are mysterious creatures, at least to me.
3353: Rough-skinned newts (Taricha granulosa) occur along the Pacific coast from central California to southwestern Alaska at elevations from zero to 2,800 m. Adults breed and larvae hatch during spring, larvae spend summer in breeding ponds, then transform into terrestrial juveniles in the fall, with variation in timing based on elevation. Using minnow-trap and dip net surveys at nine sites in northern Humboldt County, California, we observed differences in timing of breeding and length of larval period within a small geographic range. All sites were lentic and at elevations between 400 and 1,000 m. We detected overwintering larvae at five (56%) sites, but the proportion of the population that was overwintering was highly variable between sites. At two sites, larvae hatched in August and persisted through the winter and spring, while at another two sites, most larvae hatched in June and transformed by October, leaving < 4% of the larval population at those sites to overwinter. At four sites, larvae began transforming at snout-to-vent lengths (SVL) of 21-23 mm, whereas at other sites larvae did not start transforming until 30 mm SVL. Based on visual surveys of amplecting pairs, timing of breeding was variable among ponds, with some populations breeding from fall to spring, and others breeding from spring through the summer. We have yet to find an association between environmental factors and larval period, overwintering, or timing of breeding, suggesting these aspects of newt reproductive biology are plastic and influenced by a complex interaction between multiple environmental cues.
3354: The increasing global temperature, with an average increase of 1.8°C in the last century, is anticipated to induce significant alterations in wildlife habitats and populations around the world. Particularly, ectothermic organisms like reptiles, which rely on external temperatures for thermoregulation, are projected to be disproportionately affected by these climatic shifts. This research aims to explore the impacts of climate change and habitat loss on freshwater turtles in New Mexico, focusing on their dietary patterns. Employing stable isotope analysis (δ15N and δ13C), we studied the dietary habits of turtle populations across four distinct sites, correlating these with varied habitat and environmental conditions. We also conducted a temporal dietary comparison between present-day isotopic values of Western Painted Turtles (Chrysemys picta bellii) and those from the 1960s-1980s using museum specimens. The site-to-site analysis showed differences in isotopic values between species at Elephant Butte State Park and the Rio Grande Nature Center State Park. The historical comparison of Chrysemys picta bellii showed differences in isotopic values between present and historical turtles at the Sevilleta National Wildlife Refuge and the Rio Grande Nature Center State Park. Next season, we will assess the genetic structure of the turtle populations across the Rio Grande. Genetic data will allow us to calculate the effective population size, connectivity between populations and hybridization between the native Big Bend Slider (Trachemys gaigeae) and the Invasive Red-ear slider (Trachemys scripta elegans).
3355: Climate change is a primary driver of the worldwide decline in amphibians, whose functioning is highly dependent on local climate. In salamanders, temperature influences many physiological processes, including embryo development rate. This effect has been studied in many salamanders in the genus Ambystoma, but not in the ringed salamander (Ambystoma annulatum), a species of conservation concern in Missouri, USA. Determining A. annulatum’s response to rising egg incubation temperatures is crucial to conservation and management efforts and contributes to the scientific literature on this understudied species. We determined the effect of incubation temperature on survival, larval size, and egg incubation period in A. annulatum. A. annulatum eggs were collected from three wild populations in the St. Louis, Missouri, USA area, subjected to three different incubation temperature treatments, and monitored for five months after hatching. We predict that survival, larval size, and egg incubation period will be reduced at greater incubation temperatures.
3356: Understanding a species’ conservation status requires evaluating its ecological relationships, contemporary distribution, and vulnerability to future environmental change. Species distribution models (SDMs) are widely used for these purposes, but regional-scale applications often suffer from extrapolation and niche truncation, reducing model accuracy and transferability. Spatially-nested hierarchical SDMs, which integrate data across multiple spatial scales, offer a promising solution but remain underutilized in regional conservation research. Crawfish frogs (Rana areolata) are a cryptic grassland species reliant on crayfish burrows that have experienced declines across their range and are data deficient in Oklahoma. This study combines field surveys with hierarchical SDMs to determine the species’ current distribution in Oklahoma, assess environmental factors influencing habitat suitability, and predict future range shifts under climate and land use change. Additionally, we compared the accuracy of spatially-nested hierarchical SDMs to regional-only SDMs. We documented R. areolata at 303 survey locations and found no evidence of historical county-level declines. Our models suggest large amounts of suitable habitat exist in eastern Oklahoma. Our traditional regional-only SDM suffered from extreme extrapolation and niche truncation, leading to predictions of significant habitat loss under future conditions. In contrast, our  hierarchical SDMs mitigated these issues and projected an increase in future habitat suitability. Our findings highlight the advantages of hierarchical SDMs for improving model accuracy and informing conservation assessments. We advocate for the broader adoption of this approach in regional-scale studies to enhance model accuracy, improve predictions of species responses to environmental change, and more effectively assess species status at a regional level.
3357: Habitat loss through land conversion and fragmentation is the single greatest threat to biodiversity and the persistence of species in the 21st century. Decreases in carrying capacity and population size from habitat loss simultaneously increase the probability of inbreeding and inbreeding depression. Combined, these factors synergistically increase extinction risk. The Eastern Massasauga (Sistrurus catenatus) rattlesnake is federally listed as threatened in the United States and Canada, and population declines associated with loss of habitat were cited as key factors for its listing. We used a 15-year capture-recapture dataset, targeted genomic sequencing, and capture locations from >1000 individuals from two populations of Eastern Massasaugas in Michigan to estimate inbreeding (Fgrm) and the effects of inbreeding on fitness. Using capture locations, we found evidence of spatial kinship structure, and limited dispersal ability, as a mechanism driving inbreeding within populations. We assessed the effects of inbreeding on fitness by combining reconstructed multi-generational pedigrees with capture-recapture data to estimate reproductive output and size- and site- specific annual survival probabilities. Both fitness metrics showed evidence of inbreeding depression: the 5% most inbred individuals had 11.6% lower annual survival probabilities and were 13.5% less likely to have surviving offspring compared to less inbred individuals. Our results demonstrate the mechanisms that give rise to spatial structure, inbreeding, and reduced fitness via inbreeding depression and may be used to inform future conservation efforts on Eastern Massasaugas and other vulnerable species with low vagility and slow life histories.
3358: Despite consisting of over 1,500 species and representing almost four percent of described amniote diversity, skinks (Order: Squamata; Family: Scincidae) are poorly represented in the genomic era. Despite this, the scincid lizards harbor an exemplary opportunity to investigate the genomic processes underlying ecological and morphological diversification across a global radiation. Here, we highlight this disparity as well as present a chromosome-level, annotated reference genome for the common five-lined skink (Plestiodon fasciatus) and newly assembled genomes for a majority of the Plestiodon genus.
3359: The level and distribution of genetic variation in populations provides key information for conservation assessment and actions for imperiled species. Blanding’s Turtle (Emydoidea blandingii) and Spotted Turtle (Clemmys guttata) are imperiled and have overlapping geographic ranges in the Great Lakes region. As part of project to assess the status of the species in Michigan, Indiana, and Ohio, we used microsatellite allelic variation to characterize within and among population genetic structure. A total of 833 individuals from 92 localities were genotyped across 16 loci for Blanding’s Turtle, and 600 individuals from 42 localities across 16 loci for Spotted Turtle. Overall patterns were quite similar for both species. Population genetic structure among localities was limited and showed isolation by distance. Levels of genetic variation within localities were moderate in most localities and comparable to other regions within their geographic ranges. We found populations have low effective population sizes and there was evidence of inbreeding in four Spotted Turtle populations. We modeled future genetic variation in representative populations of each species and found that they are expected to lose 50% of alleles over the next 200 years. These results suggest that translocation of individuals will likely be necessary for long-term viability of populations from a genetic perspective, but doing so is not likely to cause outbreeding depression within the region.
3360: Blanding’s Turtles (Emydoidea blandingii) are Midwestern freshwater turtle species that is declining across most of their range due to habitat loss and fragmentation. The species is currently petitioned to be listed as threatened under the Endangered Species Act. Maintaining landscapes of connected wetlands and upland nesting habitat is crucial for Blanding’s Turtle survival. In this study, we are investigating the movement of Blanding’s Turtles across a mixed landscape of high-quality habitat and developed land in Northern Michigan. We attached GPS data loggers to individuals across the landscape to gather movement and habitat use data. Habitat selection was then evaluated across multiple scales, via Euclidean distance analysis. Turtles selected for wetland habitats at the local range scale, and did not show selection against any habitats at the local or home range scale. This habitat selection data was then used to create a circuit theory habitat connectivity model of the site to provide information about potential corridors and barriers of movement to land managers of the site.
3361: The genus Micrixalus, commonly known as dancing frogs, is fifth on the list of the top ten threatened amphibian genera of the world. These foot-flagging frogs are endemic to the Western Ghats of India, a biodiversity hotspot. Out of 24 species in the genus, 22 species (92%) are categorised as 'Threatened' according to IUCN’23 red-list-assessment. One of the members, Micrixalus kottigeharensis was formerly an Evolutionary-Distinct-and-Globally-Endangered (EDGE) species. Following our work, it was down-listed to ‘Vulnerable’. Through this study, and my ongoing project called the Dancing-Frogs-Project-of-India (https://dancingfrogs.in), I present the habitat association, distribution modelling and anthropogenic threats to M. kottigeharensis. Through field surveys, we assessed the distribution using ensemble species modelling approach while gaining additional insights on the ecology and habitat association, including threats. The study shows that M. kottigeharensis prefers fast to slow-flowing streams with an average stream depth of 19±17.02 cm and width of 368±193 cm along with a canopy cover of >70%. Regression modelling shows a positive association of species presence to atmospheric humidity (Z= 3.46, p=0.00). The models also show a significant negative association with drizzle (Z= -3.24, p=0.00), intermittent rain (Z= -2.65, p=0.01) and rock temperature (Z= -2.71, p=0.01) within the streams. Our habitat suitability map for four different climate and anthropogenic scenarios shows that the species is restricted to mid-elevation, moist evergreen forests of the central Western Ghats and habitat suitability-area increase with future climate scenarios implying association with increased rainfall patters. This is the first detailed study on M. kottigeharensis highlighting the need for a conservation-action-plan.
3362: Animals continually balance the rewards of activity against the risk of predation. While sensory systems are essential for detecting predators, their role in mediating behavioral trade-offs remains underexplored. For nocturnal species, moonlight—a key driver of predation risk—varies cyclically, offering a unique opportunity to study how sensory capacity influences activity. We examined four species of Neotropical electric fish inhabiting clearwater Amazon streams where visually oriented nocturnal predators are common. These species are similar in size and diet but differ in body mass-adjusted eye size—a proxy for visual acuity. Using custom loggers to detect their continuous, species-specific electric signals, we monitored foraging activity across a lunar cycle, alongside moonlight illuminance measurements. The two species with the smallest eyes exhibited strong lunar phobia, hiding during moonlit periods and sacrificing ~25% of their foraging time. In contrast, the species with the largest eyes foraged continuously, likely using vision to detect and evade predators. A fourth species with intermediate eye size showed a canopy-dependent response, hiding only under closed canopy. Active electroreception allows these fish to forage in darkness but is ineffective for predator detection beyond ~10 cm. Our findings suggest that species with large eyes adopt a “vigilance” strategy, relying on visual monitoring, while those with small eyes adopt a “hiding” strategy. These alternative responses impose distinct energetic costs: reduced foraging versus the energetic costs of maintaining larger eyes. Overall, our results highlight how sensory adaptations influence critical trade-offs between foraging and predation risk across spatial and temporal landscapes of fear.
3363: Maintenance of genetic diversity is critical for preserving adaptive potential and avoiding inbreeding depression and further population decline.  As populations become smaller and more isolated, they are more likely to become inbred, which can lead to inbreeding depression, erosion of genetic diversity, and further population decline.
