3416: Cichlid fishes (Cichlidae) are a celebrated system in evolutionary research with impressive diversity, broad geographic distribution, and well-studied natural history that make them textbook subjects in evolutionary biology. Yet, despite their “iconic” status, cichlid age estimates vary widely, with large uncertainty within and widespread incongruence among studies. A fundamental reason for these disagreements is the lack of a morphological framework within which to phylogenetically interpret and place the cichlid fossil record. Without a robust age estimate for cichlids, we are limited in our ability to discern the patterns of cichlid divergence and understand the underlying processes leading to their extraordinary evolutionary history. We present the first family-wide matrix of cichlid osteology and squamation (145 characters for 113 living and 22 fossil taxa) built from examining specimens of living and fossil cichlids, complemented with coding of fossil descriptions from the literature. Maximum Likelihood (ML) analyses demonstrate the value of this new dataset in enhancing clade diagnosability and fossil placement across cichlids in a total evidence context with genomic data for 299 species of living cichlids. We find that age estimates under ML are highly sensitive to the number of fossils included in the analyses. We also present preliminary results of Bayesian Total Evidence dating using Fossilized Birth Death models that simultaneously integrate phylogenetic analyses and fossil placement into new estimates of cichlid age, quantitatively incorporating time and rate uncertainty into phylogenetic estimates for the family.
3417: Biofluorescence (absorption of high-energy light and reemission at lower energy wavelengths) and bioluminescence (production and emission of light by a living organism) are widespread across the tree of life, and especially prevalent in fishes. These traits evolved numerous times across fishes and play key roles in their diversification. There are few studies that have investigated the intersection of the two, where organisms use their own higher-energy bioluminescent emissions to excite fluorophores, creating fluorescent emissions of lower-energy wavelengths of light. We investigate this phenomenon in the bioluminescent ponyfishes (Leiognathidae); an ideal study system to assess the interaction of bioluminescence and biofluorescence as ponyfishes are abundant, live in near-shore areas of the Indo-Pacific, and have registered bioluminescent wavelength readings. Using blue light in four discrete wavelength categories associated with known bioluminescent light we analyzed 15 of 51 species of fresh ponyfishes. We found one species, Deveximentum ruconius, to be biofluorescent. Emitted light ocured in the wavelengths of 515-520 nm, with a shoulder at 535-550 nm (green). Biofluorescence occurred under excitation light of 460 nm and 482 nm but not under 500 nm or 513 nm. This is in line with the wavelengths emitted by their symbiotic bioluminescent bacteria, which emit at ~480 nm. This is the first evidence of biofluorescence in Leiognathidae and one of only two other instances of possible bioluminescence-induced fluorescence in fishes. These findings continue to add to the important body of work investigating the complexities of signaling and communication in the marine environment.
3418: The Axillary Lymphoid Organ (ALO) is the fleshy lobe immediately above the pectoral fin in the Zebrafish, Danio rerio.  The ALO emerges comparatively late in development and is not found in embryonic or larval Zebrafish. A discrete immune system function for the ALO has recently been described. The ALO is a translucent organ with an outer cortex with immune cells, an inner medulla with a mesh-like network of fibroblastic reticular cells along which immune cells migrate, and a network of lymphatic vessels draining to a large adjacent lymph sac. The ALO is easily removed for analysis or as a source of genetic material and regenerates within two weeks following removal. A survey of museum specimens of an array of teleost taxa revealed a diversity of pectoral lobe morphologies, with some fish species possessing substantially larger or more elaborate structures than the ALO of the Zebrafish. We infer an immune system function for the pectoral lobe in other teleosts, which is open to test. The pectoral lobe is found in basal teleosts such as the Tarpon, Megalops atlanticus, osteoglossiforms, and other ostariophysans. It is absent in higher teleosts such as the Medaka, Oryzias latipes, Fugu, Takifugu rupripes, and the Three-spined stickleback, Gasterosteus aculeatus.  The distribution of the pectoral lobe evokes the distribution of the adipose fin—a somewhat fleshy dorsal fin of unclear function.
3419: Adaptation and modularity are two major features of morphological evolution that are increasingly investigated by modern macroevolutionary biologists. However, many such studies assume that adaptive processes or modularity are constant across species. Evolution of morphology and its modularity both relate to the ecological role of morphological traits. Here, we investigate whether morphological adaptation and modularity vary across families of the Neotropical superfamily Doradoidea, comprising the Aspredinidae (banjo catfishes), Auchenipteridae (driftwood catfishes), and Doradidae (thorny catfishes). We quantified morphological diversity using three-dimensional geometric morphometrics and estimated evolutionary rates, shifts between adaptive regimes, and evolutionary modularity and integration differences among families. We found that doradoids diversified into nine adaptive regimes across morphospace. We also found some significant differences in modularity and integration between families. Major morphological shifts have surprising correspondence to previously or currently recognized taxa within the Doradoidea. We found repeated, parallel evolution of body elongation across adaptive regimes, implying a role for selection in driving parallel evolution across a primary axis of shape diversification. However, modularity and integration do not necessarily shift in correspondence with shifts in morphological adaptive peaks.
3420: Most tetrapods have relatively impermeable skin, sacrificing permeability for protection and water retention. Amphibians occupy the other end of this spectrum, with more permeable skin that allows cutaneous respiration but increases vulnerability to desiccation, physical damage, pollutants, and disease (e.g. fungal susceptibility). However, anuran species show striking variation in many skin features that are hypothesized to affect anuran gas exchange and water loss rates. The importance and variability of amphibian skin texture has long been recognized but is typically categorized into a few groups, such as "smooth," "tuberculated," "granular," "warty," etc. Our study aims to move beyond these categorical descriptions to quantify external skin variation in an efficient and reproducible manner. We are building a global database of skin texture photos and data for hundreds of species using museum specimens. In addition to building this resources, we are use these new skin texture data to test whether skin varies in association with a species’ microhabitat, climate or body size. In total, our study provides a way to measure and compare skin texture among anuran species and studies and begins to test whether amphibian skin has evolved in ways that allow anurans to thrive in a range of climates across the globe.
3421: Information on reproduction in white sharks Carcharodon carcharias is critical for estimating rates of population growth and improving the management and conservation of this globally vulnerable species. However, because of their large size, low abundance, and broad oceanic distribution, it is often difficult to obtain reproductive data from white sharks, especially females, which lack external indicators of sexual maturity and reproductive status. In this study, we used the two nonlethal approaches of blood hormone analysis and transcutaneous ultrasonography to examine sexual maturity and reproductive stage in female white sharks sampled via catch-and-release fishing. Female white sharks ranging in size from 152-501 cm total length were sampled from western North Atlantic waters between Nova Scotia, Canada and Jacksonville, FL, USA from 2012 to 2024. Size measurements, blood sampling, and ultrasonography were performed. Ultrasound images of the reproductive system were used to evaluate ovarian development and pregnancy status, while blood was used to measure plasma concentrations of the gonadal steroid hormone, 17β-estradiol, which is known to increase during sexual maturity and the preovulatory period in female sharks. A significant increase in the variability of plasma estradiol concentrations was observed in individuals ranging in size from 317-379 cm TL, suggesting that this is the period of sexual maturation. Ultrasonography images also show evidence of ovarian growth in females at ~380 cm TL, suggesting that females likely mature between 400-425 cm TL. Data pertaining to male white shark reproductive activity based on measurements of plasma testosterone are also presented.
3422: The southern stingray, Hypanus americanus, is a common coastal ray in the western North Atlantic, ranging from the United States to Brazil, including the Gulf of Mexico and Caribbean Sea, and is an important resource for ecotourism in the Bahamas and Cayman Islands. It is a hardy, long-lived species that commonly reproduces in human care. Though many aspects of its life history have been described from natural and fabricated habitats, the mating system is not well understood. While behavioral polyandry has been documented in southern stingrays, genetic polyandry, or multiple paternity, has not been reported. The goal of this investigation was to document multiple paternity based upon a population of 23 reproductively active southern stingrays at the National Aquarium in 2005 with the data set examined in 2017. Amplicon deep-sequencing using next generation sequencing (NGS) technology was used to determine multiple paternity. The two-step PCR approach combined Illumina’s dual indexing strategy and species-specific primers. Results confirmed multiple paternity, and that two to three potential sires were involved. Since it was documented in this group of rays, it is likely to occur in wild conspecifics given the similar polyandrous mating events. Although the southern stingray is not a species of concern for extinction, it is an important consideration for population management. This investigation provided the first documented case of multiple paternity in a dasyatid ray, and only the second case in a viviparous batoid.
3423: There are national, regional, and local networks that coordinate responses to injured or deceased marine wildlife, mostly marine mammals and turtles. However, in Florida, there is currently no statewide protocol to respond to injured or deceased sharks. The Florida Fish and Wildlife Research Institute manages the Fish Kill Hotline (FKH), a public-facing reporting tool that can alert FWC biologists about shark mortalities, but they often have limited capacity to physically respond to the average 71 reports they receive per year. A shark stranding or mortality event can involve multiple agencies, departments, and officials, causing confusion, resulting in the animal’s disposal before samples can be collected. ASC created the Shark Reporting and Response Network (SRRN) to help build the capacity to respond, collect samples, and disseminate those samples to appropriate facilities for research. We have responded to 36 stranding reports over the past three years along Florida’s southeast coastline, including two pregnant great hammerhead sharks (Sphyrna mokarran), tiger shark (Galeocerdo cuvier), lemon shark (Negaprion brevirostris), blacktip shark (Carcharhinus limbatus), and a small tooth sawfish (Pristis pectinata). We have built a network of turtle surveyors, anglers, ocean rescue personnel, and others to report to the FKH and ASC. The value of building out a coordinated effort in responding to these events allows for the collection of samples that would otherwise require lethal sampling, but can afford critical insights into the individual’s cause of death as well as insights into the growth, diet, reproduction, and habitat use of the species.
3424: Global concern about the conservation status of the white shark, Carcharodon carcharias, has afforded the species a relatively high degree of national and international protection. In the US Atlantic, it has been designated a prohibited species by the federal government and coastal states since 1997. However, white sharks still face numerous and evolving threats including vessel strikes which may represent a previously overlooked source of mortality for the species. Though there is documented evidence of injuries and healed scars from boat strikes on white sharks throughout the species’ range, how they occur is currently not well understood. To characterize the behavioral response of sharks to approaching boats, we conducted a series of experimental approaches and collected drone footage of the shark’s behavior before, during, and after each trial. Sharks were approached from different directions and at different speeds reflective of actual marine traffic conditions to evaluate whether these factors influence their ability to detect and evade approaching boats. Preliminary results from 20 trials conducted off the coast of Cape Cod, Massachusetts, during the summer and fall of 2024 suggest that speed (> 15 kts), rather than direction, may elicit stronger reactions from sharks. Very few individuals exhibited a reaction that would adequately evade an actual oncoming boat, which provides insight into how collisions between boats and white sharks occur.
3425: Largetooth sawfish (Pristis pristis) are an endangered ray with a rostrum containing a large number of teeth. Due to population declines, live fish are difficult to study and track, limiting our understanding of their life history and behavior. Largetooth sawfish use habitat across a range of salinities, including fully fresh water. They are known to pup in freshwater, presumably to avoid predation, however their movement ecology is poorly understood outside of their stronghold in Australia. The Brazilian Amazon coast is considered the last remaining stronghold of largetooth sawfish in the Americas, but very little is known about their distribution, abundance, or movement in this region. Trace element chemistry in fish hard parts has revolutionized our understanding of migration and movement in bony fishes and increasingly in elasmobranchs. Sawfish rostral teeth grow throughout their life, making them a unique hard structure in an elasmobranch that can record chemical changes through time and across salinity. Rostra are often preserved, providing a potential archive of movement that are more accessible to study than live fish. In this study we examined rostral teeth from 121 largetooth sawfish from the Brazilian Amazon coast, for trace-element and isotopic chemistry using LA-ICPMS. Isotopic data shows for the first time the movements of Brazilian sawfish in and out of fresh water using Sr/Ca and Ba/Ca ratios, as well as river 87Sr/86Sr signatures in fresh water. This data also shows indications of habitat associations during early life and the timing of ontogenetic shifts. This data shows for the first time the range of life history exhibited by sub-adult sawfish using the detailed chemical and isotopic data preserved in rostral teeth.
3426: Tropical freshwater fishes frequently encounter hypoxia, driving the evolution of diverse adaptations, including modifications to gill morphology that increase branchial surface area. Yet, the evolutionary basis of these traits remains poorly understood. The Neotropical electric knifefish family Hypopomidae, which inhabits environments spanning a broad range of dissolved oxygen (DO) conditions, provides a valuable model for investigating these patterns. Using phylogenetic comparative methods, we analyzed three gill traits—mean filament length, mean hemibranch length, and total filament number—across 27 hypopomid species. Species specialized to hypoxic habitats exhibited significantly greater mean filament length, even after phylogenetic correction, suggesting an adaptive response to low DO. By contrast, species restricted to normoxic habitats had lower filament length, consistent with potential trade-offs involving developmental costs and structural or physiological constraints. Many hypopomid species are eurytopic, with demes occupying both hypoxic and normoxic systems; hypoxia-tolerant demes also exhibit elevated filament length, suggesting a shared morphological basis for hypoxia tolerance that spans both population-level variation and species-level divergence. Ancestral state reconstructions indicate that species with elevated filament length evolved from normoxia-adapted ancestors and that a major transition in gill morphology and habitat use occurred at the base of the Brachyhypopomus beebei group. This transition, dated to approximately 4 Ma, coincides with the Pliocene expansion of seasonally hypoxic Amazon whitewater floodplains, likely driven by increased Andean sedimentation. Our findings suggest that ancient environmental shifts promoted ecomorphological innovation in hypopomids, shaping respiratory phenotypes and potentially accelerating lineage diversification.
3427: Increasing frequency of heat waves, not just warmer overall environmental temperatures, is a signature feature of ongoing climate change. Heat waves exert adverse impacts on populations, communities, and ecosystems of a variety of biota. In globally-imperiled turtles with temperature-dependent sex determination, warmer temperatures should produce an excess of female offspring, potentially leading to long-term demographic collapse. Yet, temperature spikes in turtle embryonic development could be problematic in more immediate ways. Using experimental manipulation, we show that heat waves during key periods of embryonic development substantially increase the frequency of shell scute abnormalities in slider turtles (Trachemys scripta). Anatomical assays confirm that a considerable fraction of these scute anomalies reflect underlying skeletal malformations. In turn, large-scale field experiments link these abnormalities to reduced survival of neonates during the key life-stage of their journey from nest to water. Moreover, long-term capture-mark-recapture fieldwork further detects that the frequency of slider turtles with scute anomalies declines with age, implying ongoing adverse impacts on survival through maturity and thereafter. In sum, an increase in environmentally-induced frequency of this deleterious trait should reduce population-level fitness in turtles.
3428: Understanding the mechanisms of speciation and adaptation is a fundamental question in biology that also provides an opportunity to uncover new gene functions of clinical relevance. Highly conserved genetic regulatory pathways shared across diverse vertebrate species have been shaped by adaptive evolution to produce spectacular morphological, behavioral, and ecological diversity. Here I review a decade of my lab’s work investigating the rapid evolutionary transition from generalist algae-eating pupfishes to trophic specialists endemic to hypersaline lakes of San Salvador Island in the Bahamas and Laguna Chichancanab, Mexico. We show that colonizing these niches occurred in stages, beginning with selection on standing genetic variation for feeding behavior, then aided by adaptive introgression from diverse sources, and ending with selection on de novo mutations in key craniofacial genes. We discovered that only 157 single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) and 87 deletions are fixed between scale-eating and molluscivore specialists despite extensive phenotypic divergence in their craniofacial morphology, metabolism, and behavior. These few differences resulted in major transitions in ecological niches and the colonization of new fitness peaks and novel performance optima for scale-biting. Overall, our work provides a new microevolutionary framework for investigating how major ecological transitions occur in nature and illustrates how both shared and unique genetic variation contributes to diversification and provides a path through complex fitness landscapes for access to novel ecological niches.
3429: Identifying the molecular mechanisms underlying adaptive phenotypic changes is essential for understanding species divergence. The visual system is an ideal model for studying these adaptations due to the well-documented genetic basis of its characters and their adaptive consequences. While many environmental factors shape visual systems, most studies have concentrated solely on the role of light. This leaves critical gaps in understanding how multiple selective forces interact and shape visual systems. In aquatic systems, depth is a strong predictor of visual evolution because light availability decreases rapidly with increased depth. However, depth is also correlated with other factors, such as hydrostatic pressure, that also strongly affect vision but are often overlooked. To evaluate how multiple selective forces shape visual systems, we use 107 genomes from a diverse genus of marine fishes (Rockfish; Sebastes). We analyze sequence and expression-level variation in opsins — the proteins responsible for detecting specific wavelengths of light. We use a phylogenetic comparative approach to (a) test for changes in amino acid sequences and gene expression that tune visual systems to the available light spectrum and (b) examine amino acid sequences that enhance protein stability and reduce protein compressibility under high hydrostatic pressure. We present preliminary findings on how the rod opsin (RH1) and one cone opsin (LWS) respond to these selective forces through changes in amino acid sequence. Understanding how visual systems in rockfish simultaneously respond to different environmental factors will help identify general patterns of opsin, visual system, and species diversification across aquatic taxa.
3430: Catfish species in the genus Ictalurus (family Ictaluridae) are commercially and recreationally important fishes in the United States. Densities of Blue Catfish (I. furcatus) and Channel Catfish (I. punctatus) are high within Lake Maurepas (Louisiana), but there has been little investigation into the population dynamics and structure within the lake. Future plans are to construct a nearby clean energy complex that will utilize carbon capture and sequestration in the production of hydrogen and permanently store the carbon dioxide by-product in bedrock formations miles below Lake Maurepas. Considering the commercial and recreational importance of these catfish species, it is crucial to understand the baseline levels of genetic variability and structure among populations of these fishes. Herein we present the initial baseline genetic assessment using thousands of single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) genotyped from ddRAD sequences. Samples of Blue Catfish (n = 90) and Channel Catfish (n = 85) were collected from Lake Maurepas and the three major rivers that flow into the lake (Tickfaw, Amite, and Blind rivers). We also opportunistically examined levels of natural introgression between species. Blue and Channel catfishes are consistently artificially hybridized in hatcheries to yield traits desirable for food production, but few studies have demonstrated natural hybridization in the wild. Our results provide valuable insights into genetic diversity and structure and levels of introgression for these catfish species and provides a baseline for future studies of gene flow and genetic structure following the implementation of this large industrial project.
Conservation & Management II / Conservation Ecology and Genetics I
3431: Cuatrociénegas, in the Chihuahuan Desert of northern Mexico, is the world’s most biodiverse spring-based wetland and a federally protected area. However, water-level declines linked to largescale regional groundwater extraction, mostly for agriculture, in adjacent valleys that contribute to the valley’s aquifer clearly imminently threaten sustainability. At the same time, the area has transformed into a popular tourism destination, with rapid and massive expansion of the hotel industry and visitation. Two of the primary developers established non-profit foundations with conservation- and community-support objectives and are working together with the Federal Reserve System (CONANP), local conservation groups, regional universities, and the municipal government to assure that development is sustainable and compatible with biodiversity conservation. While aquifer management is clearly a high priority, many unknowns continue to impede develop and implementation of plans to accomplish that. At the same time, much research is still needed to improve knowledge of basic ecology and genetics of its highly endemic, diverse and endangered fish and herpetofaunas, not to mention many invertebrates and plants. There are new initiatives working to support field and laboratory research, as well as establishment of captive breeding programs. There will be opportunities for others to become involved in research and conservation efforts, and the Desert Fishes Council (https://www.desertfishes.org/) meeting in Cuatrociénegas in November of this year will provide opportunities to learn more about that.
Conservation & Management II / Conservation Ecology and Genetics I
3432: Amplified wildfire activity in western U.S. forests threatens biodiversity, yet the impacts of some fuels treatments, including slash piling and burning, have received little attention. Piling of wood from forest thinning activities may create suitable conditions for species that require cool, moist microclimates. Sacramento Mountain Salamanders (Aneides hardii), endemic to the mountains of south-central New Mexico, have been found beneath slash piles, but the extent of their occupancy by salamanders has not yet been evaluated. We quantified slash pile structure and fuel characteristics, compared soil moisture and soil temperature beneath slash piles and under nearby logs, and surveyed for salamanders in slash piles, under nearby logs, and under logs within a 1.4 ha area encompassing all slash piles. We found Sacramento Mountain Salamanders in 50% of surveyed slash piles. Pile characteristics, environmental setting, soil temperature, and soil moisture did not differ between piles occupied by salamanders and piles in which no salamanders were detected. Salamander density was highest in slash piles, nearly 10% lower under logs in the 1.4 ha surrounding the piles, and nearly 23% lower under logs nearby piles. Evidence from this study and detections of this species into mid-October indicate that pile burning is best initiated in late fall, when most salamanders are likely to have retreated below the ground surface. Constructing smaller, pyramidal piles and restricting residence time of piles on the landscape may limit their suitability as habitat, reducing the potential for adverse impacts on salamander populations when piles are burned.
Conservation & Management II / Conservation Ecology and Genetics I
3433: Ecological connectivity is critical to the survival and long-term viability of populations but is often overlooked in regulatory frameworks. We integrated landscape-level processes into a mitigation strategy for impacts to aquatic resources on the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) OakRidge Reservation (ORR) in eastern Tennessee. Wetlands on the ORR, which contain significant breeding populations of the imperiled Four-toed Salamander (Hemidactylium scutatum), will be impacted by construction of an environmental waste disposal facility. We emphasized habitat connectivity through models that prioritized an area’s importance to natural area connectivity and maintenance of population structure for an affected habitat specialist (Four-toed Salamanders). We also emphasized in-kind mitigation through the preservation and enhancement of ecologically similar resources and the translocation and establishment of a new subpopulation of four-toed salamanders elsewhere on the ORR. We translocated dozens of four-toed salamander nests, reared larvae in a unique outdoor mesocosm setup, and we ultimately released over 500 juvenile salamanders that originated from the impacted site into the chosen mitigation wetlands. This study helps show that ecological connectivity and the conservation of species that are not afforded explicit regulatory processes can be effectively and efficiently integrated into environmental decision-making and land use planning.
Conservation & Management II / Conservation Ecology and Genetics I
3434: Eurycea tonkawae (Jollyville Plateau salamander) is a fully aquatic neotenic salamander endemic to springs, spring-fed streams, and groundwater flow paths in the Austin, Texas metropolitan area. Because much of the range of E. tonkawae occurs in a developed urban area, infrastructure projects for stormwater conveyance, flood abatement, water and wastewater transport, transportation, and others have the potential to impact salamander habitat in urban streams. Our goal was to estimate rates of occupancy in tributaries throughout the salamander’s range, including those in highly developed watersheds. We conducted area-constrained surveys across 17 tributaries, with the goal of better delineating the range of the Jollyville Plateau Salamander and identifying important predictors of species occurrence. We fit a Royle-Nichols model to our repeated presence-absence data in order to describe the distribution of salamanders among sites while accounting for the impacts of detection covariates on the observation process. Jollyville Plateau Salamanders were detected at 107 of 311 survey sites included in this study. Based on our results, occupied habitat is likely to coincide with areas near municipal infrastructure that is placed in or near streams, as all surveyed tributaries in developed watersheds have predicted rates of occupancy ranging from 27 to 71%. At the same time, urban cover was negatively correlated with salamander abundance. Our study shows the prevalence of E. tonkawae throughout urban tributaries while indicating there are ample opportunities for conservation. These may serve as mitigation for projects that would otherwise harm salamanders to potentially satisfy regulatory requirements for the Endangered Species Act.
Conservation & Management II / Conservation Ecology and Genetics I
3435: Invasive species can impact native species indirectly by introducing novel pathogens or altering the epidemiology of resident pathogens. However, few studies have explored whether the introduction of amphibians causes shifts in community-wide infection dynamics. Here we assessed spatiotemporal trends in the dynamics of three amphibian pathogens in a recent invasion of Cuban treefrogs, Osteopilus septentrionalis, in Louisiana, USA. We collected toe clips from 555 O. septentrionalis and 266 resident anurans around the greater New Orleans area from September 2017 to August 2023. We attempted to sample 15 O. septentrionalis from the primary invasion range each month, and we concurrently sampled resident anurans across both invaded and non-invaded locations to determine the impact of invasion on the community. We extracted DNA and used pathogen-specific qPCR protocols to determine pathogen presence and intensity for each individual. Overall, 48/821 tested positive for Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis (Bd), 204/821 tested positive for Ranavirus (Rv), and 106/821 individuals tested positive for Amphibian Perkinsea (Pr). Across our entire sampling period, we observed no difference in body condition by infection status (p > 0.067) or intensity (p > 0.07) within O. septentrionalis, implying this species likely serves as a pathogen reservoir. We also did not observe any significant differences within resident anurans between invaded and non-invaded sites for Bd, or Pr; however, there is a slight trend (p = 0.059) towards higher Rv prevalence in locations with O. septentrionalis. This study highlights the importance of monitoring pathogen dynamics in both the invader and native community beyond the initial invasion.
Thriving in a changing world: host-pathogen dynamics in hyperdiverse communities of amphibians and reptiles (SSAR)
3436: Pathogens interact with complex microbiomes at host mucosal surfaces, yet little is known about how these microbial communities respond to infection. While pathogen exposure can drive dysbiosis and contribute to disease, an alternative hypothesis suggests that microbiome perturbations may instead reflect selection for a more defensive community enriched with anti-pathogen members. Here, we tested this hypothesis in amphibians by conducting a meta-analysis of over 25 studies examining microbial responses to fungal pathogen infection. Using data from both field surveys and experimental studies with known Batrachochytrium infection status, exposure, and/or infection intensity, we assessed how pathogen presence influences key microbiome characteristics, including alpha diversity, beta diversity, and dispersion. Additionally, we used an updated AmphiBac Database, which includes over 7,000 bacterial cultures from hundreds of amphibian hosts tested for growth-inhibiting function of Batrachochytrium pathogens, allowing us to predict functional microbial responses across datasets. Our analysis revealed that microbiome composition shifts significantly upon Bd exposure, with responses varying based on host life stage and population trajectory—i.e., whether amphibian populations are in decline or remain stable. We also identified microbial taxa that were consistently enriched following pathogen exposure, including Flavobacteriaceae and Weeksellaceae, whereas Burkholderiaceae and Mycoplasmataceae were negatively associated with Bd presence. Understanding how microbiomes respond to pathogens is critical for evaluating their role as a dynamic component of amphibian immunity. By disentangling the drivers of amphibian–Batrachochytrium disease dynamics, our findings provide important insights into host-microbe-pathogen interactions in our changing world.
Thriving in a changing world: host-pathogen dynamics in hyperdiverse communities of amphibians and reptiles (SSAR)
3437: Shifting precipitation regimes driven by global climate change alter vertebrate behavior and host-symbiont relationships, potentially compromising host resistance to pathogen invasion. In Brazil's Atlantic Forest, a biodiversity hotspot, prior research identified drought as a key factor disrupting the skin microbiome, contributing to the die-off of pumpkin toadlets due to the invasive waterborne fungal pathogen Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis (Bd). As observational studies often cannot distinguish the direct effect of moisture on Bd growth from increased amphibian activity during wet breeding seasons, we experimentally tested the impact of drought conditions on host behavior, Bd disease dynamics, and the composition and predicted Bd-inhibitory function of cutaneous bacterial communities using field enclosures. Each enclosure housed ecologically realistic densities of Brachycephalus pitanga, a micro-endemic species of pumpkin toadlet. We simulated a short-term drought in half of the enclosures using translucent tarp coverings. To track individual toadlets, we identified their unique markings and collected skin swabs biweekly over three months. Then, we implemented molecular techniques to quantify Bd loads and characterize skin bacterial diversity and composition over time. Our results show that drought suppressed Bd, but an increased host use of wet microenvironments and shifts in the protective skin microbiome partially offset the effect of drying on Bd. This study provides valuable insights into the cascading impacts of climate change on animal behavior, host-symbiont interactions, and disease dynamics. Understanding how changing environmental conditions influence the microbiome’s role in susceptibility to invasive pathogens is crucial for the survival of vulnerable hosts.
Thriving in a changing world: host-pathogen dynamics in hyperdiverse communities of amphibians and reptiles (SSAR)
3438: Amphibians face many challenges to their conservation, including major threats from emerging infectious pathogens. In diverse amphibian communities, where multiple emerging pathogens tend to co-occur, we know little about how the structural partitioning of host specificity among pathogens impacts infection dynamics in the host community. Here, we used field data from diverse amphibian communities in north Florida to investigate host-specific traits influencing the prevalence, intensity, and transmission of three emerging pathogens of amphibians: Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis (Bd), Perkinsea (Pr), and Ranavirus (Rv). We found that Bd exhibited specificity for later developmental stages, and that overall infection patterns differed between ephemeral and semi-permanent sites and across seasons. For each pathogen, we identified key hosts that overwhelmingly contributed to community transmission dynamics and found evidence of pathogen interactions that may facilitate Bd-Rv co-infections, and dilution effects of increased host diversity on Pr infection. Our findings confirm that declining species within the region are routinely infected with emerging pathogens. However, the probability of infection relied on differences in habitat characteristics and the composition of the associated host community. Thus, our study emphasizes the importance of identifying key and sensitive hosts that drive or succumb to infections in natural communities before reintroducing amphibians into the wild. This approach can help improve conservation efforts in diverse host communities as successful repatriation of sensitive species can benefit from detailed characterization of the established disease dynamics at the release site.
Thriving in a changing world: host-pathogen dynamics in hyperdiverse communities of amphibians and reptiles (SSAR)
3439: Apicomplexan parasites in the genus Hepatozoon, a relative of the better-known Toxoplasma that infects cats and rats, have a broad host range that includes snakes and lizards. While Hepatozoon has not caused documented die offs in wild reptiles, it can cause clinical disease in captive reptiles. Clinical symptoms generally occur when parasites from an asymptomatic host infect a new host species. If this process occurs in the wild, infection risk to new host species may be correlated with times of high parasite load in the reservoir host species. To understand patterns of potential risk, we quantified Hepatozoon infection load in a population of the Florida banded water snake, Nerodia fasciata, across three seasons. We captured snakes in a shallow seasonal wetland on the campus of Florida Gulf Coast University, in Ft. Myers, Florida, in winter, spring, and summer of 2022. Using Sanger sequencing, we identified infection by a Hepatozoon lineage closely related to H. ophisauri in the population. Using quantitative PCR, we found that pathogen load varied between individuals in winter and summer. In spring, sampled individuals had uniformly high loads. Several processes could explain this pattern, including higher rates feeding of by the snakes (and therefore transmission) during spring, or vulnerability to infection due to the energetic demands of breeding. The prevalence and variability in parasite load of Hepatozoon in Florida water snakes makes it an ideal system for understanding the drivers of infection intensity and transmission risk between individuals and between seasons.
Thriving in a changing world: host-pathogen dynamics in hyperdiverse communities of amphibians and reptiles (SSAR)
3440: Animals host diverse microbiomes essential for their health and ecological roles. Metacommunity theory provides a framework for understanding host-associated microbiome assembly across scales, linking regional environmental processes to local host-microbial processes. We formulated hypotheses based on community ecology theory and tested them using 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing and novel analytical approaches to analyze the microbiomes of three Appalachian salamander species and their corresponding environments: red-backed salamanders (Plethodon cinereus) in forest soils, two-lined salamanders (Eurycea bislineata) in streams, and eastern newts (Notophthalmus viridescens) in ponds. Given prior findings on evolutionary history and Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis (Bd) shaping salamander microbiomes, we hypothesized niche-based deterministic processes would be dominant. Our analysis revealed variable levels of deterministic processes: 14% for N. viridescens, 34% for P. cinereus, and 68% for E. bislineata. Environmental microbiomes in forests and ponds were highly structured by deterministic processes (91% and 86%, respectively), while stream microbiomes showed a moderate level (47%). Across all three salamander species, we found that bacterial communities were enriched with rare environmental bacteria. We further hypothesized that patch dynamics, such as competition-colonization trade-offs, would dominate metacommunity processes, given that rare environmental microbes are more likely to colonize amphibian skin. Network analyses supported patch dynamics, revealing competition and colonization processes within salamander skin microbiome networks. We identified bacteria from the genus Pedobacter, which includes Bd-inhibitory taxa, as good colonizers on salamander skin. Our findings suggest that niche-based processes shape microbiome structure at the environmental-host interface and highlight key factors predicting microbiome composition based on environment and host biology.
Thriving in a changing world: host-pathogen dynamics in hyperdiverse communities of amphibians and reptiles (SSAR)
3441: Amphibians are the most threatened group of vertebrates, with their populations continuing to decline at an alarming rate due to factors such as habitat loss, disease, and climate change, making genetic strategies aimed at enhancing resilience more critical than ever. The genomics revolution has created many opportunities to enhance amphibian resilience, increasing the potential for establishing self-sustaining populations. These strategies include identifying populations facing genetic threats such as inbreeding depression, performing genetically informed translocations, and releasing pre-adapted individuals. Genetic intervention is also supported by advances in assisted reproductive technologies, stem cell and gamete cryopreservation, and genetic engineering. I will discuss some of the tools and resources required for genetic management, as well as recent developments in the field of genetic intervention.
Thriving in a changing world: host-pathogen dynamics in hyperdiverse communities of amphibians and reptiles (SSAR)
3442: Local adaptation to parallel environmental pressures offers a powerful natural framework to investigate the genomic basis of phenotypic variation such as disease resistance. However, understanding the phylogenetic and demographic background of populations is essential to place adaptive patterns in the proper evolutionary context. Integrating phylogeographic sampling of natural populations with functional genomic data, allows simultaneous exploration of evolutionary history and the genomic signatures of adaptation. We applied this strategy to investigate population structure, phylogeography, demography, and local adaptation across several North American leopard frog species. Using a genome-wide targeted exon capture approach, we enriched our dataset for loci related to immune function and skin integrity to explore genomic responses to chytridiomycosis. We compared genome-wide variation across multiple populations that span a range of ecological conditions and disease outcomes, including chytrid susceptible, tolerant, and disease-naïve populations. Our findings reveal that populations with reduced genetic diversity exhibited greater disease susceptibility and were more likely to face local extirpation. Interestingly, some susceptible or extirpated populations also harbored unique functional alleles not found in more stable populations, which could indicate the presence of historical local adaptations now potentially at risk. We also observed strong nuclear genetic differentiation among populations in contrast to shallow mitochondrial divergence, consistent with recent population fragmentation and drift. Although genetic structure and drift can obscure conventional outlier-based scans for selection, the use of multiple complementary methods revealed candidate genes potentially involved in local adaptation and disease resistance. This study illustrates how combining functional genomic tools with phylogeographic context can provide valuable insights into both demographic history and adaptive processes in non-model amphibians.
Thriving in a changing world: host-pathogen dynamics in hyperdiverse communities of amphibians and reptiles (SSAR)
3443: With increased research and study, our knowledge of diseases of reptiles and amphibians continues to grow. However, scientists, wildlife health experts, and veterinarians all face a common challenge: a rapidly expanding and changing target. The combination of rapid global movement of people, animals, and goods coupled with growing worldwide demand for reptiles, amphibians, or related products in the private sector has created unprecedented challenges for animal health. While there are a number of well-known and well-studied examples of this concept, such as amphibian chytridiomycosis, sadly the number of emerging disease risks facing herpetofauna is swiftly increasing. Emerging pathogens, including fungi, such as ophidiomycosis in snakes, bacteria, such as enterococcosis in lizards, viruses, such as picornaviruses in snakes, and parasites, such as Raillietiella orientalis in reptiles and amphibians, are all documented to cause disease at the level of individual animals, and have the potential to have population-level impacts. This lecture will detail several emerging diseases affecting reptiles and amphibians and will place particular emphasis on the captive:wild interface to demonstrate the challenges that herpetofauna are likely to continue to face in the future.
Thriving in a changing world: host-pathogen dynamics in hyperdiverse communities of amphibians and reptiles (SSAR)
3444: Chameleons are unique amongst tetrapods for their exceptional suite of anatomical modifications which have allowed them to adapt to and diversify in arboreal environments. Specializations shared amongst this unique lizard lineage include having shortened and compressed bodies, reduced flexibility in the trunk and neck, grasping and cleft hands and feet, a prehensile and non-autotomizing tail, highly developed and independently movable eyes, and ballistic tongues. Here we study the optic nerve of chameleons and compare them with other squamates using diceCT methods. Results from the 3D modeling of the brain and associated structures reveals that chameleons developed a coiled optic nerve, which is unique among tetrapods and might be correlated with lateralized eye movements.
3445: Mastacembelus (Synbranchiformes:Mastacembelidae) is a speciose genus of eel-like fishes that is geographically restricted to the freshwaters of tropical southeast Asia and Africa. Previous studies suggest that mastacembelids originated in Asia during the early Miocene and then subsequently invaded and radiated throughout the Afro-Tropics, where 70% of species within the genus reside. Invading a new geographic region by a clade may trigger an early burst of rapid lineage and morphological diversification as species capitalize on ecological opportunity and subsequently slows as niches become saturated. The ecological diversity of Asian and African mastacembelids differ remarkably. Asian species are restricted to swampy habitats. By contrast African species include lacustrine invades, burrowing riverine taxa, and inhabitants of the dark depths of the lower Congo rapids. Ecological diversity is often coupled with morphological diversity; however, the anatomical disparity of mastacembelids remains unexplored. Here we use micro-computed tomography and geometric morphometrics to capture cranial diversity as well as linear morphometrics to capture overall body shape. We then employed phylogenetic comparative methods to compare the tempo and mode of lineage and morphological diversification of African and Asian mastacembelids. We find that all mastacembelids are characterized by rapid lineage diversification rates and African mastacembelids are more morphologically diverse than their Asian relatives. This work provides insight on how ecologically fragmented river drainages in the Afro-Tropics play a pivotal role in the evolution of tropical freshwater fishes.
3446: Ostariophysi is among the most ecologically and morphologically diverse clades of bony fishes, comprised of five orders and over 10,000 species, which together constitute nearly 70% of freshwater fish diversity. While Ostariophysi includes some of the largest orders of fishes (e.g., Cypriniformes and Siluriformes, represented by over 4,000 and 3,000 species respectively), species richness is unevenly distributed across the clade. An outlier among more speciose kin, Gonorynchiformes is a species-depauperate order, consisting of a mere 37 extant species across seven genera. It is the sister-lineage to all other ostariophysans, and despite relatively low species richness, gonorynchiform fishes exhibit striking morphological diversity. From the hefty marine milkfish to the bizarre hingemouth to the miniaturized shellears, gonorynchiform fishes present an intriguing evolutionary phenomenon in which a small order possesses a degree of morphological disparity that may be on par with lineages that are orders of magnitude more speciose. However, no study to date has sought to quantify this disparity. In this study, we employ a landmark-based geometric morphometric approach to quantify three-dimensional skull shape disparity in gonorynchiform fishes. We characterize patterns of morphospace occupation and identify regions of the skull with the greatest shape variation. We compare the gonorynchiform morphospace with that of cypriniform fishes and test the hypothesis that gonorynchiforms have evolved as much morphological diversity as other ostariophysan orders in the absence of a large species radiation.
3447: Colubrids have a near-global distribution and comprise 50% of snakes worldwide. Morphological variation has revealed mechanistic features associated with prey preference. Skeletal modifications of mollusk specialists have been studied extensively, particularly within the genus Pareas, which exhibit a shorter, more compressed snout and, in some, mandibular asymmetry. However, little attention has been paid to those that specialize on slugs (limaxivores). Unlike the snail-eating members of the Pareidae and Dipsadini, limaxivores lack the morphological traits associated with the extraction of snails from their shells. Instead, they often possess elongated, needle-like teeth, which have been hypothesized to assist with the consumption of soft-bodied prey. We used microCT imagery to examine the morphological basis for limaxivory in the two species of Contia. Their skeletal and soft-tissue morphology was compared to that of Carphophis amoenus and Diadophis punctatus. Although not always considered to be sister-taxa of Contia, Carphophis and Diadophis are members of the basal cluster of New World dipsadids to which Contia belongs (sometimes recognized as the Carphophiinae), and they appear to afford the most appropriate comparisons for distinguishing limaxivorous adaptations in Contia. We observed substantial cranial differences between taxa with respect to their trophic structures, presumable reflecting differences in both feeding and locomotor behavior. Diet appears to be the largest determinant of variation in dentition. A more extensive investigation into the prey handling exhibited by limaxivorous snakes should inform the functional interpretation of their morphological features.
3448:
We present here our preliminary findings using DiceCT imaging to visualize the cranial anatomy of front-fanged and rear-fanged snakes collected near Kindia, Guinea. Medically relevant front-fanged species included here were Dendroaspis viridis (Elapidae) with a proteroglyph dentition, and Atractaspis aterrima (Lamprophiidae; Atractaspidinae) and Causus maculatus (Viperidae) with (convergent) solenoglyph dentitions. Medically non-relevant, rear-fanged species included here were Psammophis phillipsii and P. elegans (Lamprophiidae; Psammophiinae) and Toxicodryas blandingi (Colubridae; Colubrinae) all with opisthoglyph dentitions. Highlights of our findings are as follows: The elongate venom glands of C. maculatus were expected but nevertheless impressive to see imaged in this way for the first time; The nasal glands of the lamprophiids were enlarged relative to those of the other snakes, which we speculate may be related to the role of gland secretions in their social lives.

Nous présentons ici nos résultats préliminaires utilisant l'imagerie DiceCT pour visualiser l'anatomie crânienne de serpents à crochets antérieurs et à crochets postérieurs collectés près de Kindia, en Guinée. Les espèces à crochets antérieurs d’importance médicale incluses ici étaient Dendroaspis viridis (Elapidae) avec une dentition protéroglyphe, et Atractaspis aterrima (Lamprophiidae ; Atractaspidinae) et Causus maculatus (Viperidae) avec des dentitions solénoglyphes (convergentes). Les espèces à crochets postérieurs, sans importance médicale, incluses ici étaient Psammophis phillipsii et P. elegans (Lamprophiidae ; Psammophiinae) et Toxicodryas blandingi (Colubridae ; Colubrinae) tous avec des dentitions opisthoglyphes. Les points saillants de nos résultats sont les suivants : Les glandes à venin allongées de C. maculatus étaient attendues mais néanmoins impressionnantes de voir imagées de cette façon pour la première fois ; Les glandes nasales des lamprophiidés étaient plus grandes que celles des autres serpents, ce qui, selon nous, pourrait être lié au rôle des sécrétions glandulaires dans leur vie sociale.
3449: Several studies have documented associations between the relative size of brain regions among fishes, such as chondrichthyan and cichlid fishes, and their habitats. The cerebellum and telencephalon, for example, tend to be relatively larger in species that inhabit more spatially complex environments, such as coral or rocky reefs as compared to simple benthic substrates or up in the water column. These relationships have not yet been examined in Neotropical electric fishes (Gymnotiformes), that sense self-generated electric fields. Here, we compare patterns of diversity in brain anatomy with ecological traits using principal components analysis to explore correlations between the relative size of brain regions with environmental features associated with river size (small, large, or both) and mesohabitat (small lotic, large river margins, pelagic in large rivers, benthic in large rivers, and multiple environments). We find gymnotiform species that inhabit more spatially complex environments have relatively larger telencephalic lobes as compared with species that inhabit spatially simple habitats. These analyses support the hypothesis that in Gymnotiformes, relative size of the telencephalon is correlated and perhaps influenced by environmental adaptations, as reported in other fish taxa. However, unlike other fishes, cerebellum size in gymnotiforms is not correlated with habitat complexity. The exceptionally large size of the cerebellum in gymnotiforms, used in active electroreception, may mask brain size patterns observed in other fish groups.
3450: Within Microhylidae, only two genera putatively develop keratinized feeding structures during the tadpole stage: Scaphiophryne of Madagascar and Otophryne of northern South America. Based on our current understanding of the microhylid phylogeny, it is possible that these two lineages independently regained keratinized mouthparts after the common ancestor of microhylids lost these structures. To evaluate this hypothesis, we generated histological sections of Scaphiophryne and Otophryne tadpoles and reconstructed the evolutionary history of tadpole keratinized mouthparts across the frog tree of life. We confirm that the cellular microanatomy of the keratinized jaw sheaths in Scaphiophryne and Otophryne is comparable to that of other tadpoles, composed of basal keratinocytes that proliferate into a stacked column of cone cells and supporting sheath cells. The inferred ancestral larval state in crown-group frogs is a tadpole with keratinized mouthparts, and these specialized larval structures were subsequently lost in more than 15 anuran lineages. Tadpole keratinized mouthparts were lost in the most recent common ancestor of Microylidae and independently regained in the ancestors of Scaphiophryne and Otophryne. Our findings provide new insights into the constraints and flexibility of tadpole mouthpart evolution, and we add microhylid tadpole keratinized mouthparts to the growing list of complex traits that have been evolutionarily lost and regained in violation of Dollo’s law of irreversibility.
3451: Mormyridae, a family of weakly electric fishes native to African lakes and rivers, display remarkable diversity in their craniofacial morphologies from brachiocephalic to dolichocephalic.  Despite their ecological importance, the functional morphology of these fishes remain largely understudied. The goal of this study is to investigate the functional implications of face elongation on the mechanical leverage of the lower jaw, an important proxy of force transmission in the jaws of teleost fishes. Initially, we hypothesized that mormyrids with longer snouts (i.e., the distance from orbit to end of the rostrum) would have lower mechanical advantages due to the assumed jaw elongation. We assessed the mechanical properties of the jaw lever-linkage system using simple lever mechanics measured from high resolution microCT scans. Preliminary results show that some species with extreme craniofacial phenotypes and elongated snouts exhibit lower mechanical advantages. However, this pattern is not necessarily attributed to jaw length alone. In some species with elongated snouts and lower mechanical advantages, their skeletal jaws are relatively short, which conflicts with the general assumption that mormyrids with shorter jaws would have a greater bite force. In our preliminary dataset, we see different configurations of face elongation (e.g., long faces but relatively short jaws versus long faces with relatively long jaws) and this leads to various functional outcomes from relatively weak to strong jaws.
3452: Overlap between marine megafauna and maritime activities is a topic of global concern. Basking sharks (Cetorhinus maximus; CM) are listed as Globally Endangered under the IUCN, though reported sightings appear to be increasing in Ireland. While such trends in the region are welcome, increasing spatiotemporal overlap between CM and numerous water users poses an increased risk of boat strikes to the animals. To demonstrate the risk and impact of boat strikes on marine megafauna, we present camera-enabled animal-borne inertial measurement unit (IMU) data from a non-lethal boat strike on a CM within a proposed National Marine Park in Ireland. We tagged a ~7 m female CM in County Kerry, Ireland, which was struck by a boat ~6 hrs after tag deployment. Comparison of pre-strike data with 4 hrs of video and ~7.5 hrs of IMU data following the boat strike provide critical insight into the animal’s response. While the CM reacted momentarily with an increase in activity and swam to the seafloor, it quickly reduced its overall activity (i.e., Overall Dynamic Body Acceleration, tailbeat cycles, tailbeat amplitude and vertical velocity) for the remainder of the deployment. Notably, the animal also ceased feeding for the duration of video and headed towards deep offshore waters, which is in stark contrast to the pre-strike period where the animal was consistently observed feeding along the surface in shallow coastal water. This work provides insight into a CM’s response to acute injury and highlights the need for appropriate protections to mitigate risks for marine megafauna.
3453: Scientists’ interest in highlighting and reversing the depletion of shark populations has been growing for several decades. As the number of safeguards for sharks adopted at national and international levels has increased, scientific research has expanded beyond the study of shark population status and life history characteristics to the examination of conservation measures’ effectiveness. Bans on finning (slicing off a shark’s valuable fins and discarding the body at sea) and retention of certain species were among the first measures promoted 30 years ago to address the waste and overfishing of sharks; they remain among the most common remedies in place today. The implementation of these policies has resulted in myriad effects and has sparked a wide range of recommendations for improvement. Scientific advice is particularly influential and plays an important role in the development and amendment of shark fishing restrictions, including bans on retention and finning. Policy aspects that are important for evaluation but not always obvious will be reviewed. Suggestions for maximizing the conservation benefit of associated research findings will be offered.
3454: Environmental DNA (eDNA) has emerged as a powerful tool to support the conservation of aquatic species. The value of eDNA methodologies lies in its highly sensitive detection capabilities, making it an effective tool to fill data gaps for elusive species. The sawfishes are one of the most imperiled vertebrate groups, with all five species classified as Critically Endangered on the International Union for Conservation of Nature Red List of Threatened Species. Owing to their toothy rostra, sawfishes are easily entangled in a wide range of fishing gears, with mortalities in fisheries driving global declines. The Largetooth Sawfish, Pristis pristis, had a circumtropical range historically, but has experienced severe global declines in range and abundance. Viable populations are thought to be confined to a stronghold in northern Australia, although remnant populations may persist in a handful of countries. Genetic analysis of historical DNA from sawfish rostra indicates the Eastern Pacific and Atlantic harbors a distinct genetic lineage of P. pristis which is at risk of extinction. To identify promising locations where populations may persist in the Eastern Pacific, we conducted eDNA surveys across Panama, Colombia, and Peru. A novel species-specific Droplet Digital PCR assay was designed to detect a single copy of P. pristis DNA, with functionality across its historical range. Analysis of 492 water samples revealed P. pristis persists in the Eastern Pacific, but occurrence may be limited to key regions. Additional eDNA surveys using ddPCR technology are recommended to support identification of priority areas for conservation efforts.
3455: Social media tools have revolutionized how people communicate with one another, with numerous implications for public science engagement, stakeholder outreach, professional networking, conservation advocacy, and even research. However, the social media landscape is changing rapidly. With the decline of Twitter as a professionally useful tool, how should scientists, environmentalists, and managers adapt? This talk will summarize the basic principles of using social media tools for professional science, conservation, and management purposes, highlighting case studies of success from the AES and JMIH community. It will also introduce new tools like Bluesky.
3456: The smalltooth sawfish (Pristis pectinata) historically ranged from North Carolina to Texas in United States’ waters and as far south as Uruguay in the western Atlantic Ocean. However, following a stark population decline, the species is now rarely found outside Florida. In 2003, the smalltooth sawfish became the first elasmobranch to be listed as Endangered under the U.S. Endangered Species Act. Increasing abundance is a key objective of the recovery plan, but current and baseline population sizes are lacking. Therefore, innovative approaches are needed to assess recovery and develop data-driven criteria for future population assessments. In this study, genomic data from more than 1,000 individuals were used to estimate census population size (NC) across multiple time periods using close-kin mark-recapture. Effective population size (NE) was also estimated for the same time periods, enabling the NE/NC relationship to be assessed. In addition, a subset of individuals was used to estimate NE over the past 100 generations, which allowed baseline NC estimates before the population decline to be inferred using the NE/NC relationship. The study provides crucial insights into the life history and abundance trends of the distinct population segment of smalltooth sawfish in U.S. waters. The results will inform recovery planning aimed at ensuring the species' long-term viability.
3457: Marine protected areas (MPAs) are increasingly being used in marine conservation, however, their effectiveness in protecting wide-ranging species is unclear.  The silky shark, Carcharhinus falciformis, has experienced large declines in the Eastern Tropical Pacific and may benefit from the network of MPAs in the region.  We examined silky shark use of MPAs and fisheries overlap by satellite tracking 38 individuals tagged within the Galapagos Marine Reserve (GMR) for periods of up to 639 d.  Based on movement patterns, sharks were split into three groups: males, eastern females, and western females.  Sharks from all groups tended to show site fidelity to the GMR and it was the most used MPA.  MPA use varied little between the wet (Dec-May) and dry seasons (Jun-Nov) for males and eastern females; males and eastern females spent ~55% and ~70% of their time within MPAs, respectively.  Western females spent more time within MPAs during the wet (~50%) compared to the dry season (~15%).  Combining silky shark space use with fishing effort data from Global Fishing Watch revealed that sharks were most at risk from fisheries during the dry season within the northern Galapagos EEZ.  Risk was much lower in the wet season; however, Global Fishing Watch data severely underestimates fishing effort in the region.  Overall, silky sharks spent a great deal of time within the protected waters of the GMR, but their movements extended far beyond the GMR and other MPAs, putting them at risk from commercial fisheries operating in the Eastern Tropical Pacific.
3458:
This presentation introduces a new book called Ecology and Evolution of Amazonian Fishes, which explains how the freshwater fishes of South America became the richest continental vertebrate fauna on Earth. The contributing authors, all experts on particular fish groups, produced three novel and taxonomically coordinated datasets, including a comprehensive time-calibrated phylogeny with geographic ranges and behavioral and ecological traits for all 6,345 known species. A fourth dataset provides a synthetic chronology of important paleogeoraphic events and conditions of the past 100 million years that influenced the evolution of this fauna. These ecological and evolutionary patterns are merged to evaluate prominent theories on the origins of South American freshwater fishes. The book explains now Amazonian fishes emerged from the fortuitous interactions of perennial environmental conditions, unique paleogeographic events, and characteristic organismal traits, operating over millions of years, which allowed rates of speciation to exceed extinction. These conditions included the vast area of moist lowland tropical rainforests, with diverse aquatic habitats, and a stochastic history of river capture and shoreline fluctuations across a topographically flat landscape. The result was a reticulated history of riverine connections that spurred geographic isolation and allopatric speciation in some species, merged species ranges and lowered their extinction risk in others, and isolated yet others to the continental periphery. This combination of geographic and organismal factors, under a generally stable climate through geological time, resulted in a series of fortunate events that drove sustained speciation, lowered extinction, and ultimately, resulted in the characteristic biodiversity profiles of Amazonian fishes.

Esta apresentação introduz um novo livro intitulado Ecology and Evolution of Amazonian Fishes que explica como os peixes de água doce da América do Sul se tornaram a fauna continental de vertebrados mais rica da Terra. Os autores colaboradores, todos especialistas em determinados grupos de peixes, produziram três conjuntos de dados inéditos e coordenados taxonomicamente, incluindo uma filogenia abrangente calibrada no tempo, com distribuições geográficas e características comportamentais e ecológicas para todas as 6.345 espécies conhecidas. Um quarto conjunto de dados fornece uma cronologia sintética de eventos paleogeográficos importantes e das condições dos últimos 100 milhões de anos que influenciaram a evolução dessa fauna. Esses padrões ecológicos e evolutivos são combinados para avaliar teorias proeminentes sobre as origens dos peixes de água doce sul-americanos. O livro explica como os peixes amazônicos surgiram a partir de interações fortuitas entre condições ambientais perenes, eventos paleogeográficos únicos e características organísmicas específicas, atuando ao longo de milhões de anos — o que permitiu que as taxas de especiação superassem as de extinção. Essas condições incluíram a vasta área de florestas tropicais úmidas de planícies e uma história estocástica de captura de rios em uma paisagem topograficamente plana, que produziu uma rede interligada de conexões fluviais, impulsionando o isolamento geográfico e a expansão das áreas de distribuição. Essa combinação de fatores geográficos e biológicos resultou em uma série de eventos afortunados que promoveram uma especiação sustentada, reduziram as extinções e, por fim, resultaram nos perfis característicos de biodiversidade dos peixes amazônicos.
3459: The African catfish family Auchenoglanididae presently includes the genera Auchenoglanis, Parauchenoglanis, and Notoglanidium. We conducted a phylogenetic analysis integrating genomic data from ultraconserved elements (UCEs) and a morphological dataset of 52 anatomical characters. Our results indicate that the eight sampled species assigned to Notoglanidium do not form a monophyletic group, necessitating recognition of two additional genera. We find N. maculatum, N. thomasi, and N. walkeri forming a clade sister to all other members of the Auchenoglanididae, so we restrict Notoglanidium to these three species. We additionally recognize Anaspidoglanis to include A. boutchangaii and A. macrostoma, and Platyglanis to include P. depierrei and P. pembetadi. We also redefine Parauchenoglanis to include the lower Congo River endemic P. pallidum. These findings highlight the importance of combining genetic and morphological data for resolving taxonomic relationships and provide a framework for future studies on the evolutionary history of African catfishes.
3460: The Neotropical freshwater fish (NFF) Hoplerythrinus is widely distributed throughout cis-Andean tropical South America. The type species H. unitaeniatus was described from the Rio São Francisco, and the two other valid species are known only from the type material: H. gronovii from Cayenne in French Guiana and H. cinereus from Trinidad Island. No studies have yet been conducted to assess the taxonomic status of these nominal species, and diversity in this group remains poorly understood. Here, we integrate DNA barcode sequences, a phylogenomic dataset of ultraconserved elements (UCEs), morphological information, and extensive geographic distribution coverage to investigate the diversity and evolutionary history of Hoplerythrinus. Six mtDNA lineages were identified: (i) Amazon, Orinoco, and Guianas basins, (ii) Paraná-Paraguay basin, (iii) São Francisco and Upper Tocantins basins, (iv) coastal drainages along southeastern Brazil, (v) Orinoco basin, and (vi) from upper portions of Amazonian versants draining the Brazilian Shield. Reciprocal monophyly of these clusters was not always recovered in phylogenomic analyses using UCEs data. Discordant assignments of representatives from the Orinoco basin comparing mitochondrial and nuclear datasets suggest secondary contacts between adjacent regions. Additionally, morphological characters examined to date do not distinguish among the lineages. Hoplerythrinus exhibits low species accumulation rates considering its divergence time (ca. 7.1 Ma), similar to patterns exhibited by some ecologically generalist NFF genera. Results suggest that here has not been enough time to establish full divergence among lineages. Therefore, they cannot be unambiguously diagnosed as valid species.
3461: Chameleons are a diverse clade of lizards that inhabit a wide range of habitats across the arboreality spectrum. Chamaeleo calyptratus has served as a primary model for studies on arboreal locomotion in chameleons. Studies including Chamaeleo dilepis, however, have scored their arboreality as terrestrial, semi-arboreal or arboreal depending on the species it was being compared to. Specific knowledge of the kinematics and performance of C. dilepis locomotion is somewhat limited, however, and the species is unlikely to simultaneously exhibit locomotor patterns adapted for all possible conditions along the arboreality spectrum. We performed locomotor trials with C. calyptratus and C. dilepis across substrates and orientations to compare kinematics between these two model chameleon species. Individuals were first filmed using biplanar high-speed video walking along a meter-long wooden dowel at three inclines (-45º ,0º, 45º). Individuals were then filmed walking along on a 1-meter-long flat surface at 0º incline. We quantified morphology, kinematic, and performance variables including velocity, joint angles of the forelimb and hindlimb, stride length, and stride frequency from locomotor trials for each species. Both species operated in the same kinematic space and responded to changes in substrate, but they responded to the different substrates in different manners. Our results provide insight into how an arboreal and terrestrial environment impacts the locomotor patterns and performance of these species to help establish the degree to which C. dilepis locomotion departs from a typical arboreal model chameleon.
3462: Cynoglossus n. sp. 1, described from three specimens (97.1–111.3 mm SL), and Cynoglossus n. sp. 2, described from 14 specimens (74.0–106.3 mm SL), were collected in coastal waters of the southern Red Sea. These new species feature an incomplete ocular-side dorsolateral line and are the first Tongue Soles from the Red Sea that possess a truncated dorsolateral line. These species are distinguished from congeners by the combination of: relatively small size; incomplete dorsolateral line; no blind-side lateral lines; 2 ocular-side nostrils; and single pelvic fin. The species, as defined in our study, correspond to well divergent monophyletic lineages in a phylogenetic analysis of the mitochondrial COI gene. Cynoglossus n. sp. 1 differs further from congeners in its meristic features, especially in having 10 caudal-fin rays, and its ocular-side coloration (uniform light to medium reddish-brown background without prominent crossbands or darkly pigmented spots on the center of its ocular-side scales). Cynoglossus n. sp. 2 is further distinguished from congeners by meristic features, especially its 8 caudal-fin rays, and its uniformly light- to medium-brown ocular-side pigmentation without prominent crossbands, but featuring a prominent dark spot in the central part of its ocular-side scales. Discovery of these new species, together with other recently described Tongue Soles, indicates that cynoglossid Tongue Soles are more diverse in the Red Sea than previously hypothesized. Many Tongue Soles found in the Red Sea have limited distributions or are endemic to this sea, further highlighting the uniqueness of the Red Sea fish fauna.
3463: Entering its 28th year, it may be the longest-running nomenclatural standoff in ichthyology. In 1997, Maylandia Meyer & Foerster 1984 was deemed a nomen nudum and replaced by Metriaclima Stauffer, Bowers, Kellogg & McKaye 1997. But both names continue to be used in ichthyological and aquarium references, creating considerable confusion. For example, 16 new species have been described using the Metriaclima name since 2007, but are reassigned to Maylandia at Eschmeyer’s Catalog of Fishes. Literature on the controversy, most of it appearing in aquarium publications and websites largely outside the view of professional taxonomists and the ichthyological community at large, is reviewed. Based on this review, one name best meets ICZN standards for availability and should be used moving forward.
3464: Phylogenetic reconstruction of the Neotropical freshwater fish family Anostomidae using multilocus sequence data from 97 species supports the recognition of three subfamilies: Leporellinae with one genus, Anostominae with six genera, and Leporininae with nine genera. We reassign many Leporinus species to a redefined Hypomasticus, move the species formerly known as Anostomus brevior to Petulanos, and allocate Leporinus striatus to a new monotypic genus sister to Abramites and Megaleporinus. These taxonomic changes reinforce the emerging perspective of Hypomasticus as a clade with diverse oral morphologies, not limited to species with subterminal or inferior mouths.  They also partially solve the longstanding non-monophyly of Leporinus. Though many relationships inferred herein match earlier morphological hypotheses, the subfamily Anostominae appears as the unambiguous sister to Leporellus, not Laemolyta, indicating that the superior mouths of Anostominae and Laemolyta evolved convergently. Several clades have converged on subterminal or inferior mouths, including lineages within Hypomasticus, Leporellus, Leporinus, and Schizodon. This largest-ever phylogeny for Anostomidae will support further taxonomic research and provide a scaffold for morphological, biogeographic, and evolutionary studies in this transcontinental group of Neotropical fishes.
3465: All reptiles have scientific names but the meaning of these names is not always obvious. We investigated the etymology of all extant reptile taxa, including 1,258 genera, 12,384 species and 2,085 subspecies, that is, a total of 15,727 names. 5,390 names are derived from Latin (34%), 2,471 from Greek (15%), 4,497 are eponyms (i.e., named after people, 29%), and 3,337 are toponyms (i.e., named after places, 21%).
