However, there are also 667 named that fall into different categories, e.g. 57 species named after mythological figures, including, for instance, characters in the Game of Thrones. A few taxa named after organizations (about 20), or local heroes and tribes such as the Cofan Indians. There are also species named after ships, cars, fruit, stars, TV programes, dances, or other idiosyncratic sources. Some authors, like John Edward Gray, made up dozens of names without any meaning – but at least they sound good (in Gray’s opinion). More than 20 names were sponsored through the BIOPAT program which names species after donors. We will provide a survey of the most common, most interesting, and most puzzling reptile names, including a few whose origin or meaning remains mysterious.
3466: Chameleons (Chamaeleonidae) and many lungless salamanders (Plethodontidae) can quickly project their tongues to capture distant prey. Both ballistic tongue systems feature a tubular accelerator muscle coupled with tapered skeletal elements and slender, elongated retractor muscles, but the biomechanical principles and evolutionary mechanism remain enigmatic. Here, we studied the dynamics of entire tongue projection-retraction cycles. In both groups, the tongue projection movement is characterized by an initial acceleration phase and a subsequent deceleration phase, allowing the tongue pad to collide with the prey at a limited ideal range of velocity and deceleration. When colliding with the prey, the tongue pad experiences the greatest deceleration and reaches zero speed, after which an elastic restoring force from the retractor system initiates the retraction movement. We show this rapid adhesion and recoiling (termed ‘rapting’) is modulated through the timing of eccentric contraction of the retractor muscles. With a mathematical model, we show that the biomechanical coupling between a linear accelerator (i.e. the projector system) and a muscular tether (i.e. the retractor system) modulates the dynamics of the ballistic projection-retraction cycle. Our results help to explain not only the convergence in design and performance of ballistic tongues in salamanders and chameleons but also how selection for capturing distant prey and small body size may underlie the evolution of ballistic tongue systems.
3467: The northern distinct population segment of Copperbelly Watersnakes (Nerodia erythrogaster neglecta) is found at one locality where Indiana, Michigan, and Ohio meet. This species has experienced declines over the last few decades with most recent surveys estimating between 41- 91 adults remain. Extensive efforts have been made by local agencies to manage, purchase and restore habitat in this area, but Copperbelly numbers remain low. In 2020, The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and Toledo Zoo collaborated to pilot a population augmentation project, which resulted in creation of a propagation and captive-rearing facility. Following a soft-release period at the source site, the first cohort of seven captive-reared snakes was released in July 2024 and radio-tracked throughout the rest of the season. Snakes in our study exhibited movement patterns and habitat use consistent with previous telemetry data from wild snakes and generally stayed within 20 m of their release wetland. No mortality was observed and all seven snakes survived to overwintering. Telemetry will continue in spring 2025 to assess overwintering mortality. These preliminary results are encouraging and a second group of snakes is scheduled to be released in June.
3468: Understanding how genetic diversity is structured across fragmented landscapes is critical to the conservation of imperiled species, particularly those reliant on isolated or ephemeral habitats. The Chiricahua Leopard Frog (Lithobates chiricahuensis), a federally threatened amphibian native to the arid southwestern U.S., has significantly rebounded through coordinated management efforts. However, there has been no formal genetic evaluation for the species, leaving managers unsure how to cluster management units and enact any mixing between populations. We conducted a comprehensive range-wide genomic analysis using ddRADseq data from more than 400 individuals across 55 sites in Arizona and New Mexico. Our results revealed substantial genetic differentiation, identifying up to 16 distinct clusters corresponding to geographic and ecological boundaries, with previously undocumented levels of structure at certain sites in New Mexico. Despite historic declines and ongoing habitat fragmentation, genetic diversity remains relatively high, and evidence of inbreeding is minimal—likely reflecting the effectiveness of past conservation actions. These findings offer a robust framework for genetically informed translocation, augmentation, and captive breeding, and highlight the importance of balancing genetic integrity with adaptive management. We also document hybridization with L. blairi, reinforcing the need for continued genetic monitoring. This study illustrates how genomic tools can refine recovery strategies for species with complex population structures and conservation histories.
3469: Eastern diamondback rattlesnakes (Crotalus adamanteus; EDBs) are an imperiled, heavy-bodied pitviper endemic to the southeastern Coastal Plain. Reproduction is costly for females, which are slow to mature, reproduce infrequently, and expend substantial somatic reserves during vitellogenesis and gestation. Reproductive females drive population stability, yet we have a limited understanding of what factors inform their survivorship. In 2022 and 2023, we monitored mature females (snout-vent-length ≥100 cm, n=23) via radio telemetry on a coastal sea island in South Carolina. Using a known fates framework in program MARK, we examined the effects of season (dormant, active), reproductive condition (reproductive, nonreproductive), relative fecundity, body size (snout-vent-length), and health (i.e., body condition, signs of disease) on the survival probability of females in the twelve months (October 2022‒September 2023) following the 2022 season of parturition (August‒September 2022), anticipating that reproduction would invoke delayed mortality costs. Annual survival was strongly affected by individual health; survival was positively associated with dormant season body condition and negatively associated with clinical signs of disease, which we attributed to the pathogen Ophidiomyces ophidiicola (causative agent of ophidiomycosis, also known as snake fungal disease). We report the lowest survival estimate for the species (i.e., 68%), which poses alarming implications for ongoing population viability (e.g., recruitment) and species resilience at local and regional scales. Our findings thus suggest a critical need for targeted efforts to understand and mitigate novel disease dynamics among vulnerable North American snakes.
3470: Unisexual Ambystoma salamanders are a unique lineage of polyploid, all-female salamanders that "steal" DNA from males of several co-occurring sexual species. The unisexuals therefore contain genomes from multiple species, and potentially gain benefits from greater gene expression or increased diversity in genes being expressed. One potential benefit is greater diversity in the components of their skin secretions. Amphibian skin secretions are complex mixtures that include diverse groups of molecules such as alkaloids, steroids, peptides and proteins. Some molecules discourage predation through toxicity or unpleasant taste, while others serve as a functional part of the immune system by providing protection from infection. Gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GCMS) reveals substantial differences in the components of skin secretions from sexual species and unisexuals, as well as differences between captive and wild animals. A broader diversity of components in the skin secretions of unisexual salamanders may confer enhanced protection against predation or microbial pathogens.
3471: Wood turtles (Glyptemys insculpta) in Massachusetts exhibit higher mortality rates than other aquatic turtle species in the area due to increased predation rates. Wood turtles are considered endangered by the IUCN, a Species of Special Concern under the Massachusetts Endangered Species Act, and under evaluation for listing under the federal Endangered Species Act. Wood turtle populations in Massachusetts have been monitored and supplemented through headstarting efforts for several years by Zoo New England. One goal of headstarting is to produce ‘predator-proof’ juvenile turtles which can be safely released into the wild. However, increased mortalities have disproportionately affected headstarted wood turtles in some of our field sites. To gain a better understanding of predation pressures affecting wood turtles and how to mitigate them, we assessed predator occurrence, abundance, and behavior with motion-triggered wildlife cameras placed in wood turtle habitat. We recorded ten second videoclips with 36 cameras between May and November 2024 in three different field sites. Each camera was paired with one of four treatments consisting of a visual and/or olfactory cue: 1) a realistic wood turtle model, 2) a scent tube infused with wood turtle scent, 3) a wood turtle model with a scent tube, 4) control treatment (no visual or olfactory cue). We implemented these treatments to investigate the behavior of potential wood turtle predators and if and how they would interact with visual and/or scent cues. Further, we compared data on predator abundance with location data from our monitored wood turtle populations at each site.
3472: Genetic rescue is a conservation strategy by which genetic variation is increased in small, imperiled populations by supplementing individuals using captive breeding methods. The Santa Cruz long-toed salamander, Ambystoma macrodactylum croceum, is a subspecies of Ambystomatid that is state and federally listed as endangered and has a range limited to a small area along California’s central coast. Multiple factors, including the proliferation of commercial agriculture, expansion of development, salinization of ponds, and introduction of non-native species, have led to population declines, inbreeding, and loss of genetic diversity. This loss of diversity can lead to the risk of an extinction vortex, wherein a small population can spiral into extinction. To counter this risk, we initiated a captive breeding program aimed at increasing genetic diversity in the wild. We boosted genetic diversity using an admixture design, by crossing populations with lower genetic diversity to those with higher diversity and releasing the resultant larvae into shrinking populations. We then tracked the reproductive and survival success of released individuals using genetic mark-recapture techniques and a pedigree analysis using microhaplotype markers. Preliminary results suggest that larval introductions have led to breeding success in a few ponds. Continued evaluations will assess the program's efficacy at increasing genetic diversity and reducing extinction risk. We are also evaluating the potential to introduce genetically diverse populations into new habitats within and outside its current range. Overall, this proactive conservation method can potentially help this species escape the extinction vortex as it continues to be threatened by anthropogenic stressors.
3473: Long-term monitoring is crucial to understanding how populations persist and change over time in response to both threats and active management. The Orianne Society’s survey efforts are the longest ongoing, large-scale effort to monitor Eastern Indigo Snake (Drymarchon couperi) populations at broad spatial scales. In 2010, The Orianne Society began occupancy monitoring for Eastern Indigo Snakes using visual encounter surveys at 40 sites in the Altamaha River drainage. In 2016, we expanded monitoring efforts to include sites in the Alapaha, Ogeechee, and Satilla River drainages and increased our total number of survey sites to 60 over a three-year rotation. To date, we have completed three full site rotations of this expanded design (ca. 540 total surveys over nine years). Across all survey effort, we have observed 183 indigo snakes and 137 shed skins. Detection probabilities are positively influenced by the number of Gopher Tortoise burrows at a site and are typically between 0.50–0.69 at the best sites. Our data suggest indigo snake populations in southeastern Georgia have remained relatively stable, with indigo snakes detected at 52% (2016–2019), 50% (2019–2022), and 43% (2022-25) of sites surveyed (estimated occupancy probabilities: 2016–2019 = 0.57; 2019–2022 = 0.61; 2022–25 = 0.47). However, our fieldwork has also identified concerning habitat degradation at some sites that threatens the persistence of Gopher Tortoises and consequently Eastern Indigo Snakes. Continued monitoring of indigo snake populations in Georgia will inform ongoing and future conservation and management decisions.
3474: Few freshwater turtles spend time in saline environments aside from the Emydid Diamond-backed Terrapin (Malaclemys terrapin) of North America’s brackish-water Atlantic and Gulf Coasts. It is thus surprising that vibrant and widespread populations of the declining Northwestern Pond Turtle (Actinemys marmorata) are found in the brackish waters of Suisun Marsh in the San Franscisco Bay Estuary of California, USA. The marsh has salinities that vary from freshwater to almost entirely seawater, but fluctuate daily with tides, seasonally with dry Mediterranean summers, and annually depending on climate. In a lab study, we found that pond turtles from the marsh lost more mass after two weeks of exposure to 15 ppt salinity, but were better able to maintain blood plasma osmolalities close to field values than were inland turtles, presumably because turtles from the marsh forwent feeding and drinking to manage blood solutes. Using telemetry trackers on turtles in the marsh, we found they increased home range areas and moved away from a site where tides were restored to a previously dammed portion of the marsh, with smaller turtles disappearing from the restoration site altogether. Finally, from occupancy surveys across the 470 km2 marsh, we found that pond turtle occupancy decreased as salinity increased, with an inflection around 10 ppt salinity. Our work highlights the limits some freshwater species face in dynamic coastal environments where sea level rise, droughts, and diversion of freshwater inputs are all expected to converge to increase salinities in coming decades.
3475: Geographic isolation and ecological specialization have long been implicated in macroevolutionary diversification, but quantitative methods to assess habitat connectivity on modern and paleo-landscapes have only recently become available. Here we test alternative models of macroevolutionary diversification in clades of channel-dwelling electric fishes (Apteronotidae, Gymnotiformes) from South America. We use species distribution models (SDMs) and landscape evolution models (LEMs) to assess patterns of habitat connectivity through time, of species adapted to riverine habitats across a range of stream orders. We test the hypothesis that eurytopic (i.e. broadly adapted) species, which tolerate a wider range of stream orders, are exposed to more frequent headwater tributary capture events, and therefore undergo higher rates of dispersal and speciation. We observe higher rates of net lineage diversification in clades of eurytopic species, supporting the interpretation that river capture allowed species who can inhabit smaller rivers (with Strahler stream orders 1-5) greater opportunity to disperse to, and diversify within, adjacent basins. This result is consistent with a model of continental radiation on a dynamic riverscape, where clades are subjected to river capture over millions of years, and where most sister species exhibit allopatric distributions and a high level of habitat redundancy.
3476: The world of snakes remains largely unexplored, with many aspects yet to be identified compared to other taxa. Within the genus Bungarus, this lack of attention is particularly evident. In Bangladesh, five species of Bungarus have been documented, yet Bungarus sindanus has received significantly less attention compared to Bungarus caeruleus and Bungarus walli across Asia, including Bangladesh, India, and Pakistan.  This study employs a mixed-methods approach, combining field observations and data collection from existing databases. Field studies were conducted across three distinct regions of Bangladesh during different seasons from 2020 to 2024.  The findings confirm that Bungarus caeruleus, Bungarus walli, and Bungarus sindanus exhibit distinct differences in habitat preferences, morphological patterns, and toxicity levels.  This research highlights the need for further studies on Bungarus sindanus, providing a foundation for future exploration and conservation efforts.
3477: We examine skull development in the Red Sea anemonefish, Amphiprion bicinctus, across four early life stages (preflexion, flexion, postflexion, and metamorphosis) using micro-CT scanning and 3D geometric morphometrics to assess ontogenetic allometry and shifts in modularity patterns. The mandible, premaxilla, and maxilla exhibit strong size–shape relationships, whereas the lower pharyngeal jaw and parasphenoid remain largely isometric, indicating that shape in these structures is not significantly influenced by size. PCA and morphological disparity analyses identify preflexion as the stage with the greatest shape variation, potentially reflecting increased developmental plasticity early in ontogeny. Of the six modularity hypotheses tested, based on developmental and functional bone interactions, the two developmental hypotheses were highly conserved across stages. However, during flexion, a stage characterized by structural reorganization, several hypotheses, both developmental and functional, showed increased support based on DIC values, suggesting shifts in modularity at this critical point. Across all stages, strong integration between the premaxilla and mandible was observed, including during flexion, as indicated by significant PLS scores. This integration supports the need for consistent developmental and functional coordination of these oral jaw elements during early life in the pelagic environment. Together, these findings demonstrate how allometry, modularity, and integration shape early skull morphology in a species undergoing rapid development and ecological transitions, with the oral jaws exhibiting strong between-bone integration and pronounced allometric growth likely linked to optimizing feeding performance.
3478: We combined behavioral and genetic parentage data recorded over a decade to test the fitness consequences and possible causes of delayed versus accelerated territory acquisition in first-year male Collared Lizards. Ours was an interesting study population because some first-year males acquired breeding territories whereas others delayed territory defense until Year-2, and individuals displayed long-term philopatry to habitat patches differing in structural features that influenced male behavior. Territorial longevity was under strong selection that enhanced lifetime fitness in males. Among males that survived to a second breeding season, Year-1 fitness was a strong predictor of lifetime fitness, and individuals that defended territories during Year-1 achieved higher first season fitness than those postponing defense. Nonetheless, the proportion of non-territorial first-year males remained relatively stable, suggesting that more than one social ontogeny is maintained in this population. Variation in habitat structural complexity appeared to play a key role in the maintenance of delayed territory defense. Surreptitious travel and mating via the network of sub-surface crawlspaces characterizing complex habitats allowed non-territorial males to achieve higher lifetime reproductive success than their counterparts in simple habitats lacking such interconnected crawlspaces. More frequent territory acquisition in larger first-year males hatching from first clutches suggested that the social ontogeny of individuals was conditional on their physiological capabilities, perhaps stemming from environmental factors influencing early development. Our results demonstrate the power of combining genetic parentage and behavior over the lifespan of individuals to reveal important factors driving variation in individual behavior and social system evolution.
3479: A major challenge of fisheries management is determining the rate of species mortality, especially natural mortality. This can be especially true for highly migratory species such as sharks and some rays due to their wide distributions, highly mobile behavior, and poorly-understood trophic interactions. We used acoustic telemetry detections of Atlantic cownose rays (Rhinoptera bonasus, 58 adults, 35 juveniles), juvenile dusky sharks (Carcharhinus obscurus, 29 individuals), and adult smooth dogfish (Mustelus canis, 21 individuals) to test criteria for potential mortalities, estimate annual mortality rates, and identify potential sources of mortality based on timing and location of the last confirmed detections. Criteria for potential mortality included gaps in detection between the last confirmed tag detection and the tag expiration date that exceeded the mean time between detections, abnormal movements in comparison to other individuals of the same species, and apparent stationarity within receiver arrays. Estimated mortality rates were compared with published mortality rates derived from fishery catch data and other sources. To identify temporal and spatial trends in mortality, we plotted and mapped the dates and locations of final confirmed tag detections for individuals identified as potential mortalities. These times and dates were compared with available data on fishing activity, seasonal distributions of potential predators, and other possible sources of mortality. Our analysis will assess the utility of acoustic telemetry data in answering questions about mortality in highly migratory elasmobranchs.
3480: Under rapidly changing global conditions, it is imperative that we identify the mechanisms shaping the capacity of organisms to respond to environmental variation. Ectotherms are particularly sensitive to projected changes in global climate given that their biological process are largely regulated by the thermal regimes in which they inhabit. There is growing evidence that the quality and composition of an animal’s diet may confer increased tolerance of environmental stressors. The macronutrient ratio hypothesis (MRH) states that animals will shift their macronutrient preferences under thermal stress due to trade-offs with growth and energetic demand. In particular, it is expected that the ratio of protein:carbohydrates in the diet should decrease due to the less expensive digestion of carbohydrates, and a handful of studies have found evidence for this. However, other studies find that under thermal stress, ectotherms may actually prefer diets rich in protein to maintain maximal growth rates and protein turnover. In this project, I examine the impact of dietary nutritional quality on the acute thermal tolerance of bluegill (Lepomis macrochirus). Hatchery obtained fish were raised at room temperature and fed diets that varied in protein content prior to assessment of their critical thermal maximum and minimum. It is predicted that fish fed diets high in protein will exhibit increased tolerance to acute thermal challenges, resulting in an increased thermal breadth. This project sets the foundation for determining the role nutritional status plays in facilitating tolerance of environmental stress in a common freshwater fish.
3481: Ecological factors can both limit and drive morphological diversification. Certain trophic niches may have strong functional constraints on trait diversity to optimize feeding on a specific type of prey item. For example, durophagous and piscivorous fishes often have jaws optimized for crushing hard prey and catching highly evasive prey, respectively, which may limit oral and pharyngeal jaw diversity. However, variability in selection strength and interference from competing selection pressures can lead to more diffuse trait combinations than expected. In this study we explored how trophic specialization shaped the diversity of jaws in sciaenids. Sciaenidae is a speciose clade of approximately 300 species that exhibits exceptional morphological variation of jaws, from deep, wide, and sturdy jaws to long, thin, and flexible jaws. Sciaenids also exhibit a broad range of diets, including omnivores, planktivores, molluscivores and piscivores. We used micro-CT scans to measure 18 functional morphometric traits of the oral and pharyngeal jaws. We compared morphological diversity among trophic niches and tested the hypothesis that trophic specialization results in restricted trait space. We also explored traits in multivariate space and tested for convergence in response to trophic niches. Our preliminary data shows piscivorous and durophagous lineages occupy distinct ecomorphological trait space relative to other trophic niches. Piscivorous species showed longer, thinner oral and pharyngeal jaws, likely optimal for flexibility and manipulation, while durophagous species exhibited wider, deeper pharyngeal jaws, likely to facilitate crushing hard prey. Our study shows trophic niche variation can drive morphological diversity in a clade of globally distributed fishes.
3482: Thanks to a unique mode of locomotion, lateral undulation, snakes are able to move on land, in grass or bushes, on/in sand, in tunnels, in mud, on and under water. This versatility raises biomechanical and evolutionary questions and stimulated considerable research, particularly in robotics. However, the relationships between undulatory kinematics, morphology, ecology and swimming efficiency were unknown less than 5 years ago; it was impossible to describe/predict how a given snake species would swim, or even if it was capable of doing so in most cases. One of the main reasons for this lack of knowledge is that only a handful of species, almost all of them closely related, have been studied, leaving aside the immense diversity of snakes. The Dragon-2 project (ANR) aimed to fill these gaps. The swimming kinematics of hundreds of individuals from more than 100 species distributed across the snake phylogenetic tree were studied, allowing contrasting morphologies and ecologies to be taken into account. 3D particle image velocimetry was used to observe and measure the vortices generated by the undulations of swimming snakes. A bio-inspired continuous autonomous robot was developed. Thanks to the combination of ecology, fluid mechanics, robotics and digital modelling, and thanks to four PhD students, we now know much more about how snakes swim. Broad patterns of lifestyle (e.g. arboreal, fossorial, aquatic snakes), surprises (e.g. truly marine snakes are slow swimmers) and complexity have emerged. There are many fundamental and applied perspectives and questions. One of the main findings is that amphibious or semi-aquatic snakes are unlikely to be intermediate forms between land snakes and truly marine snakes. Rather, they may represent a distinct evolutionary pathway.
3483: Despite their ecological significance, frogs receive far less public support and funding for research and conservation than that afforded to more charismatic animals. An emerging perspective suggests that conservation success is dependent on understanding the cognitive, emotional, and behavioral aspects that impact attitudes and behaviors towards biodiversity. This mixed-methods study attempted to shed light on how three communities in the vicinity of Nature’s Valley in the Western Cape province of South Africa, perceive, interact with, and consider the protection of frogs. Overall, the three communities slightly disliked frogs, however, geo-specific variability between demographic profiles, cultural beliefs and myths, and memorial background evidently strongly impact human-frog interaction and willingness to tolerate and protect them. This complex interplay between cultural and personal factors, as well as grouped bio-spherical values, led to the conclusion that to ensure the success of frog conservation efforts, a generalist approach to pro-frog behavioral change should be followed by focusing on pro-environmental behavior in general first rather than attempting to change a specific aspect of human-frog interaction from the outset.
3484: Road density is projected to substantially increase over the next 50 years. Roadways have severe direct negative impacts on migratory amphibian populations via vehicle collisions. Roads commonly bisect amphibian migration pathways as adults move to and from breeding areas in Spring and juveniles disperse from natal wetlands in Fall. While the impact of roadways on adult amphibians is well studied and commonly mitigated using volunteer road patrols, recently metamorphosed juvenile amphibians are severely understudied despite constituting a major component of amphibian population viability. In addition, despite their popularity, the efficacy of volunteer mitigation in reducing adult and juvenile amphibian road mortality is also understudied. We will fill this gap by investigating (1) the road mortality rates of juvenile Ambystoma salamanders, and (2) the efficacy of volunteer mitigation at reducing adult and juvenile road mortality. We began monitoring Ambystoma maculatum road mortality in March 2025. To measure mortality rates, we marked salamanders moving towards the study roadway and monitored individual survival immediately before and after crossing using a novel drift fence/camera trap design. To test volunteer efficacy, volunteers mitigated road mortality at only half of the study area. Over 1.5 months of monitoring, we marked 76 adult spotted salamanders, observed the mortality of and successful crossing of marked salamanders, captured over one million photos, and organized 12 volunteer patrols with a total of 15 individuals. In addition to the spring, we will also monitor road mortality rates and evaluate volunteer mitigation of juvenile salamanders in the summer and fall.
3485: The Highly Migratory Species Management Division of the National Marine Fisheries Service (NOAA Fisheries) is responsible for the management of the U.S. federal shark fishery in the Atlantic Ocean, including the Gulf of Mexico and Caribbean Sea. Federal management of the Atlantic shark fishery began in 1993. At that time, management was focused on rebuilding various shark stocks. In the early years of my career working in NOAA Fisheries managing the shark fishery, I focused on ways to ensure commercial and recreational shark fishers had fishing opportunities while also ensuring shark stocks were rebuilding. While there were the occasional incidents when someone was injured or killed due to an unexpected interaction with a shark, most of my interactions were with fishers who wanted to fish for sharks or conservationists who wanted to save sharks. My recent interactions have changed dramatically with the issue of shark depredation combined with more overall restrictions on fishing coming to the foreground. In this presentation, I will provide my perspective as a fishery manager regarding how human and shark interactions have changed over the past 30 years.
3486: Blanchard's cricket frog (Acris blanchardi) is a state-endangered species in Wisconsin and Minnesota but is relatively widespread further south. However, the local- and landscape-scale characteristics that affect this species’ ability to persist and disperse are poorly understood. We combined a four-state dataset of call surveys with novel Bayesian hierarchical multi-species occupancy models to estimate detection and occupancy probabilities and to test for the effects of local- and landscape-scale covariates and non-random species associations. Models indicated negative associations between occupancy probabilities and crops and forest cover within 500 m of a site. Latitude had a negative effect as well. The size of the largest stream within 1 km, a proxy for ease of dispersal through the surrounding landscape, did not correlated with cricket frog presence. Probability of detection during a 5-minute survey was about 59%. Our results contribute to ongoing discussions about the influence of land cover on habitat suitability.
3487: The theoretical and experimental purpose of this project was to investigate aspects of Wood frog (Lithobates sylvaticus) breeding site selection and communal oviposition. Two related experiments sought to advance previous work on communal Wood frog oviposition, introducing the concept of proximate decision rules to the Wood frog communal oviposition research program started in the early 1980’s. By examining the relative contribution between external cues (thermal and acoustic templates) and self-organization (mediated by social cues), egg mass transplant experiments within an array of forested constructed vernal pools will test the role of previously laid egg masses vs. temperature and chorus density in an egg mass aggregation pattern observed across the wood frog’s range. We coupled field manipulative transplant experiments with mesocosm choice experiments to assess the relative strength of signals transmitted by previously laid egg masses. Using a computational framework, we then applied the use of hybrid agent based cellular automata models to explore general “behavioral rules” thought to be performed by wood frogs during mating and compared similarities between simulations and observed egg mass distributions. Lastly, during these experiments, measurements of within-pool parameters will be made to construct predictive models of oviposition spatial patterns of Wood frogs and co-occurring Mole salamanders (Ambystoma sp.) within constructed vernal pools using habitat structure parameters.
3489: An age-structured Leslie matrix model previously developed for the US population of smalltooth sawfish, Pristis pectinata, was updated to determine their ability to recover under new scenarios of bycatch from the US southeast shrimp trawl fishery and a a large-scale mortality event in 2024, which killed many large juveniles and adults.  From 2019, population projections under updated levels of shrimp trawl mortality indicated the population was relatively stable but when the mortality event was introduced in 2024, the population significantly declined. In all scenarios evaluated, there was at least a 25% probability of population extinction. In scenarios with lower initial population sizes, the median (50%) predicted outcome was population extinction. In a scenario with lower initial population sizes, higher than average bycatch mortality, and the assumption that all reported spinning fish perished in  2024, the model predicted a >75% likelihood of extinction. However, in scenarios with higher initial population sizes, the population slowly recovered from the mortality event, with faster recovery at lower bycatch levels. Model outcomes suggest the US population of smalltooth sawfish is in jeopardy and the next few years will be critical to the viability of this endangered species. The moderately high rate of intrinsic increases suggests they have the capacity to recover, but only if bycatch remains low and another large mortality event does not occur.
3490: Human-made noise in the ocean can negatively affect fish by masking biologically-relevant sounds, inducing avoidance behaviour, triggering physiological stress and even inducing auditory damage. However, most research has focused on adult bony fishes, while the impacts on cartilaginous fishes (sharks, rays, and chimaeras) remain largely unexplored. These species are particularly vulnerable due to their slow reproductive rates, with many species laying eggs that are anchored to benthic structures by tendrils and develop externally (oviparity). Embryos develop over months to years before hatching, after which juveniles often inhabit specific coastal nursery areas to avoid predation. During these early stages, embryos, hatchlings, and juveniles are immobile or have limited mobility, making them especially susceptible to local environmental stressors, including noise pollution. This study examines the effects of anthropogenic noise on the early life stages of three species of cartilaginous fishes. We characterised the soundscapes of their nursery habitats, identified the main sources of human-made noise, and exposed egg cases, hatchlings, and juveniles to ecologically-relevant noise levels. We monitored their behaviour, physiology, development, and inner ear morphology. Our findings reveal that the morphology of the inner ears of the tested species exhibit plastic responses to noise exposure, suggesting developmental changes at the sensory level. We discuss these results in the context of bioacoustics, auditory ecology, and conservation, highlighting the need to consider vulnerable life stages of cartilaginous fishes in marine spatial planning and noise regulation.
3491: With record-setting rainfall and winds, Hurricane Helene resulted in the tragic loss of over 100 lives and the devastation of infrastructure and property throughout western North Carolina. Both terrestrial and aquatic ecosystems throughout the region were similarly impacted, with the extent of the damage still being assessed. The Swannanoa River, a tributary to the French Broad River, and its tributaries were among the most heavily impacted areas from Helene. Immediate impacts to the Swannanoa River watershed included those stemming from intense flooding, such as the destruction of riparian vegetation, the accumulation of human debris and sediment into streams and their floodplains, prolonged turbidity, and the major reconfiguration of stream channels and associated microhabitats. Semi-quantitative stream fish surveys conducted in November-December 2024 throughout the watershed indicated that fish assemblages were largely similar to pre-Helene data, with some noted variability. These data will be discussed in the context of observations of the impacts of Helene on physical habitat structure and on-going restoration throughout the watershed, along with the results of fish surveys conducted in Spring and Summer 2025. The full effects of Hurricane Helene on aquatic biodiversity in the region will likely take years to assess.
3492: Peters’ Rock Agamas (Agama picticauda) are petrophilic lizards native to Eastern sub-Saharan Africa and are established in multiple areas in Florida. Where established, this species is conspicuous and numerous and has been the top reported nonnative reptile to Florida’s state wildlife agency since 2021. There is a need to identify effective removal methods that can be applied at scale in different habitats and by homeowners and professionals in both public and private lands. For example, while air rifles are an effective method employed by U.S. Department of Agriculture Wildlife Services personnel, there are various risks that make this method inappropriate in most public settings. We evaluated three removal methods for Agama picticauda in Martin County, Florida, USA. Using a before-after-control-impact design, we evaluated targeted removals by lizard fishing (baited line on the end of an extendable pole), air rifle, and fabric minnow traps baited with crickets at 3 sites per treatment across two seasons (Fall 2024 and Spring 2025) compared to control sites with no removal treatment applied. Each method was applied to each site for three one-hour treatments per season. We discuss efficacy of different removal treatments in terms of cost, catch-per-unit effort, and population reduction potential. This information may be applicable to other management efforts on small invasive lizards and may be informative for non-lethal capture efforts of similar lizard species.
3493: Ocean acidification can have negative effects on many species. However, the long-term responses of species will depend critically on the degree to which populations can evolve to become more tolerant of high CO2/low pH conditions as the ocean environment changes. To investigate this phenomenon, we evaluated genetic variation in both feeding rates and growth rates for larvae of a coastal fish, the California Grunion. We combined breeding experiments (66 families in a half and full-sib breeding design) with experimental manipulation of seawater conditions (4 pCO2 levels) to examine heritable variation in sensitivity to CO2. Our results suggest that elevated CO2 can strongly impair feeding efficacy, but these results do not emerge until later in the larval phase when the supply of maternal yolk was exhausted. By 11 days post hatching, there was significant, heritable variation in sensitivity of feeding to CO2 (e.g., ~20% of families were unaffected; ~20% experienced over a twofold drop in mean feeding efficacy at the highest CO2 levels). Moreover, sensitivity of feeding rate to elevated CO2 was genetically correlated with sensitivity of growth rate to elevated CO2 (rG = 0.29). These results suggest that tolerance to ocean acidification conditions may be better understood by considering a suite of related, performance-based characteristics. For Grunion, genetic variation in tolerance may facilitate adaptation, offsetting some of the harmful effects of ocean acidification.
3494: Sex chromosomes have evolved repeatedly in animals. Evolution of sex chromosomes is particularly interesting in reptiles, as they have frequent transitions among systems, with transitions between XX/XY and ZZ/ZW systems as well as changes to which chromosomes in the genome are acting as sex chromosomes. However, we lack data for many reptile species. The Mediterranean house gecko (Hemidactylus turcicus), for example, is an invasive gecko that is now found across the globe. While we know both its karyotype (2n=44) and sex determination system (XX/XY sex chromosomes), we have until now not been able to identify which chromosomes in the genome are the sex chromosomes. To address this, we assembled and annotated a high-quality reference genome for a male H. turcicus using PacBio HiFi, Hi-C sequencing, and multi-tissue RNASeq for annotation. We used this reference genome, in combination with RADSeq of 7 males and 7 females and Illumina resequencing of 3 males and 3 females, to identify the previously unknown sex chromosomes. This genome assembly will also be useful for the broader herpetological community for studying this widespread and biologically important species.
3495: Despite extensive study, several species of freshwater sculpin fishes in the subgenus Cottopsis (native to western North America) remain difficult to classify due to overlapping traits, unclear geographic boundaries, and limited genomic data. These challenges are particularly evident in Cottus asper (Prickly Sculpin), Cottus perplexus (Reticulate Sculpin), Cottus marginatus (Margined Sculpin), and Cottus gulosus (Riffle Sculpin). While historical morphometric evidence and early molecular data suggest these species are distinct, additional molecular studies propose C. perplexus and C. marginatus as junior synonyms of C. asper, further complicating species boundaries. To address these issues, we generated high-throughput sequencing data from vouchered museum specimens to construct a robust phylogeny. Here, we present results from this molecular work, including a large panel of single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) used to resolve phylogenetic relationships within Cottopsis. These data reveal strong genetic separation among C. asper, C. perplexus, C. marginatus, and C. gulosus, and uncover at least five genetically distinct, previously unrecognized clades. These findings also clarify the geographic distributions of these lineages, revealing new patterns of spatial differentiation. In parallel, we are conducting ongoing phenotypic analyses using CT scans, photogrammetry, and meristic data to assess morphological variation in a genomic context. While these morphological results are still in progress, we will briefly discuss the approach and how it complements the molecular findings. Together, these efforts help resolve long-standing taxonomic uncertainty and lay the groundwork for forthcoming species descriptions, providing a stronger framework for understanding sculpin evolution, ecology, and conservation in western North America.
3496: The U.S. Atlantic Shark Research Fishery is a cooperative research program between NOAA Fisheries and commercial bottom longline shark fishing vessels. The fishery has 100% observer coverage allowing detailed biological and fishery data collection, while fishing vessels receive exemptions from certain regulations that incentivize participation. From 2021-2024, participating vessels collected data to measure the effect of soak time on shark at-vessel and post-release mortality rates. Vessels were outfitted with experimental electronic monitoring (EM) sensors that recorded time and direction of mainline spool rotation to examine the potential to remotely monitor longline soak times. The EM data were validated against observer-recorded soak times. Additionally, observers deployed high-rate pop-up satellite archival tags (PSATs) on dusky shark (Carcharhinus obscurus), spinner shark (C. brevipinna), and bull shark (C. leucas) to identify post-release mortality or recovery. Data were collected from 51 sets on 6 vessels, and included the deployment of 30 PSATs. Preliminary results demonstrate the feasibility of using EM to monitor soak times in longline fisheries, and better characterize the effect of soak time on mortality rates. They also show the value of fishery observers and cooperative research in deploying electronic tags to cost-effectively answer critical questions for shark stock assessment and sustainable fisheries management.
3497: The Atlantic Highly Migratory Species (HMS) Management Division of the National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS) is responsible for managing federal HMS fisheries in U.S. waters of the Atlantic Ocean. A number of fishing gear related management measures have been implemented by NMFS since the 1999 Federal Fishery Management Plan (FMP) for Atlantic Tunas, Swordfish, and Sharks, and Amendment 1 to the Atlantic Billfish FMP. Over the years, these management measures have been put in place to achieve conservation and management goals including preventing or stopping overfishing; reducing impacts on bycatch species; increasing post-release survivability; reducing lost and derelict gear; and other objectives. However, HMS fishing gear and techniques have evolved over time, and there have been changes in species distributions, market conditions, and fishing interests. Considering all of these factors, NMFS is proposing changes to fishing gear regulations for HMS fisheries related to buoy gear and speargun requirements. We are also considering overarching changes regarding gear used for the collection of bait.
3498: Research on Cuban ichthyofauna began in the 18th century with Don Felipe Poey, who described 758 fish species in his work "Ictiología Cubana". However, this compendium remained unpublished until 2000, when University of Havana released Poey’s transcriptions edited by Dr. Dario Guitart Manday. Since then, several updates and taxonomic revisions have been made, resulting in a more detailed knowledge of Cuba’s fish diversity. To date, 1,120 fish species have been recorded in Cuban waters, of which 1,031 are bony fishes. However, fishes of Cuba face serious threats due to overfishing, pollution, and the introduction of exotic species. Currently, 3.4% of these species are threatened, while 1.2% are considered near threatened. Information on population status is crucial for prioritizing conservation efforts, and the IUCN Red List is used as a reference for assessing extinction risk. This study provides an updated annotated list of bony fishes in Cuban waters, serving as a valuable tool to guide conservation and fisheries management strategies. Beyond national efforts, this resource also contributes to broader Caribbean-wide strategies, where the sustainability of marine resources is essential.
3499: Morphological differences among sexes is considered a fundamental outcome of sexual selection. In snakes, however, some sexually dimorphic traits have been hypothesized to arise through sex-specific ecologies rather than mate choice and competition. Skull traits involved in feeding are predicted to be particularly sensitive to variation in feeding ecology. We used micro-CT scanning to measure and compare the sexes' skeletal morphology of five species of sea snakes. Additionally, we collected basic external morphometrics of each specimen. Based on previous work, we predicted that Aipysurus laevis and Emydocephalus annulatus will show sexual dimorphic traits, while Hydrophis platurus, H. cyanocinctus, and H. fasciatus will not have sexually dimorphic traits. We found that Sexual dimorphism within the aipysurine lineage does extend past the external measurements and body size and there are dimorphic traits in the cranial skeletal morphology including !!. Meanwhile, we found no significant difference in any measured cranial skeletal morphology between the sexes of any of the Hydrophis species. Hydrophis species have sexual size dimorphism (SSD), but their skeletal morphology was not dimorphic when corrected for body size. Because cranial skeletal dimorphism is rare in snakes compared to SSD and dimorphism in tail size, sexual dimorphism in sea snake skull morphology may represent an evolutionary innovation with important links to sex-biased ecological pressures. This study also suggests the critical importance of ecological and behavioral data in testing the drivers of dimorphism across clades and provides an example of how new scanning technologies can help generate new field-based hypotheses for future tests.
